Former Polish PM urges Poland and Ukraine to resolve historical disputes and look ahead
Former Polish Prime Minister Jan Krzysztof Bielecki expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Regardless of how we look at the future, the issues of the past will always weigh on us. So the only thing we can do is to ‘clear’ that past,” Bielecki said.
He stressed the need to conduct exhumations and provide dignified burials for the victims of the tragic events in Volyn during World War II.
“If it is important for Poles to conduct exhumations and ensure dignified burials for the victims of Volyn, then this should be done. If Poles want to carry out excavations during the war, they should be given that opportunity,” the former Polish Prime Minister said.
According to Bielecki, once these issues have been resolved, Polish-Ukrainian relations should be guided by the principle of “forgive, but remember.”
“No one expects us to agree on everything concerning the past, but everyone should remember their own history and the wrongs that were inflicted,” Bielecki said.
At the same time, he stressed that historical disputes should not become an obstacle to the development of Polish-Ukrainian relations.
“I am a pragmatist, and therefore, regardless of what politicians do, this intensive cooperation will continue because it is needed by both Poles and Ukrainians,” Bielecki said.
He noted that Ukrainians play an important role in the Polish economy.
“There are large companies in Poland where 20–30% of the workforce are Ukrainians, and if they left, it would have a painful impact on businesses,” the former Prime Minister said.
According to him, Poland and Ukraine also have close cultural ties that will not change regardless of the political climate.
Bielecki expressed hope that common sense would prevail in Poland and that incidents targeting Ukrainian citizens would come to an end.
“I think more and more politicians will have the courage to speak out about this,” he said.
The former Prime Minister also stressed Poland’s strategic importance to Ukraine due to its geography and logistics.
“It is also important to look at the map: the land corridor to Europe through Poland is a natural window for Ukraine to the world, a link in Kyiv’s logistics chain,” he said, adding that this was another important element uniting the two countries.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine’s Ambassador to Poland Vasyl Bodnar said that Ukrainians in Poland were increasingly defending their rights through legal means, including by turning to law enforcement agencies in cases of aggression or discrimination.

Nepal-Tibet death toll rises amid new flood fears and race to free group trapped in tunnel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:39:04 UTC
12:39:04 KST

Thousands of people remain missing after the catastrophic flash flood that has killed more than 700 people in Nepal and Tibet as authorities warn search and rescue teams of rising waters.
The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet has climbed to 750 dead and more than 3,000 people missing. Chinese authorities on Sunday reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, of whom 261 were foreign nationals, while Nepali officials confirmed 734 dead and 2,498 people missing.
In China’s update, the state broadcaster said the missing foreign nationals included 104 from Nepal, 49 from India, 33 from Latvia, 18 from the US and 15 British citizens.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far.
In a breakthrough late on Saturday, the Nepali army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where workers are believed to be trapped.
The home minister, Sudan Gurung, said: “We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside.”
More than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside such tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.
Nepal warned on Sunday of rising flood waters and urged rescue teams to exercise caution. “We have received information that the flood flow in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa has increased further,” the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said in a warning issued at 7.20 am.
In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority listed 933 hydropower workers among the missing, including trekkers and Hindu pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash.
The foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, on Saturday estimated Nepal’s reconstruction bill could run into the “billions of dollars”.
“The urgency is on rescue and saving lives as much as we can,” he said, appealing for specialised assistance, including heavy-lift drones and technology to help locate people who are trapped.
He also called for forensic testing kits to identify bodies and freezer units to store them, saying bodies that have been in water could decompose at a faster rate.
Survivors face an agonising wait to learn the fate of missing relatives, and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away,” Buddhi Ram Dangol told Agence France-Presse in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. “There is nothing left.”
Fears of further flooding have compounded the search for the missing.
The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes, and one of these formations has become a risk of further floods.
The Chinese and Nepali foreign ministers spoke on Saturday and discussed sharing satellite and hydrological data, both sides said.
In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, rescue operations were temporarily paused at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of more flooding from a newly formed lake.
A total of 2,141 rescuers were near the Gyirong site, the Xinhua state news agency reported, including more than 500 in the worst-hit area.
In Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, relatives and friends gathered outside the main government hospital from early morning, desperately searching for news of missing loved ones.
Many shuffled between the help desk and the hospital noticeboard, clutching photographs and scanning injured patients’ lists in the hope of finding them.
Dil Maya Lama stood weeping outside the help desk at the hospital, searching for information about her missing 26-year-old brother, a driver for a hydropower company in Rasuwa. She had traveled from Ramechhap, about 130km (80 miles) away.
“I came here with the hope that I might find him,” she said. “There is no information about him.”
Nelza Moktan anxiously sought information about her missing cousin, who also worked as a driver in Rasuwa.
“I feel hopeless. It has already been four days,” she said.
With Associated Press, Agence France-Presse and Reuters

Iceland polls close in referendum on reopening EU membership talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:31:56 UTC
12:31:56 KST

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
30 August 2026•Update: 30 August 2026
Polling stations closed in Iceland Saturday at 10 pm (2200GMT) following a closely contested referendum on whether to reopen EU membership negotiations.
The campaign was dominated by concerns about the cost of living, security, sovereignty and control of the country's fisheries.
Polling stations opened as early as 9 am local time, with closing times varying between counties and voting continuing into the evening.
Nearly 400,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote, with preliminary results expected early Sunday, according to RUV, Iceland's public broadcaster.
The referendum does not decide whether Iceland will join the EU.
A majority “Yes” vote would give the government a mandate to resume accession talks, while any eventual membership agreement would require approval in a second referendum.
Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009 after its banking system collapsed during the global financial crisis.
Accession negotiations began in 2010 but were suspended three years later after a Eurosceptic government took office. In 2015, Reykjavik informed Brussels that it no longer wished to be considered an EU candidate.
The European Commission maintains, however, that Iceland's membership application remains legally valid and that negotiations are only on hold, according to a report by the European Policy Centre (EPC).

Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez has said that an energy agreement with the United States will remain in force for 25 years, target an increase in crude output to 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd), and preserve the nation's sovereignty over its natural resources.
Rodriguez hailed the accord in a late-night address as a "historic" deal that would help revive the economy and boost government revenue, saying it would shape the country's future.

US involvement

Trump stated that Washington secured majority control of over 65 billion barrels of proven reserves through private business partnerships.
Venezuela holds the world's largest proven oil reserves, but currently produces roughly 1.25 million bpd following years of underinvestment and sanctions.
Rodriguez estimated the agreement could generate around $209 billion for the Venezuelan state, based on a $65 per barrel benchmark price, with approximately $19 per barrel flowing directly to the government.
She stressed that Venezuela retains "ownership of and sovereignty" over its natural resources, "while leveraging capital, technology and operational expertise to support the recovery of a strategic industry that has been severely affected by sanctions."

Taiwan expects 6 new rapid minelaying ships by year-end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:30:17 UTC
12:30:17 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Navy plans to operate a fleet of 10 rapid minelaying ships to boost its nearshore defense.
Four are already in service in the Navy’s 192nd Fleet, Liberty Times reported. Lung-Teh Shipbuilding Corp. is building the remaining six ships, which are expected to be delivered by the end of this year.
A military officer said the new rapid minelaying boats can significantly shorten response times in combat, thanks to an automated minelaying system developed by the National Chung Shan Institute of Science and Technology, per Liberty Times. The new system is fully digital, allowing a single operator to control mine deployment from a console on the bridge or by remote control.
The system can deploy a range of mines, including the domestically produced Wanxiang Type I and II bottom and moored mines, as well as US-made Mk-6 mines. Once a mine is deployed, the computer instantly records its precise coordinates. This improves accuracy during operations and facilitates safe clearance after a conflict.
Once the fleet is operational, it is expected to deter enemy naval forces from imposing a blockade or launching landings near Taiwan.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) attended the opening ceremony of Palau’s Pacific Prosperity Exhibit on Friday, where he viewed the results of long-term regional cooperation among Taiwan, Palau, other Pacific allies, and like-minded partners.
The exhibit was held in connection with the 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), which Palau is hosting. Lin said Taiwan has long participated in the PIF as a development partner and supports the shared vision outlined in the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, according to the foreign ministry.
In the face of transnational challenges, Taiwan is willing to continue sharing its development experience and work with like-minded partners to address the practical needs of Pacific nations through mutually beneficial cooperation, Lin said. He added that the Taiwan government is bringing together resources from government agencies, industry, and civil society through its Diplomatic Allies Prosperity Project.
By leveraging Taiwan’s strengths in technology, healthcare, agriculture, energy, digital governance, and sustainable development, the project helps address the development needs of diplomatic allies and like-minded countries, Lin said.
The foreign minister said the Pacific Prosperity Exhibit is a concrete example of this cooperative model, showcasing accumulated achievements and underscoring Taiwan’s commitment to sharing its experience.
This year’s PIF centers on “Building Economies, Life, Action, and Unity.”

Iceland referendum initial tally narrowly favors reopening EU accession talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:28:51 UTC
12:28:51 KST

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
30 August 2026•Update: 30 August 2026
Initial results of Iceland's referendum show a narrow majority backing the reopening of EU membership negotiations as vote counting continues, according to public broadcaster RUV.
The latest result showed 46,589 votes, or 50.5%, support restarting accession talks, while 45,682, or 49.5%, oppose the proposal.
Support for reopening negotiations is strongest in the Reykjavik North constituency, where 59.4% of voters back the proposal. Opposition is highest in the Southern constituency, where 60.1% are against it.
The Southwest constituency, which accounts for roughly 30% of Iceland's electorate, was evenly divided.
The campaign was dominated by concerns about the cost of living, security, sovereignty and control of the country's fisheries.
Polling stations closed at 10 pm local time (2200GMT) Saturday after voting began as early as 9 am.
Nearly 400,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote.
The referendum does not determine whether Iceland will join the EU. A majority "Yes" vote would give the government a mandate to resume accession talks. Any eventual membership agreement would require approval in a second referendum.
Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009 after its banking system collapsed during the global financial crisis.
Accession negotiations began in 2010 but were suspended three years later after a Eurosceptic government took office. In 2015, Reykjavik informed Brussels that it no longer wished to be considered an EU candidate.
The European Commission, however, maintains that Iceland's membership application remains legally valid and that negotiations are only on hold, according to a report by the European Policy Centre (EPC).

UN says Special Rapporteurs are independent, not ‘out of control’ after Guterres interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:22:33 UTC
12:22:33 KST

Stéphane Dujarric, Spokesman for the United Nations Secretary-General, said on Friday that, contrary to previous reports in The Jerusalem Post and the Financial Times, the Secretary-General did not say that UN special rapporteurs are "out of control"; he said that they are independent actors outside the Secretariat's control.
The Spokesperson was responding to a report in The Jerusalem Post, which claimed that UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres admitted in an interview with the Financial Times on Tuesday that several UN special rapporteurs are "totally out of control" regarding their views on Israel.
Guterres was referring to the process of the work Special Rapporteurs do, not the content or the output of that work, Dujarric claimed.
"I think it's a misreading of what the Secretary-General said," explained Dujarric. "What he said in the interview, and I think people should look at the video, is that he can't speak for the entirety of the UN system. Many in the UN structure are independent of the Secretariat and therefore totally out of the Secretariat's control… out of the Secretary-General’s control."
In response to a follow-up question about the potentially controversial nature of some rapporteurs' reports, Dujarric affirmed that the UN Secretary-General's office "defend[s] their right to speak."
"We defend their right to work," he continued. "We will always do so. But, given their independence, it is not for the Secretary-General to say, 'we like what this rapporteur says, we don't like what this rapporteur says,' right? They're independent. Their strength is in their independence."
Guterres denies claims that the UN has a bias against Israel
In his interview with the Financial Times, Guterres also strongly denied that the UN as a whole has an institutional bias against Israel.
"I totally refuse the idea of bias," he said. "On the contrary, I think we have been on the right side of history."
He added that, from his perspective, the UN had been "defending what is necessary for peace to come to the Middle East.
"There are two peoples, with a few million each one," he explained, "And there is no way one can destroy the other. So it's probably better to do everything possible to reconcile."
Tzvi Jasper contributed to this report.

Greece to sign $3.6b. Israeli air defense deal, creating 'Achilles Shield' against Turkey and Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:22:23 UTC
12:22:23 KST

Greece is set to sign a $3.6 billion defense deal with Israel on Monday in Tel Aviv, a major agreement that will provide Athens with a multilayered air defense system against potential threats from Turkey and Iran.
The agreement, negotiated over three years, will become the largest defense export deal in Israel's history.
A Greek delegation will sign the agreement with Israel's Defense Ministry to purchase air defense systems valued at $3.6 billion, slightly below earlier estimates. The deal will provide Greece, for the first time, with an integrated, multilayered defense network.
Most of the funds will go to Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, which will supply Greece with David's Sling systems designed to intercept heavy rockets and ballistic missiles, as well as mobile SPYDER systems designed to counter unmanned aerial vehicles and drones. Israel Aerospace Industries will provide the Barak MX system, which is designed to defend against aircraft and missiles.
The agreement also includes a national-level command-and-control center to operate the systems and manage launches, similar to the system used in Israel. The center will incorporate artificial intelligence capabilities.
Greek companies are expected to receive about €700 million of the deal's total value as subcontractors for Rafael and IAI.
Project 'Achilles Shield'
The project is known in Greece as "Achilles Shield" and will include deploying SPYDER batteries on Greek islands, including popular vacation destinations visited by many Israelis.
The largest defense export deal in Israel's history to date was IAI's first export sale of the Arrow 3 missile defense system to Germany, worth $3.5 billion, signed in 2023. Elbit Systems announced a $2.3 billion deal with a foreign customer this year, according to reports from the Persian Gulf, while Rafael signed a framework agreement with Romania this year to sell SPYDER systems worth $2 billion.
Greece is already a major Israeli customer
Greece has already become a major customer of Israel's defense industry, purchasing Spike missiles and Spice precision-guided bombs from Rafael, Rampage missiles from Elbit Systems and IAI, and Heron 2 drones from IAI.
The air defense agreement is expected to further strengthen the strategic partnership between the two countries, with Israel playing a key role in helping protect Greek airspace.
Greece, Cyprus, and Israel have strengthened their security coordination in recent years amid growing tensions with Turkey. Cyprus has also reportedly purchased Israel's Barak MX system to defend its airspace, according to foreign reports.

IDF general warns talks with Hamas, Hezbollah lack a clear strategy for victory - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:22:14 UTC
12:22:14 KST

The diplomatic efforts underway between Israel and Gaza and Lebanon "are largely ineffective... half-baked in terms of what we will actually achieve," Brig.-Gen. (res.) Oren Avman told 103FM on Friday.
Avman, who is a former commander of the Kfir Brigade, made these comments when weighing in on a recent report that said Prime Minister Netanyahu permitted former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar to maintain direct contact with Hamas officials during the war.
He added, "I don’t know if we’re being played or if a false reality is being manufactured - on top of the state’s overall conduct, which already draws plenty of valid criticism - but in this false narrative, we're pretending to run a process that will ultimately disarm Hamas."
Avman noted further: "Over the last generation, state entities have virtually ceased to exist in our strategic reality. We have to recognize that - it's been the case for over 25 years."
Despite his criticism, Avman emphasized that he does not reject diplomacy itself. "Diplomatic efforts and dialogue are always vital and must continue regardless. The real question is where they ultimately lead and whether we are being forced to compromise on essentials," he said.
"The diplomatic efforts of 2026 must persist. We are in a completely different era. Over the last generation, we negotiated with Arafat and the Palestinian Authority, reached understandings with Hezbollah following Operations Accountability and Grapes of Wrath as well as the Second Lebanon War, and now, in one way or another, we are pursuing understandings with Hamas."
'When human lives are on the line, it's legitimate to negotiate with the devil'
Avman's skepticism of the diplomatic process stopped short of criticizing the diplomatic process when it comes to the lives of hostages.
"When saving human lives is on the line, especially regarding the hostages following our terrible failure on October 7 - it is legitimate to negotiate even with the devil," he said.
"As long as we succeed in bringing them home safely, you make deals with enemies, not friends, just like prisoner exchanges between sovereign states. That's why I draw a clear line between an operation aimed at saving lives, like the hostage situation, and all these recent reports about talks before and after, funding, Qatar, and the like."
'The IDF in Lebanon is like Home Alone 2'
Turning to the Lebanese front, Avman sharply criticized the lack of a clear political objective. "Regarding the talks on Lebanon, the IDF finds itself in a 'Home Alone 2' situation - full of holes like Swiss cheese, operating without a clear political compass while locked in localized battles of attrition," he said.
"The question is whether we're stuck in a game of ping-pong - they launch a drone, we scramble F-16s or hit back somehow. The IDF is bogged down in a security zone, and when it comes to dealing with Hezbollah, the problem is that reality is dictating our actions instead of us shaping reality."
In closing, Avman highlighted two core issues that he believes plague Israel across all fronts.
"Looking at all fronts, there are two underlying drivers. One is decision-making paralysis, and the second, highly problematic driver is the immense strain on the IDF, coupled with a complete lack of grasp of the reality facing reserve, career, and active-duty soldiers. Managing these two factors simultaneously makes this an extraordinarily complex situation."

California legislature votes to ban child marriage and empower forced marriage victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:22:06 UTC
12:22:06 KST

California's state legislature passed two bills this week that close long-standing legal loopholes by establishing an absolute ban on child marriage and enabling victims of forced marriage to secure civil restraining orders.
Assembly Bill 1267 institutes a ban on child marriage by repealing "the authorization for a person under 18 years of age to be issued a marriage license or to establish a domestic partnership."
AB 2534 empowers individuals to protect themselves against forced marriage by incorporating it into the state's Domestic Violence Prevention Act, allowing victims to secure civil restraining orders against anyone who coerces, facilitates, or arranges an unwanted union.
The two bills are yet to be signed into law, as they await Governor Gavin Newsom's signature. If confirmed, the legislation will take effect on January 1, 2027.
According to the nonprofit legal advocacy organization, Tahiri Justice Center, AB 1267 will make California the 18th state in the nation to completely ban child marriage. AB 2534 will create the first forced marriage protection order in the country.
Child marriage currently legal in California, with consent of a guardian
According to Bill 1267, which amends and repeals sections of California's Family Code and Health and Safety Code, "Existing law authorizes an unmarried person who is under 18 years of age to marry upon obtaining a court order granting permission and the written consent of at least one of the parents or the guardian of each underage party to the marriage, as specified."
According to the text of Bill 2534 forced marriage is defined as "a spousal relationship in which one or both parties do not or cannot consent and one or both parties are compelled, through force, fraud, coercion, duress, abuse of power, or coercive control, to enter, attempt to enter, or maintain, a marriage, regardless of whether the marriage is legally valid."
It legislates that "If a protective order is sought to protect against a forced marriage, the bill would authorize all persons engaged in conduct to arrange, officiate, finance, or facilitate a forced marriage or attempted forced marriage to be included in one action as respondents," and authorizes a court to "grant relief regardless of whether a marriage has occured or whether a purported marriage would be legally valid in this state or any other jurisdiciton."
Survivor: 'I know what it feels like to have your choices taken from you'
According to the Tahiri Justice Center, Sara Tasneem, a survivor of an abusive child marriage and advocate for ending the practice, said, “The passage of AB 1267 is a huge win for all of us - survivors, advocates, and allies - who have been fighting to end child marriage in California for nearly a decade. The new law will set the legal age of marriage at 18, without exceptions, protecting future children from the severe harms of child marriage and bringing California one step closer to ending the practice.”
Sadia Khan, another survivor of forced marriage and an advocate against the practice, said in response to the bills' passing in the legislature, “As a survivor, I know what it feels like to have your choices taken from you, to believe no one can stop what’s happening, and to discover that the law doesn’t have a clear answer for your situation.
"As a domestic violence policy advocate, I’ve learned that our greatest responsibility is not simply responding to abuse after it occurs; it is preventing it from happening in the first place. Nothing can give me back the years I lost. But now, California is making sure no one else is forced to lose theirs.”

Israeli army intensifies siege of West Bank village, seals sole entrance: Official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:05:59 UTC

Layan Bsharat and Tarek Chouiref
30 August 2026•Update: 30 August 2026
The Israeli army has kept the sole remaining entrance to the Palestinian village of Al-Mughayyir in the occupied West Bank closed for 20 consecutive hours, preventing residents from entering or leaving, an official told Anadolu on Saturday.
Amin Abu Aliya, head of the Al-Mughayyir village council, said Israeli restrictions and attacks on residents and farmers have intensified in the last 20 days.
He said the village’s only remaining entrance is repeatedly closed in the morning to prevent workers from reaching their jobs and later in the day to stop those outside from returning.
Abu Aliya said the measures were aimed at creating conditions that force workers to stay outside the village and ultimately drive Palestinians from the area.
He said Israeli forces raided Al-Mughayyir on Friday with dozens of military and police vehicles alongside Israeli occupiers on the claim that sheep belonging to an occupier had been stolen.
Abu Aliya rejected the claim as false, saying Israeli forces nevertheless pursued Palestinian livestock owners, raided a home and attempted to seize sheep, sparking confrontations in which Palestinians were injured.
He said Israeli forces have kept the village entrance closed since the raid and prevent ambulances and Civil Defense vehicles from entering during the closures.
Abu Aliya added that while residents were dealing with attacks Friday in the southern part of the village, more than 50 Israeli occupiers entered the northern area, assaulted a Palestinian farmer and stole 25 sheep.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry warned earlier Saturday that Al-Mughayyir had been subjected to a “suffocating siege” for around 20 days.
It said Israeli forces control access through village gates, at times allowing residents only two hours a day to enter or leave.
It said the restrictions and attacks by Israeli occupiers were aimed at isolating the village and creating conditions for forced displacement.
Three Palestinians were injured Friday in an occupier attack in Al-Mughayyir, while Israeli forces and occupiers blocked an ambulance en route to transport those who were injured.
The occupied West Bank has seen an escalation in Israeli military raids and attacks by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians since the outbreak of the war in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

MOSCOW, August 30. /TASS/. Ukraine's national debt grows by an average of $4-5 billion a month, according to TASS calculations based on data from the country's Finance Ministry.
The debt stands at about $218-219 billion at the end of August and is expected to reach around $240 billion by the end of 2026 and at least $290 billion by the end of 2027. This would amount to about $8,500 in debt per Ukrainian by the end of 2026 and around $10,400 by the end of 2027.
However, the Ukrainian Finance Ministry's estimates are likely to fall short of the actual additional borrowing needed. Kiev will require at least $6-7 billion this year to fund military operations and pay service members, with no domestic sources to fill the gap.

Ofer Winter might offer Israeli voters a new political slate, even supporting Netanyahu - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:04:48 UTC
12:04:48 KST

Ofer Winter launched his new People of Israel party on Tuesday, kick-starting what could become a bloc-busting run for the Knesset.
Beyond the retired IDF general’s stated ideology and firm position within the right-wing bloc, Winter is offering something few other candidates can: a genuinely new political slate.
Shaped by a goal of having as broad an appeal as possible, Winter’s list includes some very well-known and some lesser-known faces, all with one thing in common: They have never done this before.
After October 7, the need for fresh faces in both the legislative and executive branches of government has become evident.
The Hamas massacre exposed failures that had been systemically ignored for years, not only by individuals in government but across Israel’s political and security establishment.
That does not mean every newcomer will be better than every veteran. Experience matters, particularly when governing a country facing threats on multiple fronts.
But there is a legitimate argument that the people who helped shape the system that produced Israel’s current crisis should not be the only ones entrusted with fixing it.
Right-wing voters want new faces in politics
Winter appears to have identified a chunk of right-wing voters who, while not ready to vote for the opposition, have become disillusioned with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition and want new faces on the Right.
Yoseph Haddad is a known quantity across the political spectrum for his pro-Israel activism abroad and his hardline right-wing stance on Arab sector issues at home.
Former Jerusalem deputy mayor Fleur Hassan-Nahoum has municipal experience without the baggage of national politics. Laly Derai, mother of slain IDF soldier Saadia Derai, is a respected social activist making her first venture into politics.
They, and the rest of Winter’s new list, will be able to go to voters and argue that the faces we see running for the Knesset today are the same people who have dominated Israeli politics through years of instability, including five elections in three years.
They are the same people who allowed Israel’s security to fall by the wayside in favor of partisan political ambitions, and the same people who failed to bring Hamas and Hezbollah to their knees despite a plethora of promises.
That alone is not enough to win votes. Winter must show that his candidates are capable of offering new thinking and, ultimately, competent government. And this is where People of Israel has an opportunity to offer something genuinely different.
The public is not necessarily looking for politicians who have never made a mistake. It may be looking for politicians who were not part of the political system that produced the current impasse, and who can approach its problems without years of partisan baggage.
Ofer must reconcile his party's position for political renewal while endorsing Netanyahu for PM
But one issue Winter must address over the coming weeks and months is the political contradiction staring him in the face.
On Thursday, following nearly 48 hours of speculation on Israeli news channels, Winter clarified that his party would only recommend Netanyahu for prime minister after the election.
“We do not work for any person, only for the people of Israel,” he said. “We are in the right-wing camp, the leader of the right-wing camp is Netanyahu, and we will only recommend him.”
Winter is entitled to take that position. If his voters want a right-wing government led by Netanyahu, he should be clear about it. But he also needs to explain how that position squares with the broader message of political renewal on which his campaign is being built.
The two positions are not irreconcilable. Winter can argue that Israel needs new political forces while Netanyahu remains, for now, the natural leader of the Right. But if that is his argument, he should make it explicitly.
Whether one agrees with Winter’s politics or not, announcing a list free of anyone who held national political office before October 7 offers something Israel has been missing: a genuine chance to start over.
Winter’s positioning within the blocs, and especially his relationship with Netanyahu, will help determine whether People of Israel’s reliance on new faces is merely a political gimmick or the beginning of a post-October 7 model of Israeli politics.
If Winter can offer voters both a fresh slate and a convincing answer to what that slate is actually meant to change, other politicians may soon find themselves trying to follow his example.

Abdul El-Sayed apologizes to Jewish Democrats over past Temple Israel attack comments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:04:29 UTC
12:04:29 KST

Michigan US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed apologized for his past comments regarding the March attack on Temple Israel in suburban Detroit during a meeting with the state Democratic Party’s Jewish caucus at the party convention on Saturday.
The Democratic nominee told the room that his remarks following the attempted targeting of the West Bloomfield synagogue preschool, in which he had said, in part, “Hurt people hurt people,” were intended to provide “context.”
Reflecting on them, he said on Saturday, “I made a mistake.”
“If my statement caused pain, I’m sorry. It was not what I intended to do,” El-Sayed continued. Referencing the first of two statements he had made about the attack, he added, “We issued a statement, of course, condemning it, and that just should have been it, full stop.”
El-Sayed’s initial Temple Israel comments, which many Jews interpreted as justifying the attack, have alienated Jewish voters in the state. After an initial statement condemning the attack, El-Sayed then followed up with one referencing Israel’s war in Lebanon, where the attacker had lost family in an Israeli airstrike.
New round of outreach efforts in vie for votes
On Saturday, El-Sayed, a former county health director, insisted that his push for “context” to the attack was broadly appropriate, but not at that moment, explaining that such “conversations” could happen “in the fullness of time.”
“Sometimes you can’t really see context in the moment of acuity or pain,” he said. “The intention for me was not to trample that pain. It was not to discount it. It was not at all to justify any sort of domestic terrorism. That’s wrong, full stop.”
El-Sayed’s apology, which was in response to a question posed to him by a Jewish Democrat in attendance, came amid a new round of outreach efforts he has been making with Jewish voters since he won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary earlier this month.
He also plans to attend a Sunday Jewish caucus gathering honoring state Attorney General Dana Nessel with congressional nominee Jeremy Moss in attendance, both of whom the candidate has publicly been at ideological odds with over Jewish issues.
In recent days, El-Sayed has also minimized some of his harsh critiques of Israel in his stump speeches and issued a statement distancing himself from onetime campaign ally Hasan Piker, the left-wing anti-Israel streamer.
His nomination acceptance speech later that day made only one, oblique, reference to American support for Israel: “It shouldn’t be this hard to pay your taxes and know that that money’s going to be spent on you, and your kids, and your schools, instead of being dropped in the form of a bomb on somebody else, and their kids, and their school.”
But skepticism was still palpable among the 30 or so Jewish Democrats in the room, a crowd that included one delegate who said his daughter and grandson had been inside Temple Israel when it was attacked.
“Our safety as Jews in America relies on, I think, what’s said by public figures, and how they present themselves in public, and how they advocate for Jews in public,” he said just prior to El-Sayed’s apology.
Not all of El-Sayed’s answers pleased the room. Fielding another question about whether he would support the longstanding Democratic platform of a two-state solution in the Middle East if elected senator, the candidate pivoted.
“It’s incoherent to start with a solution and say, ‘Figure out how to work here,’” El-Sayed said. “To me, it’s about starting with a process and saying, ‘How do we dignify equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination for Palestinian people and Jewish Israelis alike?’”
He added, as he has in other interviews, that he was open to the possibility of a two-state solution “if that’s what a free Palestinian and free Jewish Israeli people decide.” But he qualified, “Our country, under the guise of a two-state solution, has been aiding, arming, and abetting a government that wants to foreclose on the possibility of a second state.”
That didn’t sit well with some in attendance, even as El-Sayed’s apology for his other comments was broadly appreciated.
“I really liked him apologizing for mispeaking. We’ve all made comments that we regret later on,” Rebecca Kasen, a Lansing-area Michigan Jewish Democrat in attendance, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. “I was less comfortable with what he said about not supporting a two-state solution.”
Overall, Kasen said, her opinion of El-Sayed had improved after the Jewish caucus meeting as a result of his apology.
“I was probably a more reluctant voter for him” beforehand, she said. That had changed: “Instead of just going to vote now, I am going to be enthusiastically voting for him.”
Senate race a tipping point in midterm congressional makeup
As the Senate race is shaping up to be the potential tipping point to decide control of the chamber in a crucial midterm year seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump, the views of the state’s Jewish Democrats regarding their party have been placed under a microscope for more reasons than just El-Sayed. That has led some longtime Jewish Democratic voters to defect to the Republican opponent, former US Rep. Mike Rogers, and also led to some awkward moments at the convention.
In one example, Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit, the party’s progressive Jewish nominee for state attorney general, addressed the Jewish caucus by declaring, “We’re going to win and keep the attorney general’s office in the hands of a Michigan Jewish Democrat.” Conspicuously absent from the day’s events was Nessel, the Jewish Democrat currently holding the seat.
Prior to the Saturday convention, Nessel, the state’s highest-ranking Jewish official, had announced she would not be attending for fear she would be targeted by antisemitic harassment. Earlier this week, in a podcast interview with The Atlantic, Nessel had reiterated her issues with El-Sayed’s comments about Temple Israel and expressed hope he would walk them back soon.
Nessel’s son Zach Nessel, secretary of the state Jewish Democratic caucus, told the caucus that his mother’s absence stemmed from “agitators” who had targeted her at the party endorsement convention in the spring. Attendance at Saturday’s event was less than one-third of what the Jewish caucus had drawn at the spring convention, organizers said.
Zach Nessel criticized the state Democratic Party for failing to take prompt action to remove the agitators from the earlier convention. He told JTA that Jews in the party “have a right to be concerned.”
“I think the Democratic Party needs to put more work into addressing their concerns,” Zach Nessel said. “But I think that can’t happen without showing up.”
Moss, the Michigan state senator who has recently been at the center of another El-Sayed-related controversy, was spotted at the convention on Saturday but did not attend the Jewish caucus events.
One ally of El-Sayed’s who also addressed the caucus is University of Michigan Board of Regents nominee Amir Makled. He is an attorney for members of the school’s pro-Palestinian encampment movement who had pushed out a Jewish pro-Israel incumbent at the previous convention. During his own address to Jewish delegates, Makled did not mention his history of social media posts, including retweeting far-right antisemitic conspiracy theorist Candace Owens and sharing praise for Hezbollah leaders.
Makled’s speech later that day at the nominating convention alluded to his work with the encampments as he declared that Michigan “will never have a university where students are punished simply because their speech makes the powerful uncomfortable.”
In between candidate meet-and-greets, Jewish caucus members shared their anxieties about their closely scrutinized role in the midterm elections. They were gravely concerned about protecting democracy and election security from Republican threats, and felt that flipping the Senate was crucial.
Yet it was hard, they said, to get much of the Jewish community on board this time, given the positions of El-Sayed and some other members of the Democratic slate. Michigan is home to an estimated 100,000 Jews, and the Senate race is currently polling in a dead heat, making their votes potentially pivotal.
“How do we unify our community to put the country first?” one attendee asked the group. “I have a hard time doing that

Australia should look 'very seriously' at UK-style ban on strangulation porn: minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:02:34 UTC
12:02:34 KST

In brief
- There are growing calls for better protections against harmful online content consumed by young people.
- Consent advocates have flagged growing concerns about the rise in sexual strangulation.
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek says the government is considering further reforms around online safety and should be looking "very seriously" at following the United Kingdom's lead by outlawing depictions of strangulation in pornography.
Her comments follow the recent death of a 16-year-old girl after a suspected sexual strangulation act.
The death has sparked renewed concern over the rising rate of sexual violence among young people.
According to the Breathless campaign, strangulation — often referred to as "choking" — has become a common sexual practice for young Australians.
The campaign found 57 per cent of young Australians reported being strangled by a partner during sex, while 51 per cent said they had strangled a partner during sex. Among women, 61 per cent said they had experienced strangulation during sex.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Last year, the UK government moved to criminalise porn featuring strangulation or suffocating, introducing a bill that would make it illegal to create or share any such content.
It was recommended in a UK government-commissioned review of online pornography, which found that dangerous practices were being normalised, particularly for young people, through porn.
New South Wales Liberal leader Kelly Sloane has written to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to call for a similar ban in Australia.
"When pornography depicts an act capable of causing brain injury, unconsciousness or death, it should not be treated as just another form of adult entertainment," she said in a statement on Sunday.
Speaking on ABC's Insiders, Plibersek said the government should look seriously at such a ban.
"There is something wrong with a situation where 60 per cent of young people say they've experienced strangulation during sexual encounters," the federal minister said.
"There is no safe way to strangle someone."
Revisiting consent education
Plibersek said it would be crucial to educate young people that pornography is not real life.
"We know that children as young as 10 are seeing pornography before they've had their first kiss; they're getting their sex education from pornography," she said.
The government has already introduced age restrictions for social media and pornography in a bid to limit what young people view online, though concerns have been raised about loopholes.
Federal Education Minister Jason Clare announced on Sunday that the federal government would review the existing consent and respectful relationships program in schools to determine whether it needs strengthening.
Last week, three teen students were charged with the sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl in Bondi, and three boys were charged with the sexual assault of a 17-year-old girl in a separate incident in Sydney's McCarthur region.
In an interview with The Daily Telegraph, Clare said recent events had been "devastating".
"At a time where young people — especially boys — are being targeted with poisonous content online, this is more important than ever," he said.
Plibersek said the government was also open to examining the issue of algorithms, and whether social media companies should be forced to allow users to opt out.
Research has found that dangerous and misogynistic ideas are reaching young men at scale through social media algorithms.
The government is also developing a new digital duty of care framework that would force tech companies to identify potential risks of harm from their services and take reasonable steps to prevent them.
A ban on smart glasses?
Plibersek said the government would also closely consider whether so-called "smart glasses" should be banned, and if not, what safeguards should be put in place around their use.
The devices, which look like ordinary glasses and can now be bought for less than $100, can be used to film people covertly without their knowledge or consent, prompting growing support for a ban.
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland called on Australia's Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) earlier this month to investigate the potential privacy implications of the products.
Plibersek said the attorney-general would "have more to say about the import of the glasses soon".
The Greens are calling for a 12-month ban on the import of the devices in order to first implement urgent reforms to privacy laws.
"These covert wearables are a disturbing technology," Greens spokesperson for digital rights, Senator David Shoebridge, said this week.
"They're built to let someone film you without your knowledge in a change room, on the street, or at your kid's swimming lesson, and our law does nothing about it."
“While some of these devices have lights when they are recording these are far from any real privacy protection, and many have no warnings at all."

Reviving Kuala Lumpur: can Malaysia modernise without pricing out its past?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
03:00:18 UTC
12:00:18 KST

Reviving Kuala Lumpur: can Malaysia modernise without pricing out its past?
Urban renewal aims to regenerate the capital’s historic core, but polish and authenticity don’t always share the same street
A yellowing receipt, framed behind glass near the entrance of Abdul Razak Gold House, records an address that no longer officially exists: “63 Ampang Street, Kuala Lumpur (Malaya)”.
For six decades, this family business has reinvented itself in step with the city around it. What began as a modest goldsmith’s counter beneath a row of old shophouses is now a brightly lit jewellery and bullion store.
Today, skyscrapers and overhead train tracks loom over the capital’s commercial core, and many of the businesses along Lebuh Ampang – the modern name for Ampang Street – that the shop’s proprietor remembers from his childhood have long since vanished.
Mohd Razalie Abdul Rasul, 37, is the newest custodian of Abdul Razak Gold House. He has expanded the business into bullion trading, bought the property next door and is, ultimately, preparing for a handover to the next generation.
“My dad is still a mentor, but the way he thinks and I think is totally different,” he said. “We have to think very modern. We have to stay one step ahead.”
Their family drama is a microcosm of the soul-searching currently sweeping Kuala Lumpur: how do you hold on to the past while still moving forward?

Venezuela’s interim president says US energy deal will last 25 years

Venezuela’s interim president says US energy deal will last 25 years
- Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez announced a 25-year US-Venezuela energy deal aiming to boost crude output to 1.5 million barrels per day and preserve resource sovereignty.
- The agreement could generate about US$209 billion in revenue, with US$19 per barrel directly benefiting Venezuela despite fluctuating oil prices.
- Venezuela plans to grant new oil exploration rights to companies including US firms like Chevron, amid protests against US presence in Caracas.
AI generated
CARACAS - Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez said on Aug 29 that an energy agreement with the US would remain in force for 25 years, target an increase in crude output to 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) and preserve the country’s sovereignty over its natural resources.
Rodriguez hailed the accord in a late-night address as a “historic” deal that would help revive the economy and boost government revenue, saying it would help shape the country’s future.
“This 25-year bilateral project envisages the development of 17 strategic oilfields with a production target of more than 1.5 million barrels per day,” Rodriguez said on state broadcaster VTV.
“That figure relates solely to the bilateral agreement between Venezuela and the United States.”
Rodriguez added that the agreement’s target of 1.5 million bpd was only an initial goal and that the broader plan also included the development of eight greenfield oil blocks as part of a wider expansion of the country’s energy sector.
US President Donald Trump on Friday announced plans for the US to take partial control of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves, betting that American companies can help revive the South American nation’s battered energy industry while providing a new source of crude to help lower US fuel prices.
Trump provided few details on the agreement, saying only that the US had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves through a partnership with private business.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven oil reserves, but it produces only about 1.25 million bpd - far below its potential - after years of underinvestment, mismanagement and sanctions.
Rodriguez said the agreement could generate about US$209 billion (S$266.16 billion) in revenue for the Venezuelan state, based on a benchmark oil price of US$65 per barrel, though she acknowledged crude prices could fluctuate.
She said roughly US$19 from each barrel produced and sold under the arrangement would flow directly to Venezuela, providing a significant boost to government revenue.
She said that the country retained “ownership of and sovereignty” over its natural resources, “while leveraging capital, technology and operational expertise to support the recovery of a strategic industry that has been severely affected by sanctions.”
Earlier onAug 29, dozens of pro-government groups gathered in downtown Caracas to protest against the US presence in Venezuela.
Rodriguez welcomed the agreement following Trump’s announcement, saying it would bolster economic growth and increase government revenue.
Venezuelan officials are preparing to sign agreements next week granting new oil exploration and production rights to several companies, including US firms.
Two sources close to the negotiations said on Aug 28 that Chevron was among the companies expected to finalise talks to transition its Venezuelan joint ventures into the country’s new energy framework. REUTERS

Iceland's EU referendum edges closer to 'no'
Published August 30, 2026last updated August 30, 2026
Partial results from Iceland's referendum on resuming European Union membership talks showed a slim lead for the "no" camp on Sunday morning.
With final results counted from five of six constituencies, 52.5% of voters opposed the government's proposal to resume EU negotiations, while 47.5% backed the plan, Iceland's public broadcaster RUV reported.
Some 270,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote. There was no information yet about voter turnout.
Election officials warned that a more reliable result might not be available until midday on Sunday.
Iceland has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming the bloc's 28th member. Talks were suspended 13 years ago by the euroskeptic government at the time.
Iceland's current left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a vote next year but brought it forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.

Iceland referendum initial tally narrowly favours reopening EU accession negotiations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
02:45:26 UTC
11:45:26 KST

Initial results of Iceland's referendum have shown a narrow majority backing the reopening of EU membership negotiations as vote counting continues, according to public broadcaster RUV.
The latest result on Saturday showed 46,589 votes, or 50.5 percent, in support of restarting accession talks, while 45,682, or 49.5 percent, oppose the proposal.
Support for reopening negotiations is strongest in the Reykjavik North constituency, where 59.4 percent of voters back the proposal. Opposition is highest in the Southern constituency, where 60.1 percent are against it.
The Southwest constituency, which accounts for roughly 30 percent of Iceland's electorate, was evenly divided.
The campaign was dominated by concerns about the cost of living, security, sovereignty and control of the country's fisheries.
Polling stations closed at 10 pm local time on Saturday after voting began as early as 9 am. Nearly 400,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote.
Not final referendum
The referendum does not determine whether Iceland will join the EU. A majority "Yes" vote would give the government a mandate to resume accession talks. Any eventual membership agreement would require approval in a second referendum.
Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009 after its banking system collapsed during the global financial crisis.
Accession negotiations began in 2010 but were suspended three years later after a Eurosceptic government took office. In 2015, Reykjavik informed Brussels that it no longer wished to be considered an EU candidate.
The European Commission, however, maintains that Iceland's membership application remains legally valid and that negotiations are only on hold, according to a report by the European Policy Centre (EPC).

Israel pounds southern Lebanon as Iran vows to stand by Beirut
Israel continued attacks across southern Lebanon on Saturday, carrying out airstrikes, artillery shelling and demolitions, while Tehran pledged continued support for the country amid stalled negotiations over an IDF withdrawal.
Most of the day’s attacks were concentrated in Nabatieh Province, RT’s Lebanon correspondent Steve Sweeney said. Two explosions were reported near Aita al-Jabal, while Israeli drones carried out two strikes on Nabatieh al-Fawqa on Saturday morning. Israeli forces separately set fire to homes in Beit Yahoun.
The latest strikes came two days after an Israeli attack on Arab Salim killed 28-year-old Saja Sharara just 48 hours after her wedding, according to Sweeney, who recently visited the southern Lebanese village. Six others were wounded, including a child, a woman, and two elderly people.
Israel, however, said Thursday’s strikes followed the launch of two Hezbollah drones toward Israeli troops.
The escalation comes as Tehran reaffirms its support for Lebanon. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Sheikh Ali al-Khatib, vice president of Lebanon’s Higher Shiite Islamic Council, in Tehran on Friday. According to Lebanese L’Orient Today, Khatib described a deteriorating situation in the south, saying many displaced residents had exhausted their savings and had been left without homes or work. He appealed in particular for financial assistance for affected communities.
Araghchi said Tehran was working to revive the US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed in June, the first clause of which called for an end to Israeli attacks on Lebanon. He argued that implementing the agreement remained the way to resolve the crisis, while acknowledging that “the circumstances are difficult,” as cited by L’Orient Today.
The memorandum followed a renewed escalation between Israel and Hezbollah after the latter resumed attacks two days after the US-Iran war began on February 28. Hezbollah said its operation was retaliation for the killing of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
Hezbollah says it has observed the ceasefire reached under the subsequent US-Iran agreement. Israel, however, has continued strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon and currently occupies more than 600 square kilometers of Lebanese territory.
Beirut and Israel have meanwhile been holding direct negotiations aimed at securing an Israeli withdrawal and ending the hostilities. Another round is reportedly expected in Rome in September, but progress has been limited.

Killing of Palestinian children and teens by Israel surges in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
02:43:00 UTC
11:43:00 KST

Killing of Palestinian children and teens by Israel surges in West Bank
- The killing of Palestinian children and teenagers by Israeli forces in the West Bank has surged since October 2023, with an average of seven deaths per month compared to one per month previously.
- Many teenagers are killed during clashes when Israeli troops shoot youths accused of throwing stones, while younger children are often victims of indiscriminate fire.
- Families suffer deep grief and struggle for justice, with investigations by the Israeli military often disputed and Palestinians expressing that they rarely receive accountability for such deaths.
AI generated
RAMALLAH, Palestinian Territories - Alia al-Hallaq’s son Mohammed was nine when he was killed by an Israeli army bullet last October, but the Palestinian homemaker still speaks of herself as a mother of five, not four.
“I still haven’t accepted the idea of the loss. I often sit in the courtyard of the house and look at Mohammed’s grave below, and I cry while making sure that my children don’t see me,” she told AFP.
She said Mohammed was killed after running away from soldiers patrolling their village of Al-Rihiya, in the south of the occupied West Bank.
Hallaq’s uncle, also named Mohammed Hallaq, told AFP that his nephew was killed by a stray bullet during a confrontation between the army patrol and a group of older youths.
The bullet travelled through Mohammed’s abdomen, according to emergency services.
“Mohammed’s killing was the end,” his mother said.
The Israeli military, contacted by AFP for comment on Mohammed’s death, said at the time that soldiers opened fire during an altercation while deployed in Al-Rihaya.
“Soldiers responded with fire toward the suspects in the rock-hurling. Hits were identified,” it said, using language it generally employs to say troops shot and hit someone.
The killing of Palestinian children and teenagers by Israel has become increasingly common since the start of the war in Gaza.
B’Tselem, an Israeli rights group, reported 235 children and teenagers killed by Israeli forces in the West Bank since Oct 7, 2023 – when Hamas launched a massive attack on Israel from the Gaza Strip – through June 2026, including five killed by Israeli settlers.
The Palestinian Authority’s Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission, a Palestinian government institution, reported 250 such deaths over the same time period.
In the 17 years between 2005 and 2021, an average of roughly one Palestinian child or teenager was killed by Israeli forces every month, according to B’Tselem, a frequent but much lower rate.
For the period since the Oct 7 attack, the average using B’Tselem figures is around seven killed per month.
Bullets for stones
AFP spoke to 12 women who lost children since Oct 7, 2023.
Although the details of each case differ, all spoke of family life stopped in its tracks and a lack of accountability.
In 2025, of the 54 Palestinian children or teenagers killed according to B’Tselem, the youngest was just two years old, while the majority were aged between 14 and 17.
Teenagers are often killed when Israeli forces engage with Palestinian youths throwing rocks, whom they routinely label terrorists, and shoot them.
The Israeli military commander for the West Bank, Major-General Avi Bluth, said in early 2026 that the army had killed 42 Palestinians for throwing stones in 2025, not specifying how many were minors.
In several other cases, usually involving younger children such as Mohammed, witnesses said the army had fired indiscriminately at Palestinians and killed children who were present.
One such casualty was seven-month-old Sam Abu Haikal, shot in the face by Israeli troops in the West Bank city of Hebron in June 2026.
‘Palestinians don’t get justice’
His mother, Dania Abu Haikal, 28, told AFP she was also wounded when the troops fired at their car while Sam was on her lap, with a bullet entering through her cheek and exiting through her ear.
She bore a large scar on her face when she met with AFP at her home in Bethlehem, holding a stuffed fox that had belonged to her son.
“Why would anyone shoot an infant? What did a little baby, a seven-month-old infant, do to harm the soldiers?”Abu Haikal, a university lecturer, said.
After a preliminary investigation, the army said one of its soldiers had opened fire on “uninvolved civilians” after their vehicle accelerated in the direction of the troops.
Abu Haikal disputes this, and said her husband had brought their car to a stop before the soldiers started shooting.
She carries the agony of losing her only child on top of the physical pain from the shooting.
“I cry every day; now my life is empty without him,” she said.
Like others whom AFP spoke to, Abu Haikal consulted a lawyer to push the army to investigate the incident fully.
“Palestinians don’t get justice for being killed by Israelis. But we hope that we get justice.” AFP

Tests loom for popular British PM Andy Burnham as Parliament returns
- Andy Burnham has had a positive first month as British Prime Minister, gaining popularity with cost-of-living measures and a relaxed public image.
- Parliament returns on Sept 1, bringing challenges like prison reform decisions and Burnham’s first Prime Minister’s Questions session.
- Key issues ahead include funding his budget without tax rises, North Sea oil drilling debates, and managing relations with the EU and possibly Donald Trump.
AI generated
LONDON – Andy Burnham has enjoyed a honeymoon first month as Britain’s leader, but the hard trade-offs involved in governing are about to get real for the Prime Minister as Parliament returns from its summer break in the coming days.
Since succeeding Keir Starmer on July 20, Burnham has pleased voters with several low-cost sweeteners, including cutting electricity bills and bus fares, while burnishing his casual man-of-the-people vibes.
He has poured pints of beer with his finance minister, played guitar in Ukraine, and kept up a prolific output of slick social media videos during a self-styled “listening tour” of Britain.
Projecting a sunnier outlook than the straitlaced Starmer, and benefiting from the woes besetting hard-right rival Nigel Farage, Burnham has sparked a poll bounce for his ruling Labour Party.
A YouGov survey published on Aug 18 found that 46 per cent of Britons view him favourably, up 12 percentage points from when he first arrived at Downing Street.
With lawmakers on holiday, the new Prime Minister has largely been able to avoid thornier issues during his first weeks in office.
“He’s benefited enormously from Parliament not being there,” former senior civil servant Jill Rutter told AFP, adding that it had allowed the 56-year-old Burnham to “control the narrative” so far.
MPs return to Westminster on Sept 1, when Burnham is expected to deliver his first speech to Parliament as prime minister.
His government is set to announce that day whether it is watering down contentious plans to release thousands of prisoners early to ease chronic overcrowding in jails.
Then on Sept 2, MPs and the public will learn whether Burnham is any good at facing down the weekly grilling by the leader of the opposition when he takes part in his first Prime Minister’s Questions session.
Looming on the horizon is his government’s first budget on Oct 28, when Burnham must demonstrate that he can fund his pledges regarding cost-of-living support and ending rough sleeping, all while plugging a huge gap in defence spending.
He must do so against a backdrop of strained public finances and with limited levers to pull due to his commitment not to raise income tax, employee payroll contributions, or a value-added tax on consumer goods.
“That might be when reality starts to hit,” former minister Tony McNulty, who served alongside Burnham in Labour governments of the early 2000s, told AFP.
McNulty, now a politics lecturer at Queen Mary University of London, insists Burnham is capable of taking tough decisions and “sticking” to them, despite opponents labelling him a “people pleaser”.
Trump meeting?
Plenty of sensitive issues lie ahead, including welfare reform, how to fund social care, and whether to proceed with the scrapping of jury trials for many offences.
Whether to extract oil and gas at the controversial Jackdaw and Rosebank fields in the North Sea could be one of the most divisive questions.
“You either alienate the unions by saying no and get noises off from (US President) Donald Trump in a very unhelpful way,” explained Rutter.
Or Burnham gives drilling a green light and “you alienate the Labour net zero (supporters) who say we’re going to lose more support to the Greens”.
Burnham will host his first European leader since taking office when French President Emmanuel Macron visits London this week.
It comes as he must decide how to proceed with a “reset” with the European bloc that was championed by Starmer ahead of a bilateral summit expected in 2026.
Burnham has said Britain must be “bolder” in getting closer to the bloc, but has ruled out rejoining the single market, customs union or allowing freedom of movement.
“The EU isn’t handing out sweets just because we’ve got a sort of fun prime minister who likes (1980s English rock band) The Smiths,” added Rutter.
A likely first meeting with Trump, possibly at the United Nations General Assembly in September, will be tricky for Burnham who once described the US President’s policies as “poisonous”.
Labour lawmaker Jess Phillips said on a Sky News podcast last week that Burnham must “show what his actual priorities are” but in doing so runs the risk of disappointing many MPs.
MP Luke Akehurst told AFP that Burnham’s positive start “gives him a significant bank of political capital” among Labour colleagues “who will need to trust his judgement in addressing the range of complex policy issues that the government faces”. AFP

NEW YORK, August 30. /TASS/. NASA has postponed the planned mid-September launch of the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station (ISS), which includes Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, the US space agency said.
"NASA and SpaceX are adjusting the launch date for the agency’s Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station to address an oxidizer leak on Dragon’s propulsion system which was detected during standard prelaunch spacecraft processing. Joint NASA and SpaceX teams are performing additional tests and data review and will complete any necessary rework prior to launch. A new target date will be announced once available," NASA said on its website.
Earlier, Dana Weigel, who oversees NASA's low-Earth orbit programs, said Crew-13 was scheduled to launch no earlier than September 12. Teteryatnikov will travel to the ISS with NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk. Teteryatnikov and Kutryk will serve as mission specialists, Watkins as commander and Delaney as pilot.

China's Chang wins first ranking event title at snooker's Wuhan Open (updated)
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:39:07 CST
11:39:07 KST

Chang Bingyu poses for photos during the awarding ceremony after the final match between Zhao Xintong of China and Chang Bingyu of China at Wuhan Open 2026 snooker tournament in Wuhan, central China's Hubei Province, Aug. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Zhizun)
WUHAN, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's Chang Bingyu won his first ranking event title at the World Snooker Wuhan Open, beating new world No.1 Zhao Xintong 10-7 in an all-Chinese final here on Saturday.
Chang, 24, held his nerve in a dramatic deciding frame. With the final black remaining and Zhao already ahead on points, Chang used a snooker to force a foul before clearing four colors close to the cushion. He then potted the final black to win the frame by two points and seal the title.
After shaking hands with Zhao, Chang covered his face with a towel and struggled to contain his emotions.
"This title means a lot to me," Chang said. "There was a period when I couldn't participate in matches, then I came back and regained my professional status. Last year I reached a final, and now I finally won the title. I have really put in a lot over these years, that's why I'm so emotional."
Chang reached his first ranking final at the Scottish Open in December 2025, where he led Chris Wakelin 2-1 before losing eight consecutive frames.
"After that loss, I reminded myself every day that if I reached another final, I had to seize the opportunity," Chang said.
His path to the Wuhan title included victories over fellow Chinese player Liu Hongyu, Ali Carter, former world No. 1 Judd Trump and his idol, seven-time world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan.
"I never thought I could beat Zhao," Chang said after the final. "I came into the match with the mentality of learning from him. I've watched most of his matches in recent years. His game is both attractive and practical, and I have imitated many aspects of his style."
Zhao, who had won all seven of his previous ranking finals, praised Chang despite the loss.
"Although it's a little disappointing, Chang Bingyu deserved to win," Zhao said. "Many young players, including him, have already reached a very high level. I believe they will continue to get better."
The Wuhan Open has now been won by Chinese players for three consecutive editions. This year's semifinals also featured three generations of Chinese players, with Xiao Guodong (born in the 1980s), Zhao (born in the 1990s) and Chang (born in the 2000s) all reaching the last four.
Chang said he still has plenty to improve despite the breakthrough.
"The gap between me and the world's top 16 is still big," he said. "There were a lot of ups and downs emotionally in this match. I still need to work on my mentality and make myself more composed." ■

PM Narendra Modi with Uzbekistan Shavkat President Mirziyoyev
Prime Minister Narendra Modi received a warm and personal welcome from Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev after arriving in capital Tashkent on Saturday for a two-day state visit.From the airport, the two leaders travelled together by car to the presidential palace, marking the latest instance of PM Modi sharing a car ride with a world leader. They held a dinner meeting at the presidential palace.During the visit, the first leg of the prime minister’s two-nation tour, PM Modi will hold delegation-level talks with the Uzbek president to further strengthen the strategic partnership between the two countries.The discussions will cover cooperation in trade and investment, defence, digital connectivity, energy, education and people-to-people ties, while also setting the agenda for future bilateral engagement.
In his departure statement, PM Modi noted that the India-Uzbekistan Strategic Partnership had witnessed “significant advancement” in recent years.“I look forward to my discussions with President Mirziyoyev on further deepening our cooperation in trade and investment, digital connectivity, defence, energy, and on advancing our shared visions of Viksit Bharat and Yangi Uzbekistan,” he wrote on X.The visit marks his fourth trip to Uzbekistan since taking office.
He previously visited the country in 2015, 2016 and 2022.From Tashkent, PM Modi will travel to Bishkek at the invitation of Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov to attend the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit, which will mark 25 years of the organisation.
PM Modi first “carpooled” with a world leader during his 2014 visit to the United States, when he shared a car ride with then-US President Barack Obama.However, since last year, car rides with world leaders have become a recurring feature of what has been described as the prime minister's "informal diplomacy."In September last year, during his visit to China for the SCO Summit, PM Modi travelled in the same car as Vladimir Putin, reciprocating the gesture months later when the Russian president visited New Delhi in December.Since then, he has shared car rides with world leaders including French President Emmanuel Macron, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

High-level review meet held over proposed 'ARISE' project for coastal projection and climate resilience in Odisha
Edited by: Ayush Pandey / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 30, 2026, 08:16 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
