One Nation declares there are 'no safe Labor seats' after historic by-election win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
23:28:45 UTC
08:28:45 KST

In brief
- One Nation has declared it has won the Secret Harbour by-election.
- The WA state seat was seen as a test of the right-wing party's support.
Labor has pledged to listen to the message from voters after One Nation's historic victory in a formerly safe West Australian seat.
Government-backed candidate Georgia Tree conceded on Sunday after her One Nation opponent Luke Herdegen claimed a state by-election victory the night before.
Voters delivered an 18.6 per cent swing against Labor in the outer Perth electorate of Secret Harbour, handing One Nation its first lower-house seat in the state.
WA Premier Roger Cook, whose party still enjoys an overwhelming parliamentary majority, said the result was a reminder that many people were struggling with high living costs.
"The voters of Secret Harbour have spoken and we will listen," he said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"My team will continue to get out and talk to our communities, listen to their concerns and do everything within our powers to make their lives better."
People needed to take the electoral threat posted by One Nation seriously given the party now enjoyed support from a large part of the community, the premier added.
One Nation federal MP Barnaby Joyce said the party's success in WA sent another strong message to Canberra.
"The world's changed, hasn't it, politics has changed," he told News24.
"What we've seen there is quite a number of people who basically would have been former Labor Party voters ... they find it easy to make the jump to One Nation."
With about three-quarters of ballots counted, Herdegen had secured 39.1 per cent of first preference results, ahead of Tree's 24.4 per cent and Liberal candidate Ryan Robertson's 17.3 per cent share.
WA One Nation leader Rod Caddies noted the historic moment as he declared "the two-party system is dead".
"You're witnessing a result they said was impossible," he said.
"Labor have owned this part of Perth. But a safe seat does not stay safe if you ignore it long enough."
Joyce said traditional Labor-held seats could no longer be taken for granted.
"If you think 'oh, these people will just vote for me', then that's a sense of arrogance and arrogance will get your political hide delivered to you on a plate," he said.
Opposition home affairs spokesman Jonathon Duniam said the Liberals should not have admitted the by-election would be a challenge for the party before it even took place.
"When we start talking about conceding or coming in second or finding ways to work with other people before we've even run the race, then yeah, people are not going to back us," he said.
"We've got to fight hard and we've got to give people a reason to vote for us."
One Nation's performance in WA has been closely watched across the nation, particularly in Victoria and NSW, where state elections are due in November and March respectively.
Cost-of-living top of mind
Cost-of-living pressures, housing shortages and a perceived lack of community amenities topped the list of concerns for voters in Secret Harbour.
Local Luke Pors voted for One Nation, believing the minor party would do a better job than either Labor or the Liberals.
"We know what their true goal is and I think just in One Nation we trust," he said.
The WA result follows One Nation securing four lower-house seats in South Australia's March state election, the first lower-house spots the party had ever secured outside of Queensland.
The anti-immigration party also won a maiden lower-house seat in the federal parliament in May when it triumphed in the Farrer by-election.

Aussie qualifer completes rare grand slam feat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
23:26:22 UTC
08:26:22 KST

In short:
Storm Hunter has become the only active Australian tennis player to enter all four grand slams as a qualifier.
Hunter will play her first US Open since 2023 when the New York grand slam begins on Monday.
What's next?
Hunter is one of six Australians playing on Monday.
There is a very good reason why facing big-hitting French Open and Wimbledon semifinalist Marta Kostyuk in the US Open first round holds no fears for late-blooming Australian trailblazer Storm Hunter.
The 32-year-old has just sent tennis officials scrambling through the record books after qualifying for the Open's main draw for the first time.
Historians could only confirm Hunter is the first active Australian player to successfully qualify for all four grand slams, a rare feat few others from anywhere have accomplished.
Hunter did not do it easily, taking out compatriot and great mate Maddison Inglis in her first match, fending off two match points in her second and waiting through a 24-hour weather delay to advance with a third straight sudden-death victory.
"This is the last slam on my list to tick off to get through qualies and coming in I hadn't played many singles matches in the last few months so, yeah, it feels amazing," Hunter said.
Having missed more than a year after rupturing an Achilles tendon, Hunter is back in the Flushing Meadows main draw for a first time since 2023.
Her "reward" is a first-round tussle on day one with the 11th-seeded Kostyuk, who is coming off charges to the last four at both Roland Garros and the All England Club.
"Yeah, it's tough," said the one-time world number one doubles ace.
"She's obviously having a really good year. She's a great player, very physical with the way she plays and a really good competitor.
"So it's going to be tough. Obviously a very quick turnaround from playing qualifiers to my first round tomorrow, but I'm feeling good and she's the one who's under all the pressure to play against me and I have practised with her before.
"I know what her level is and I know it's going to be a challenge, but I'm up for a challenge. It's going to be fun. I'm going to enjoy it.
"There's been lots of times in my career I didn't think I'd be back playing at this level, so to be back in the main draw of a slam is awesome, and I'm just going to go out and enjoy it and give it a good crack."
Hunter is among six Australians playing on Monday.
Kim Birrell faces Petra Marcinko, Talia Gibson also plays a Croatian in veteran Donna Vekic and fellow rising star Taylah Preston takes on American Alycia Parks.
Adam Walton, up against China's Yibing Wu, and Aleksandar Vukic playing Japan's Rei Sakamoto are the only Aussie men in first-round action.
Sixth seed Alex de Minaur opens his campaign on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST).

Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
23:25:07 UTC
08:25:07 KST

Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week
This is the 27th time since Russia invaded Ukraine that the Zaporizhzhia plant has had to rely on emergency diesel supplies.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station in southeastern Ukraine has been without off-site power for more than a week, the world’s nuclear energy watchdog has warned.
The plant, which Russia has occupied since 2022, is currently relying on emergency diesel generators, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Saturday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Zaporizhzhia’s mayor says Russian advance reaches city’s outskirts
- list 2 of 3Russia reports Ukrainian drone strike near Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
- list 3 of 3Russia warns it could target UK in response to Kyiv firing British missiles
The plant needs power to keep its six non-operating reactors cool and has only a 10-day diesel supply on site, the IAEA said in a statement.
“The availability of diesel fuel is of paramount importance whenever a nuclear power plant loses off-site power,” IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has not had a delivery from an off-site storage facility in about six months but was supplied with diesel on Thursday and Friday from another off-site location, the IAEA said.
The Vienna-based agency is now trying to negotiate a local ceasefire to allow repairs to electrical lines.
Zaporizhzhia is Europe’s largest nuclear power plant. It has not generated electricity since September 2022, over six months after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February that year, but the plant’s reactors must be kept cool to prevent a meltdown of the fuel inside.
“This is the 27th blackout at the plant since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion,” Ukraine’s deputy head of military law enforcement, Gyunduz Mamedov, wrote on X on Saturday.
The IAEA has had a permanent presence at the site since September 2022, after Russia took control of the Ukrainian facility in March that year.
Both sides in the conflict regularly accuse the other of attacking the site, which sits on the banks of the Dnipro River and demarcates the front line in the sector.
On Friday, the IAEA said there had been three incidents that week with drones at the plant, injuring two employees. It did not say who launched the drones.
Earlier this month, a drone strike close to the plant killed one nuclear specialist and wounded 17, with Moscow asserting that Kyiv was behind the attack.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that Russian actions in and around the plant constitute nuclear blackmail against Ukraine and Europe more widely.
In 2024, footage emerged of a fire in one of the power plant’s cooling towers, prompting Ukraine to accuse Russia of nuclear blackmail.

'RSS vision is to see the world as one': Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat at New York event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
23:19:46 UTC
08:19:46 KST

'RSS vision is to see the world as one': Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat at New York event
Edited by: Prisha Patnaik / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 30, 2026, 06:35 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
'Unity in diversity in Bharat's DNA: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat
NEW DELHI: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat, addressing around 5,000 members of Indian-American organisations at Madison Square Garden in New York, spoke about unity, pluralism, individual responsibility and the obligations of the Indian diaspora, while arguing that material success alone cannot define a fulfilling life.Bhagwat was speaking at the “Universal Oneness Celebration”, organised by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue. He framed his address around the idea of “oneness”, drawing parallels between the pluralism associated with the United States and what he described as Bharat’s “unity in diversity”.“When we say America, United States of America, one word is often discussed frequently. That is pluralism,” Bhagwat said. “And when we say Bharat, another word, another phrase is discussed: unity in diversity.”“For Bharat, this unity and diversity, both are in their DNA,” he said.Bhagwat said differences between people were a natural feature of life, but argued that these differences existed alongside an underlying sense of oneness.“So many styles of living. We appear different. We are different,” he said, pointing to differences in people's everyday needs and circumstances.
“But there is innate oneness. That is why we feel for each other,” he added.He described diversity as the “decoration of oneness”, presenting unity not as the absence of differences but as something that exists beneath them.Bhagwat also linked this idea to what he described as the responsibilities of individuals, societies and nations. Nations, he said, should not be seen merely as geographical entities but as having a larger purpose.“These nations are not merely geographical entities. In the design of this universe, nations have to carry out a duty,” he said, quoting Swami Vivekananda's formulation that every nation has a message, a mission and a destiny.
‘Be true to America’: RSS chief message to diaspora
Turning to the Indian diaspora in the United States, Bhagwat said Indians living abroad had a primary responsibility towards the country where they lived and worked.“So we are Americans, and we should be true to America,” he said.He described this as a duty towards one's “karma bhumi” — the land where a person lives and works.“The diaspora, Indian diaspora, they have a duty to their karma bhumi. They must fulfill that. They should be loyal to their karma bhumi,” Bhagwat said.At the same time, he said Indians abroad could maintain a connection with Bharat as their “janma bhumi”, or birthplace, and could contribute to the country if they wished to do so after fulfilling their responsibilities to their adopted home.“But it is not obligatory,” he said.Instead, he said, the connection with Bharat should be reflected in the values carried by the diaspora.“Your janma bhumi expects you to live the values it has imparted on you,” Bhagwat said.Bhagwat also questioned the idea that professional success should be measured primarily through earnings and material possessions.“How much we earn is not important. How much we distribute is important,” he said.He asked whether a career could be reduced to money and material happiness, while acknowledging that material aspirations had a legitimate place in Hindu philosophy.“You think of career? Is career only money? Is career only material happiness?” Bhagwat asked.He referred to the four Purusharthas, saying that Artha and Kama represented important material dimensions of life alongside spiritual pursuits.“It is not denied. In four Purusharthas, Artha and Kama are two important Purusharthas related to material life,” he said.Bhagwat also referred to the traditional four stages of life — Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha and Sannyasa — arguing that people acquire different responsibilities as they move through life.“So you have to learn, you have to sustain life, and you have to give the advice, your experience to next generation,” he said.He argued that material abundance by itself could not guarantee fulfilment.“So the material happiness is transient, cannot satisfy,” Bhagwat said. “And if abundance of material happiness is there, it may fail also. And therefore there is no satisfaction.”
Highlights responsibility towards others
Bhagwat's broader argument centred on the idea that human intelligence carried with it a responsibility towards others.Using the example of a hungry person watching someone eat, he said people instinctively recognise another person's suffering and cannot simply ignore it.“A simple experiment you can do, or I can challenge you to do. When you are taking your lunch or dinner, let a hungry man stand before you, and let him stare at your full platter with hungry eyes,” he said.“You can try; you will not do. Because we are human beings.”He contrasted human beings' ability to think and plan with the instinctive behaviour of animals, but said the ability to think also brought a responsibility to use that capacity correctly.“If you think in the right way, you go nearer to God. If you think in the wrong way, you go nearer to the animal kingdom,” he said.
Bhagwat offers interpretation of Dharma
Bhagwat also offered a broader interpretation of “Dharma”, saying it should not be understood simply as religion or worship.“Dharma is not religion. It is not worship. It is beyond all this,” he said.He described Dharma as a sustaining principle that allows people and society to manage competing aspects of life and maintain balance.“It is the balance which sustains everything at once, simultaneously, and simultaneously everyone can progress,” Bhagwat said.He similarly argued that progress should not require either individuals or society to be suppressed.“Individual, society and environment, they have to proceed together, progress together,” he said, adding that different aspects of an individual's own life — body, mind and intellect — also had to advance together.
Bhagwat concluded by returning to the idea of responsibility towards both one's place of work and birthplace.He called on people to fulfil their duties towards their “karma bhumi” as well as their “janma bhumi”, saying such an approach could help a world struggling with multiple challenges.“To that destiny and fulfill our duties in our karma bhumi as well as our janma bhumi,” he said.“If we do that, that will be a boon for the world struggling with all these problems and stumbling at every step.”
Prisha Patnaik is a journalist with The Times of India, writing across geopolitics, international affairs, culture, history and internet culture. With over two years of experience in social media and digital content, she is interested in how news, politics and culture are shaped for digital audiences. She holds a master’s degree in Media and Communications from Goldsmiths, University of London.

The US could gain control over part of Venezuela’s oil reserves for 100 years – The Telegraph
Kyiv • UNN
The US is discussing control over Venezuela’s 65 billion barrels of reserves for 100 years. More than $100 billion is planned to be invested in the oil industry.
The United States could gain control over a significant share of Venezuela's oil reserves for 100 years under a major agreement that U.S. President Donald Trump called "the largest oil deal in world history." The Telegraph reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the agreements provide for long-term U.S. control over Venezuela's oil fields, while the American side could receive rights to use them for the next 100 years.
This concerns control over more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves. That is more than one-fifth of Venezuela's total proven reserves, estimated at approximately 303 billion barrels and considered the largest in the world.
The agreement is designed to last for decades
The agreements cover 17 strategic oil fields. Private companies are planned to be brought in to develop them, while investment in Venezuela's oil industry could exceed $100 billion.
Trump said the agreement would more than double the oil reserves available to the United States and, in the long term, help lower fuel prices for Americans.
At the same time, the detailed legal and commercial terms of the agreements have not yet been disclosed. In particular, it remains unclear in exactly what form the United States will obtain long-term rights to Venezuela's oil fields and how the 100-year control mechanism will be implemented.

Ontario’s Doug Ford prods Trump with sign rejecting ‘Lake America’ name
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
22:50:27 UTC
07:50:27 KST

Ontario’s Doug Ford prods Trump with sign rejecting ‘Lake America’ name
The ‘Lake Ontario’ sign comes in response to the US president’s efforts to rename the body of water ‘Lake America’.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has unveiled a new – and very blue – response to United States President Donald Trump’s controversial order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.
On Saturday, Ford recorded a video of himself along the lake’s shore near Hamilton, Ontario, where he revealed a baby-blue, billboard-sized sign that reads “Lake Ontario” in large white letters.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US President Trump signs order renaming Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’
- list 2 of 3Can Trump really rename Lake Ontario, ‘Lake America’?
- list 3 of 3With the US and Canada locked in a trade war, fears of a recession lurk
Underneath, a subheading underscores Ford’s message about the name: “Now and Always.” The message is also repeated in French, Canada’s second official language.
Ford, who has made a habit of needling the US president, explained that the sign was erected to reaffirm the Great Lake’s name “in case President Trump — or anyone else — forgets”.
“Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in his social media video. “And long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario.”
The White House did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
With Canada and the US embroiled in a spiralling trade war, Trump signed an executive order on Thursday that changed how the US federal government would refer to the body of water.
The order, however, drew pushback from allies and critics alike. Vermont Governor Phil Scott, a fellow Republican, called the move “petty and disappointing”, and several politicians urged Trump to return to the negotiating table, rather than antagonise Canada, a longtime ally.
Canada is ranked as one of the US’s top two trading partners, and as of 2024, it is the largest destination for US exports.
The trade tensions, however, have led to a popular backlash in Canada, with boycotts of US goods and bans in several provinces against US liquor.
Ford, a right-wing populist, has emerged as a vocal proponent of Canadian retaliatory actions. Since Trump took office for a second term in 2025, he has called for Canada to cede its sovereignty and become a US state, and has issued several waves of tariffs against the northern country.
Ford’s “Lake Ontario” sign marks the premier’s latest salvo in his ongoing feud with Trump.
Earlier this week, Ford escalated his attacks against Trump after trade negotiations between the two countries fell apart, resulting in US tariffs of 50 percent on $20bn worth of Canadian goods.
“He can kiss my a** as far as I’m concerned. We’re going to go at him full steam,” Ford said about Trump during a Monday interview on a Toronto radio show.
Trump fired back on his Truth Social platform by mocking Ford as “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive” compared with his late brother, the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford.
“Someone should get these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE,” Trump added.
Saturday’s billboard is not the first stunt Ford has undertaken to stand up against Trump, either. Some of those actions have had international consequences.
Last year, Ford’s government spent $75m on an anti-tariff advertisement featuring the voice of former US President Ronald Reagan, which aired in the US.
“Over the long run, such trade barriers hurt every American worker and consumer,” Reagan can be heard saying in the message.
The US and Canada were in the midst of trade negotiations at the time, and Trump cancelled the talks in protest against the advertisement. Some members of the Trump administration compared the advertising campaign with election interference, as the advertisements aired before 2025’s off-year races.
Ford ultimately pulled the advertisement from the airwaves in October, saying he had achieved his goal “to initiate a conversation” about “the impact of tariffs on workers and businesses”.
Since 2018, Ford has led Ontario as its provincial head of government. The province is considered the centre of Canada’s automotive manufacturing industry, and its factories are tightly integrated with US car manufacturers across the border.
A prominent conservative and longtime leader in Toronto, Ford formerly drew comparisons with Trump. His entry into provincial politics coincided with Trump’s first term as president.
Early on, some of Ford’s supporters rallied around the tagline “Make Ontario Great Again”, a play on Trump’s “Make America Great Again” campaign slogan. The phrase, in turn, had been popularised during Reagan’s 1980 run for president.
But Ford has rejected any comparisons with the US president, saying he and his family were involved in politics long before Trump.

What’s behind the US deal to seize control of Venezuelan oil reserves?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
22:33:01 UTC
07:33:01 KST

What’s behind the US deal to seize control of Venezuelan oil reserves?
Few details have emerged about the arrangement between Washington and Caracas, criticised as a takeover of Venezuela’s resources.
The United States has announced that it has secured control of a substantial portion of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves, after President Donald Trump pledged to “take back” the South American country’s energy resources.
On Friday, Trump announced that his government and that of Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez had reached a deal to give the US majority control over more than 65 billion barrels’ worth of proven oil reserves.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump announces ‘biggest oil deal in world history’ with Venezuela
- list 2 of 3US nears deal to secure stake in Venezuelan oil fields, insiders say
- list 3 of 3Venezuela and Israel restore consular ties as relations warm
Details remain unclear. But the deal will involve 17 strategic oil fields in Venezuela. The US government has said it will partner with a private business to extract the fuel.
“The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” Trump wrote in a social media post celebrating the announcement.
What has been said so far, and what could the new deal mean for US-Venezuela relations? We answer those questions and more in this explainer.
How much oil is involved?
The deal reportedly involves 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.
That amounts to roughly a fifth of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves. As of 2023, the US government estimates that Venezuela has 303 billion barrels of oil reserves, the largest known deposit in the world.
Approximately 17 percent of the world’s oil supply is estimated to be in the South American country.
But some analysts have questioned the 65-billion-barrel total Trump announced. With no fixed terms released, there has been speculation that Trump may have made a splashy announcement to help jumpstart the US economy.
“The 65 billion barrel number is a red herring and will have little relevance to any actual deals — the real relevant details of which are still almost entirely unknown,” oil market researcher Rory Johnston said in a social media post.
“It’s just a classic big number that Trump was sure to jump all over and will repeat ad nauseam going forward.”
How will this affect US oil supplies?
Trump has said that the deal “MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves”.
Government estimates indicate that proven US oil reserves are declining, standing at approximately 46 billion barrels by the end of 2024.
The US government also operates a Strategic Petroleum Reserve, an emergency supply of oil to help ensure steady domestic supplies.
But the emergency stockpile is shrinking, with only 289.7 million barrels in storage facilities designed to hold up to 714 million barrels. Trump has indicated that Friday’s deal will help restore the US oil reserves, which have hit their lowest levels since 1982.
What led to this moment?
The year 2026 has seen dramatic changes for Venezuela and its relationship with the US.
Since 2013, the South American country had been led by socialist President Nicolas Maduro, whose tenure had been defined by a series of disputed elections and crackdowns on political dissent.
Trump and Maduro had repeatedly clashed, with Trump accusing the Venezuelan leader of sending drug-traffickers into the US, and Maduro accusing Trump of foreign interference in domestic politics.
Their conflict came to a head on January 3. For weeks, US military vessels had been amassing off the shore of Venezuela, and during the early morning hours, Trump authorised an operation to abduct and imprison the Venezuelan leader.
Maduro now awaits trial on drug- and weapons-related charges in New York.
In the aftermath of the attack, Trump backed Maduro’s former vice president, Rodriguez, to lead the government in Caracas. She was sworn in shortly afterwards.
The Trump administration also announced that Washington would take control of Venezuela’s oil exports “indefinitely”.
Critics have pointed out that the Trump administration has pressured Rodriguez to comply with its demands. “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” Trump told The Atlantic magazine in January.
What are Trump’s claims to Venezuela’s oil?
Experts have denounced US intervention in Venezuela as illegal under international law.
But the Trump administration has made the claim to Venezuelan oil resources a key pillar in its involvement in the South American country.
In the lead-up to the January 3 attack, Trump and his allies advanced an argument that Venezuela’s oil supplies belonged to the US, due to a history of early fuel exploration in the country.
They also denounced the Venezuelan government’s efforts to expropriate oil resources from private companies, as part of an effort to nationalise the fossil fuel industry.
In December, Trump announced a blockade around Venezuela to prevent the sale of oil, its largest export. As justification, he accused Venezuela of having “stolen oil fields” from the US.
His adviser, Stephen Miller, separately called the nationalisation of Venezuela’s oil industry “the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property”.
International law, however, gives countries “permanent sovereignty” over their resources, to protect them from unwanted foreign exploitation.
Why announce a deal now?
Friday marked the six-month anniversary of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Once the war began on February 28, Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic. Nearly one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supply passed freely through the strait before the war.
The shutdown has resulted in a spike in global oil prices, including in the US, where voters will head to the polls in November for midterm elections.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) announced this week that it expects this month to be the most expensive August on record for petrol prices, with US consumers paying an average of more than $4 a gallon (3.8 litres).
The dispute over the strategic waterway is ongoing, as is the war itself. Ongoing military actions have also strained US oil supplies.
How is the Trump administration framing the new oil deal?
Trump has repeatedly held up Venezuela, under Rodriguez’s leadership, as a model for how it would like to deal with foreign adversaries like Iran.
He has also touted Washington’s control over Venezuelan oil supplies as a boon for the US economy during the midterm election period.
“We’re doing great in Venezuela. We’re taking a lot of oil from Venezuela, and we’re getting along great with them,” Trump told supporters at a rally in Las Vegas this month.
He then claimed to have “paid for the war” against Venezuela “with what we’ve taken out” from the country.
“That’s the old-fashioned way, right? The old-fashioned way,” Trump told the crowd. “To the victor belong the spoils, right?”
In announcing Friday’s deal, Trump pledged that the resulting increase in the US oil supply “will substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans”. The cost of living is expected to be a key issue in this year’s midterm races.
Separately, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a foreign policy hawk, framed the oil deal as a victory for Trump’s America First platform.
“It demonstrates how President Trump’s bold foreign policy is driving America First wins: securing stable reserves and low-cost oil in our Hemisphere and lowering gas prices here at home,” Rubio wrote.
He also asserted the deal would be mutually beneficial to Venezuela. The agreement, he said, will increase the private investment needed for “the reconstruction of Venezuela’s economy”.
How has Delcy Rodriguez responded to the deal?
Rodriguez has likewise presented the deal as a win for her administration.
In a message on the social media platform Telegram, she called the agreement “historic” and said that it would have “a significant impact on our nation’s revival”.
“It will facilitate a significant flow of investment aimed at the recovery and reconstruction of strategic infrastructure for the development of our hydrocarbons industry,” Rodriguez wrote.
Venezuela has long struggled with an economic crisis that has caused shortages of basic supplies and spiralling inflation. Nearly 8 million Venezuelans have left the country since 2014 due to political repression and economic concerns.
Critics have pointed to government corruption and mismanagement of state industries, including the oil and mining sectors, as one of the reasons for the economic decline. Another commonly cited reason is the impact of heavy US sanctions on the Venezuelan economy.
Since taking office as interim president, however, Rodriguez has led a campaign to increase private investment in Venezuela’s industries, at the behest of the Trump administration.
Her government has estimated that Friday’s deal will net $209bn in taxes for Venezuela, plus $100bn in investments.
How long will the deal last?
Media reports indicate that the Rodriguez government has given the Trump administration the right to use the oil reserves for 100 years.
What are the criticisms?
Washington has a long record of intervention in Latin America, and Trump has sought to assert US dominance over the Western Hemisphere as part of a policy he calls the “Donroe Doctrine”.
Critics have depicted Friday’s arrangement as a bid to seize Venezuela’s resources, akin to what Western powers did during colonial times.
Shortly before the deal was announced, energy analyst Gregory Brew likened reports of the impending agreement to oil concessions sought by the British Empire in the early 20th century.
“Such a thing is without precedent,” Brew wrote on social media. “The closest thing would be BP [British Petroleum] (back when it was majority owned by the UK govt) claiming ownership of Iraqi and Iranian oil reserves pre-WWII.”
Trump himself has embraced the colonial-era slogan “Manifest Destiny”, as part of his plan for a “growing nation” that “increases our wealth” and “expands our territory”.
Could the Venezuela model be applied elsewhere?
Trump has floated the possibility of claiming oil reserves in other parts of the world, too.
In 2011, long before he made his first successful bid for public office, Trump suggested that the US should use its military power to extract oil from other countries.
“I would take the oil,” Trump said of the US military intervention in Libya. That same year, he repeated the remark in reference to the US occupation of Iraq.
During his second term as president, Trump has voiced similar intentions towards Iran. In April, he posted on social media, “With a little more time, we can easily OPEN THE HORMUZ STRAIT, TAKE THE OIL, & MAKE A FORTUNE.” He has also proposed making the Strait of Hormuz a US territory.

Iceland votes on its future in knife-edge EU referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
22:26:49 UTC
07:26:49 KST

Iceland votes on its future in knife-edge EU referendum
Icelanders have turned out in unusually large numbers to decide whether to reopen accession talks with the European Union, with the founding NATO member split almost exactly down the middle over its future relationship with Brussels.
Polling stations closed at 10 PM local time on Saturday, with the latest partial results showing “no” narrowly ahead after an exceptionally tight count. With around 152,000 votes counted, the nationwide tally stood at 50.1% for “no” and 49.9% for “yes,” as election officials warned that a reliable final result might not emerge until later on Sunday.
Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, who backed reopening negotiations, said she hoped the extraordinarily close contest would neither divide the country nor leave lasting wounds.
“The main thing is that we remain united ... whether the result is yes or no,” she said.
Interest in the referendum has been exceptionally high. More than 63,000 people – close to a quarter of the electorate – had already cast advance ballots by Friday night. Turnout on election day was also running ahead of the 2024 parliamentary election in parts of Reykjavík.
The ballot asks voters a single question: “Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?”
A “yes” would not automatically make Iceland an EU member. It would restart negotiations abandoned more than a decade ago, with any eventual membership agreement expected to be put to voters in a second referendum. The vote itself is legally advisory, although Frostadottir has pledged to respect the result.
The campaign went down to the wire. A final Maskína survey put the “yes” camp at 50.4% and “no” at 49.6%, while a Gallup poll shortly beforehand showed essentially the reverse picture, with opponents narrowly ahead.
Iceland first applied to join the EU in 2009 after its devastating banking collapse and began negotiations the following year. The process was suspended after a change of government in 2013 and effectively abandoned in 2015 as the economy recovered and enthusiasm for surrendering powers to Brussels faded.
Supporters of restarting the talks have argued that closer EU integration could bring greater economic and currency stability and give the country of fewer than 400,000 people more influence over rules it already adopts through the European Economic Area. The country is also part of the Schengen zone and deeply integrated into European markets.
Opponents have focused heavily on sovereignty, agriculture and, above all, Iceland’s fishing grounds, warning that eventual membership could subject the strategically vital industry to the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy.
The geopolitical argument has also loomed unusually large. Frostadottir’s allies have portrayed the EU as additional protection in an increasingly unstable world, particularly after US President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to take control of neighboring Greenland.
Unease was further fueled in January when Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Iceland, Billy Long, joked that the country itself could become the “52nd state” of the US, with him serving as governor.
Euroskeptics, meanwhile, have argued that Brussels itself is becoming increasingly militarized and confrontational. Iceland is already a founding NATO member and maintains extensive military ties with Washington.

'Slippages reveal design flaw on Kanpur-Lucknow e-way'

Slippages on Kanpur-Lucknow Expressway point to design issue, not construction defect; stretches will need bottom-up rebuild. (AI-generated image)
NEW DELHI: Slippages on sections of the Kanpur-Lucknow Expressway within days of its inauguration point to a design issue, not a construction defect, a top govt official has said, adding that simple patchwork repairs will not solve the problem. "The affected stretches will have to be rebuilt bottom up. We need to ensure there is no laxity at the designing stage of projects. This is a major concern for us, especially since the expressway has been executed under Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM)," the official said.
The Centre is awaiting the final report of an expert who conducted a detailed investigation into the slippages. "There was no deficiency in the thickness of the road or in the pavement layers beneath it," the official added. In HAM projects, the private developer is responsible for the operation and maintenance of the project through the entire concession period, which, typically, is 15 years.A preliminary investigation by an IIT Kharagpur professor had identified the use of weak, highly plastic soil beneath parts of the expressway as one of the main reasons for the slippages. Plastic soil loses strength when wet and can get deformed under load. The preliminary report shows poor drainage as a contributing factor.

Chinese FM holds phone talks with Nepali counterpart
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:18:43 CST
07:18:43 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's package of assistance to Nepal is being implemented, including emergency cash assistance and humanitarian aid, with some relief supplies set to arrive in Kathmandu soon, said Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi during his phone conversation with Nepali Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal on Saturday.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said that a severe mudslide disaster, triggered by a sudden glacier collapse in Nepal's border area, has caused significant casualties and left people missing on both sides. It has been the most serious cross-border disaster between the two countries in recent years, and the relief efforts are unprecedentedly complex and arduous.
He said that China attaches great importance to the situation. Chinese President Xi Jinping immediately issued important instructions, setting clear requirements for rescue and emergency response work. Chinese Premier Li Qiang traveled to the disaster-hit area to guide the work on the ground.
Wang said that while urgently carrying out rescue and relief efforts on its own side, China extended a helping hand at the earliest opportunity and supported Nepal in its emergency disaster relief efforts.
Xi has sent a condolence message to Nepali President Ram Chandra Poudel, and Li has expressed condolences to Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah, Wang noted.
China will provide emergency aid to the disaster-hit area in Nepal and carry out international rescue cooperation, according to a meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee. This is an important political decision made by China and demonstrates China's friendship with Nepal, he said.
Wang said that two teams of Chinese tunnel rescue experts had rushed to the disaster-stricken area and Kathmandu to offer assistance, and China has shared with Nepal important information such as images, satellite and hydrological data of the disaster-stricken area, including early warning information of the upstream barrier lake.
He said that for Nepalese citizens stranded on the Chinese side, China has made proper arrangements and will assist them in returning to Nepal as soon as possible, expressing his gratitude and hope that Nepal will continue to assist and transfer Chinese citizens in Nepal.
Wang said that China and Nepal are a community linked by mountains and rivers and sharing a common destiny. In the face of the disaster, the two countries should stand together firmly, join hands to deal with it and overcome the difficulties together, and interpret the traditional friendship across the Himalayas with concrete actions.
Shisir conveyed condolences from Nepali leaders to the Chinese government and people and to the families of the victims, and expressed sincere gratitude for China's emergency humanitarian assistance.
He said that although both Nepal and China had been hit by the disaster, China had overcome its own difficulties to extend condolences and provide assistance to Nepal at the earliest opportunity, fully demonstrating the high level of Nepal-China relations.
The Nepali side once again expressed its gratitude to China and will continue to work closely with China to make every effort to rescue Chinese nationals who remain stranded or unaccounted for, while jointly working to locate and rescue missing foreign nationals, he said.
Nepal stands ready to strengthen cooperation with China in areas such as post-disaster reconstruction, disaster prevention and mitigation, and climate change response, and to further advance the strategic partnership of cooperation between the two countries, he said. ■

People participate in the Bubble Run in Pomona, Los Angeles County, California, the United States, Aug. 29, 2026. More than 10,000 people took part in the annual Bubble Run on Saturday at the Pomona Fairplex in Pomona, east of Los Angeles, enjoying a day of running, colorful bubbles and family fun. (Photo by Zeng Hui/Xinhua)
LOS ANGELES, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- More than 10,000 people took part in the annual Bubble Run on Saturday at the Pomona Fairplex in Pomona, east of Los Angeles, enjoying a day of running, colorful bubbles and family fun.
The Bubble Run is a family-friendly, non-competitive 5-km event featuring participants running and walking through clouds of colorful bubbles.
Held in cities across the United States each year, the event brings together runners, walkers, children and grandparents for a fun-filled day.
According to the organizer, more than 1 million people have participated in the event so far, which has been held in more than 80 cities across the United States. ■

====================================================================================================

Brain network rhythms reveal why some people are better at keeping their focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
22:00:44 UTC
07:00:44 KST

A person’s ability to maintain focus and resist distractions is embedded in the stable, large-scale dynamic rhythms of their brain. A new study published in PNAS reveals that individuals with better attention control naturally coordinate activity across major brain networks more effectively, both while resting and when cognitive demands rise.
Attention control is the cognitive ability to concentrate on relevant information while filtering out distractions. Psychologists often distinguish between momentary fluctuations in focus, like getting distracted because you are tired, and a person’s baseline capacity to pay attention over time. As a stable characteristic, this baseline capacity reliably predicts academic performance, career success, and general physical health.
Despite its importance, the neurological foundation of this enduring mental trait has remained somewhat elusive. Past neuroimaging research has mostly focused on how the average brain responds to momentary tasks or examined resting brains in isolation. Few researchers have looked at how stable, individual differences in attention control dictate the way brain networks shift their behavior from a state of rest to a state of high cognitive demand.
Psychologists Dolly T. Seeburger and Randall W. Engle from the Georgia Institute of Technology led a team to investigate this gap. They suspected that attention control relies on the frontoparietal control network, a distributed brain system that acts like a central executive. This network spans regions in the prefrontal and parietal cortices, managing goals by communicating with other systems in the brain.
Specifically, the control network frequently interacts with the default mode network, which handles internally directed thoughts like daydreaming, and the dorsal attention network, which directs focus toward the outside world. The researchers hypothesized that people with strong attention control are simply better at managing these neural connections as their environment demands more mental effort.
To test this, the research team recruited nearly 200 adults for a multi-day experiment. During the first two sessions, participants completed a battery of computerized behavioral tests. These tests measured their baseline attention control, their working memory capacity, and their general problem solving skills, known as fluid intelligence.
Because these three cognitive abilities are highly correlated, the researchers used statistical modeling to isolate attention control. This mathematical step ensured that any brain activity they observed later was uniquely associated with the ability to focus, rather than general intelligence or memory limits.
During a third session, participants underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging. Researchers recorded their brain activity under three different conditions. First, participants lay awake with their eyes open for ten minutes to establish a resting baseline.
Next, they completed a low-load memory task that required them to press a button when a shape on the screen matched the one shown immediately before it. Finally, participants completed a high-load memory task. In this difficult condition, they had to remember if a shape matched the one shown three steps back in the sequence, requiring continuous updating of their mental workspace while resisting distractions.
To analyze the brain scans, the researchers looked for quasi-periodic patterns. These are slow, rhythmic waves of brain activity that repeat over time. By tracking these low-frequency signals, the team could observe how different brain networks synchronized or decoupled as the participants moved from resting to the easy task and then to the hard task.
The analysis revealed distinct differences between individuals based on their attention control abilities. For the network associated with internal thought, people with lower attention control showed a strong positive connection with the manager network while at rest. This connection dropped abruptly as soon as they started the easy task.
In contrast, highly attentive people showed a different rhythm. Their connection between the manager network and the internal thought network changed very little between rest and the easy task. When the hard task began, however, their brains strongly segregated the two networks, suggesting they successfully pushed away internal distractions only when maximum focus was required.
A similar pattern emerged for the external attention network. People with lower attention control showed their largest shift in connectivity when moving from rest to the easy task. Those with higher attention control experienced their biggest boost in connectivity under the highest cognitive load, recruiting their goal-directed attention systems exactly when the difficulty peaked.
The researchers also tracked the ventral attention network, which acts as an alert system for unexpected or important events. At rest, highly attentive individuals exhibited a positive connection between the central manager and this alert network. As cognitive load increased, this connection gradually faded.
Individuals with lower attention control showed a much more erratic pattern in this alert system. Their brain activity shifted from negative coupling at rest to positive coupling under low load, and back to negative under high load.
The researchers also examined the locus coeruleus, a small structure in the brainstem that produces norepinephrine. This chemical messenger regulates physical arousal and helps coordinate global brain states. Traditionally linked to basic alertness, the locus coeruleus is increasingly recognized for its role in complex cognition.
During the most difficult memory task, highly attentive individuals showed positive synchronization between the brain’s control manager and the locus coeruleus. Conversely, people with low attention control showed a negative correlation between these regions during the hard task. This suggests that people with lower focus may have reduced their mental effort, or partially disengaged, when the demands exceeded their capacity.
While the results provide a deep look at the physical nature of attention, the study has several limitations. The locus coeruleus is tiny and varies physically from person to person. Standard brain imaging techniques are somewhat imprecise when measuring such small structures, meaning specialized scans could provide greater accuracy in the future.
Additionally, the low-load and high-load memory tasks may not simply represent different difficulties of the same mental process. Participants often adopt entirely different mental strategies to handle the harder memory sequences, which could influence the observed brain rhythms in ways unrelated to pure attention.
Because the study relies on observational data, the results cannot establish that these brain network patterns directly generate attention control. Interventions using noninvasive brain stimulation could help determine if altering these neural pathways actively changes a person’s ability to focus.
The study, “Attention control ability is associated with frontoparietal control network interactions,” was authored by Dolly T. Seeburger, Jason S. Tsukahara, Nan Xu, Vishwadeep Ahluwalia, Shella D. Keilholz, and Randall W. Engle.

What we thought was certainly sweet in taste might begin to seem sour before seeming sweet again. What once appeared square might now appear oblong or round, even though our perspective has not changed. What was once loneliness might suddenly become joyful solitude before transforming back into loneliness.
It is not necessarily the case that our experiences are changing in these situations, but only that the applicable category in language seems to shift and we are inclined to describe the experience differently. When this happens we can feel frustration at our inability to accurately translate our perceptions into words.
But all that is happening is that we are realizing something about the nature of language. We are learning that its categories are not as clear or distinct as they might seem. Using language is always messy, with regular overlap in the meanings of words, which means our attempts at description are always only attempts.

Feature: Families search for missing loved ones as conflict shatters Sudan, South Sudan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:31:48 CST
06:31:48 KST

JUBA, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Thousands of families across Sudan and South Sudan remain trapped in the anguish of searching for loved ones who disappeared amid years of conflict.
Among them is Mary Justine, a 48-year-old resident of Juba's Limon Gaba suburb, who was separated from her 16-year-old son during an outbreak of violence in South Sudan in 2016. A decade later, she struggles to come to terms with his absence.
"That experience was extremely painful for our family. Losing a child without knowing what happened to him leaves a wound that is difficult to describe. The memories remain with you, and the tears continue to come whenever you remember those difficult days," Justine told Xinhua on Friday.
She is now a member of the Association of Families of Missing Persons, a support network connecting relatives who share the hope of reuniting with missing family members.
With assistance from two organizations -- the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the South Sudan Red Cross -- the association has helped members turn shared grief into lasting bonds of mutual support.
"The suffering has brought us closer together. We now understand that despite our different backgrounds, we share the same pain and the same hope for peace. We must support one another and refuse to remain silent about the suffering caused by conflict," Justine said.
Similarly, 52-year-old Sudanese refugee Sadia Habib is struggling to trace her daughter and son, who vanished after conflict erupted in Khartoum in April 2023.
"The war has caused tremendous suffering for my family. I lost my daughter and her children, and I also lost my son during the conflict," she said.
"We have not stopped looking for them. The South Sudan Red Cross has continued searching and following up on the case. I was told that if they find any information, they will inform us and help us reunite with our loved ones," Habib added.
In a rare moment of relief, 54-year-old Sudanese national Mahmoud Al-Tijani Ahmed Bashir was recently reunited with the last of his six children, who went missing during South Sudan's 2016 conflict.
Hailing from Sudan's Blue Nile State, Bashir welcomed his son home after the ICRC successfully traced him to neighboring Uganda.
"We did not know where he was for a long time. We continued searching and remained hopeful. When we received information that he might be in Uganda, we contacted ICRC and provided the information necessary to help trace him," he said.
Daniel Bunnskog, head of delegation for the ICRC in South Sudan, noted that the organization helped trace and reunite 188 missing persons with their families out of more than 6,200 open cases between January and June.
"In the first half of the year, something positive that we want to share is that 188 cases of missing persons were clarified, which shows that there is a possibility to find answers. We hope that this positive resolution will continue," Bunnskog said.
He said the ICRC has worked closely with the South Sudanese Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management to draft a missing persons bill, describing it as a crucial piece of legislation that will strengthen the capacity and competence of authorities tasked with searching for missing individuals. ■

China Focus: How adjacent Hengqin island facilitates Macao's diversified development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:31:35 CST
06:31:35 KST

GUANGZHOU, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- A roughly 106-square-kilometer island linking Macao with Guangdong in south China, Hengqin has emerged as a key platform for Macao's efforts to diversify its economy, a central policy objective of the special administrative region government.
The Chinese government first decided to develop the island in 2009. Efforts accelerated in September 2021, when it released an overall plan to construct the Guangdong-Macao In-Depth Cooperation Zone in Hengqin. In the five years since, the boundary between Hengqin and Macao has significantly reduced, while enterprises and research institutions have been quickly established across the island.
Hengqin is about three times the size of Macao, which means it offers the space that Macao needs to develop diverse industries, specifically those that involve laboratory experiments and mass production.
"Macao needs technological innovation as a new engine for appropriately diversified economic development, while Hengqin provides an unprecedented platform for commercializing scientific achievements," said Lee Shuit-tong, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, who led the establishment of the Macao Institute of Materials Science and Engineering in Hengqin in 2021.
The institute, under the Macau University of Science and Technology, has since served as a new platform for advancing cross-disciplinary innovation initiatives and turning research findings into products, making breakthroughs in sectors such as OLED-based technologies and devices.
Lee, who also serves as the institute director, said they have operated under the model of performing research in Macao and carrying out commercialization in Hengqin. "We need to leverage the unique advantages of Macao and Hengqin to forge our own path in scientific and technological innovation," he said.
"Working complementarily, Macao can focus on basic research and serve as an international hub, while Hengqin can facilitate industrial application and commercialization," said Cheong Hou Iam, founder of Guangdong True Health Medical Technology Development Co., Ltd.
Founded in 2018 by Cheong, a Macao resident, True Health has settled its headquarters in Hengqin, with a production base in Guangdong's Zhuhai. The company specializes in intelligent medical devices for clinical tumor treatment. Its puncture-surgery navigation and positioning system can help doctors reach lesions more precisely in complex cases. It has been used in more than 100 Chinese hospitals and assisted in over 7,200 operations.
In late June, True Health was listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange, becoming the first Hengqin-based listed company.
Cheong stressed that while playing its role in technological research and development, Macao also benefits from commercialization of the research outcomes through revenue, public access to the new products, and potential expansion of local employment. "This is a core path toward appropriately diversified economic development," she said.
As of June 2, the number of Macao-funded enterprises operating in Hengqin had exceeded 8,000, up 72.6 percent from the establishment of the cooperation zone in 2021, accounting for 15.9 percent of all enterprises in the zone.
For Lei Zhen, founder of Nanometals Technology, which settled itself on the island in 2021, Hengqin's appeal lies in its ability to draw on resources from both sides.
"Companies can rely on Guangdong's well-developed supply and industrial chains, while also making use of Macao's international platform, abundant capital, and links to overseas talent and global markets," said Lei, a Macao resident.
Nanometals develops flexible transparent conductive materials, which can be used in the production of a wide range of display screens. It has become a first-tier supplier to several leading Chinese home-appliance companies.
Lei noted that in Hengqin, the company can more conveniently source professionals from the Chinese mainland, while leveraging Macao's international advantages to attract overseas talent.
With favorable customs policies reducing cumbersome border-crossing procedures previously faced by scientists traveling between the two sides, Hengqin can serve as a meeting point for the mainland and overseas researchers, he said.
At the same time, Macao universities and research institutions are also extending their presence in Hengqin, building up educational facilities and experimental laboratories.
"People are increasingly realizing that universities can serve as an important driving force for Macao's economic diversification," said Chen Guokai, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Macau and executive vice president of the University of Macau Advanced Research Institute in Hengqin.
Dedicated to technological innovation and technology transfer, the Advanced Research Institute focuses its core operations on key areas such as microelectronics and integrated circuits, traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), and advanced materials.
Chen said when the institute began construction several years ago, a one-way trip from Macao to Hengqin, including border clearance, took about one and a half hours, and now it takes less than 30 minutes.
"Teachers can finish their classes in Macao and then come here to meet representatives of mainland TCM companies in the laboratory to discuss the commercialization of research outcomes," he said.
With more efficient cross-boundary flows of people and other resources, cooperation among industry, universities and research institutions in Hengqin and Macao will have broader room to grow, he added.
Convenient travel has also underpinned the development of the Macao-Hengqin International Education (University) Town, a project included in the national 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) and the third Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Macao Special Administrative Region that was released last week.
The University Town currently hosts three public institutions -- the University of Macau, Macao Polytechnic University and the Macao University of Tourism. Its first-phase campus, covering 50,000 square meters, has recently begun operation with the first batch of more than 1,400 students starting their new semester.
Kong Chi Meng, director of Macao's Education and Youth Development Bureau, said the University Town will later add faculties of medicine, design, engineering and information science, and other disciplines in science, engineering, interdisciplinary and emerging fields.
"This will support both Macao's economic diversification and the country's need for talent in building national strength in science and technology," Kong said.
Liao Jianhao, a doctoral student at the Macao University of Tourism who has just started the new school year at the University Town, said the campus offers both an internationalized education system and a comfortable living environment.
Liao said that after graduation, he hopes to stay and work in Hengqin. "Boosted by both the 15th Five-Year Plan and Macao's third Five-Year Plan, Hengqin is bound to embrace better development," he said. ■

2026-08-30

06:31:24 KST

HARARE, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Zimbabwe's drive toward electric mobility is gaining momentum, with growing interest in electric vehicles (EVs) signaling a shift toward more sustainable transport systems, as showcased at the Zimbabwe Agricultural Show.
At the six-day show, which ended Saturday in Zimbabwe's capital, Harare, the Central Mechanical Equipment Department (CMED), a state enterprise providing transport and logistics services to both the public and private sectors, drew public attention by displaying a range of EVs, including Chinese models such as the Nio Firefly, Geely Riddara, and King Long electric commercial vehicles.
Through these demonstrations, the enterprise aims to introduce green technologies, build public confidence, and lay the groundwork for a national e-mobility ecosystem.
"Our motivation is not simply to introduce electric vehicles but to demonstrate that sustainable mobility can work in Zimbabwe. We want to create awareness, give Zimbabweans an opportunity to experience electric vehicles, and ultimately contribute to the development of an e-mobility ecosystem," Tarisai Muzorori, CMED public relations officer, told Xinhua.
Recognizing that EVs remain a relatively new concept in the country, CMED is tailoring its portfolio to meet sector-specific needs while addressing consumer hesitation.
"Our approach is to introduce electric vehicles based on the needs of different sectors rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all approach. Currently, our portfolio includes passenger vehicles, and we are also looking at opportunities around electric buses and other commercial vehicles," Muzorori said.
She noted that as awareness grows, lower operating costs and integration with renewable energy are emerging as key drivers of interest, adding that hurdles to EV adoption include consumer concerns over driving range, battery life, charging time, and resale value.
Harare resident Prestige Nota echoed these concerns, noting that establishing charging infrastructure and local service centers is vital to building market trust.
"We have seen Chinese brands such as BYD opening showrooms and offering support services in Zimbabwe. If people can be assured of after-sales services, maybe confidence in electric vehicles will increase with time," Nota said.
To encourage adoption, the Zimbabwean government reduced customs duty on EVs from 40 percent to 25 percent in 2025, while providing duty rebates on solar equipment and charging infrastructure.
The green transition is also urging auto technicians to adapt. Farirai Majaya, a local auto technician, noted that while some traditional mechanics are hesitant to embrace new systems due to the current small market size, upskilling is essential.
"Those professionals who are already in the industry need to upgrade their skills," Majaya said, emphasizing that resisting the shift to electric mobility means ignoring an inevitable global future. ■

ALGIERS, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Algerian communities have been rallying to support families affected by devastating wildfires in the country's northeast, with volunteers organizing donation drives and convoys carrying essential supplies from across the country to the hardest-hit areas.

Volunteers and local associations have set up collection points to gather drinking water, food, infant formula, baby diapers, clothing, blankets, and other necessities for displaced families.

The campaign also extended to the Algerian diaspora, with fundraising efforts organized abroad.
Meanwhile, authorities continue efforts to contain the remaining fires and assess the damage.
The Civil Protection Authority said in the latest statement on Saturday that 123 fires were recorded between Aug. 28 and 29 as of 7 a.m. local time (0600 GMT), of which 118 had been extinguished while five remained active.
Two of the ongoing fires were in Jijel, two in Setif and one in Tebessa, according to the statement.
In Jijel, crews continued battling five ongoing fires and hotspots, supported by two AT-802 firefighting aircraft, a Mi-26 heavy transport helicopter, and an amphibious water-bomber jet BE-200.
Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Jijel on Friday, inspecting the affected areas by helicopter and meeting with residents.
Ghrieb reiterated the state's commitment to supporting those affected and attended a collective funeral for 39 people in the town of Djemaa Beni Habibi, as search operations continued for the missing, according to local reports.
The prime minister also visited the Dr. Said Chibane Major Burns Hospital in Zeralda, where injured people from the affected areas were receiving medical treatment. He said that President Abdelmadjid Tebboune had ordered full medical mobilization for the injured.
The official death toll remains at 12, as announced by Interior Minister Said Sayoud on Wednesday evening, with no updated nationwide figure released since.
The fires come amid a severe heat wave affecting the North African country. The meteorological service warned that temperatures could hit 49 degrees Celsius in some areas this week.
According to Civil Protection data, around 4,000 fires were recorded from May 1 to July 20, a sharp rise of almost 167 percent from the 1,501 recorded during the same period last year. ■

China Focus: Ancient Silk Road passage in northwest China expands global ties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:30:55 CST
06:30:55 KST

LANZHOU, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Alejandro Delgado, Deputy Army Attache of the Peruvian Embassy in China, beamed at a cultural event in Beijing on Thursday as he displayed a bookmark featuring the Chinese calligraphy characters "Jixiang," a phrase that means "good fortune."
"I love the Chinese language," Delgado said.
He was among more than 200 guests from 42 countries and international organizations at the special promotion event on the Hexi Corridor. Stretching over a thousand kilometers, the Hexi Corridor served as a key artery on the ancient Silk Road more than 2,000 years ago, connecting China to Central Asia, West Asia and Europe, thereby facilitating the exchange of diverse civilizations.
Five cities along the Hexi Corridor, namely Wuwei, Jinchang, Zhangye, Jiuquan and Jiayuguan in northwest China's Gansu Province, promoted their cultural, tourism and industrial resources at the event. The event also showcased intangible cultural heritage items, cultural and creative products, and local specialties.
"This kind of activity is great for promotion. It helps people see China's diverse products and understand the country from within," Delgado said.
The roadshow has previously traveled to Shanghai and other cities. This year, representatives from the corridor cities converged on Beijing to showcase their history, culture, landscapes and development opportunities to a broader global audience.
"It makes me want to learn more about the province," said Lebanese ambassador to China Milad Raad, who has never visited Gansu.
"Both personally and in my country, we really have an interest in promoting culture. I'm truly impressed by the cultural environment here in China," he added.
Manuel Carvalho, Portuguese ambassador to China, has never been to Gansu either, but he has long known about Dunhuang, home to the Mogao Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site dating back to the 4th century.
In April, he took part in the "Global Linking of Dunhuang Culture" event, which linked Dunhuang and Lanzhou in Gansu, Beijing, and Portugal's Aveiro in a hybrid online-offline format. Since 2022, the series has traveled to countries including Armenia, Russia, Germany, Japan and the United States.
"The thing that interested me first was the Mogao Caves," Carvalho said. "But then I saw so much more, from the landscapes to the cities, from the fields to the mountains, and the many facets of Chinese culture. You are sharing with the world the beauty that you have."
As outlined in China's latest Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), which calls for expanding high-level opening-up, cities along the Hexi Corridor are now taking the initiative to go global, strengthening their ties with the world through trade, economic cooperation and people-to-people exchanges.
Jiuquan, at the western end of the Hexi Corridor, enjoys abundant sunlight and sharp day-night temperature swings, making it a major seed production base serving overseas markets.
At a seed company's research center in Jiuquan, staff are cultivating new varieties of fruits and vegetables using molecular breeding techniques. "We have developed hundreds of new vegetable varieties, which are sold both on the domestic market and abroad," said Ta Wenshan, head of the company.
Data from Lanzhou Customs showed that Gansu exported 2,500.2 tonnes of seeds in the first half of this year, up 23.5 percent year on year, with a total export value of 300 million yuan (about 44.24 million U.S. dollars). The products were sold to 160 countries and regions worldwide.
Greater openness is also bringing more two-way exchanges. In 2025, Gansu recorded 393,900 inbound tourist visits, a 60.8 percent year-on-year increase.
As more overseas tourists arrive, Gansu is standardizing multilingual signs at scenic spots to improve the travel experience. "We welcome more international visitors to Gansu and the Hexi Corridor to discover Silk Road history and the desert scenery, strengthening people-to-people ties through cultural exchanges," said Lyu Xinglai, an official with the Gansu provincial department of culture and tourism.
"The promotion event serves as an important bridge, connecting Gansu with the world and creating reliable platforms for international exchanges and cooperation," Bulgarian ambassador to China Andrey Tehov said.
He added that Bulgaria looks forward to deepening practical cooperation with Gansu in areas such as new energy, modern agriculture, trade and investment, and cultural tourism, sectors where the Hexi Corridor is now showing new development potential. ■

August rainfall fails to reduce India's monsoon deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
21:27:29 UTC
06:27:29 KST

Erratic distribution leads to 2% dip in acreage of kharif crops
NEW DELHI: Better-than-expected rainfall in many parts of the country in August has failed to reduce India's cumulative monsoon rainfall deficit. While the country's cumulative rainfall deficit (since June 1) was 13% as of July 31, it touched nearly 14% a month later due to a huge shortfall in Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and some northeastern states.This deficit led to an acreage gap in the sowing of kharif (summer-sown) crops, with paddy, the major seasonal crop, reporting a decline of more than 3% compared with the corresponding period last year.Maize that contributes the most as feedstock for ethanol production in the country reported an even bigger decline of more than 4% compared with the corresponding period in 2025. This may eventually create pressure for sugarcane to be used as feedstock for ethanol production.
The acreage of all kharif crops, taken together, was reportedly down nearly 2% as of Friday compared with the corresponding period last year. The acreage deficit was nearly 3% at the end of July.
The acreage could not be increased due to erratic distribution of rainfall in both the key monsoon months of July and Aug.Though many parts of the country defied El Nino-linked predictions and got normal rainfall, 12 states have reported a rain deficit of more than 20% since June 1, with Bihar, Andhra Pradesh and three northeastern states - Meghalaya, Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh - reporting a huge deficit of more than 40% in cumulative (June 1-Aug 29) rainfall.
El Nino is a climatic condition which sees the warming of surface waters of the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. It is associated with weak monsoons and harsher summers in India.Good rains in eastern India during the remaining two days of the month, as predicted by IMD, may slightly reduce the deficit for the region, but it won't help much overall, as the Met department Saturday predicted the continuation of "subdued rainfall activity" over peninsular India during the next week.
Peninsular India has, so far, reported a deficit of more than 23% in cumulative rainfall, leaving Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Kerala largely dry for most of the southwest (summer) monsoon season. Predicting good rains in the east for the next two-three days, IMD said isolated "heavy to very heavy rainfall" is likely over Gangetic West Bengal on Sunday, Jharkhand on Monday and Odisha till Sept 1 due to the "influence of low-pressure area over northwest Bay of Bengal and adjoining West Bengal-north Odisha coasts".
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

Germany has postponed indefinitely the procurement of up to 75 AGM-158B/B2 JASSM-ER cruise missiles, with a range of approximately 900 km, for F-35A fighter jets. The reason was a restructuring of the Air Force’s priorities following russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, reports Defense Express, writes UNN.
Details
Berlin inquired about the possibility of procuring JASSM-ER missiles as early as 2022, together with the purchase of F-35A Lightning II aircraft. However, the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support confirmed that the missile deal was never implemented.
The agency said that the procurement of JASSM-ER missiles had been "postponed indefinitely in favor of other projects." At the same time, it did not name the specific programs that had been given higher priority.
The war in Ukraine changed the Luftwaffe’s plans
According to Defense Express, the decision to review the procurement is linked to a "sharp change in the geopolitical situation" following the start of russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. This led to a comprehensive restructuring of the capabilities of the German Air Force.
