Tina Arena, the 'worst album ever made', and more music doco highlights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
20:54:14 UTC
05:54:14 KST

From Tina Arena to 'worst band ever' The Shaggs, MIFF's must-see music docos
Settling in for an enlightening documentary with a compelling soundtrack is a unique cinematic delight.
It's the key appeal of the Music On Film program at Melbourne International Film Festival (MIFF).
This year it's included the world premiere of Jebediah: Are We OK?, a candid doco on the Perth alt-rock icons, and a 25th anniversary screening of influential queer classic Hedwig And The Angry Inch with creator John Cameron Mitchell.
Beyond those, here's our take on program highlights and where you might view them beyond MIFF.
Tina Arena: Unravel Me (Dir. Adrian Russell Wills)
Tina Arena's six-decade career is more than deserving of a silver screen examination.
The Australian singer's enduring success marks her as a survivor who has had to "kick against the system time and time again," as manager Michael Parisi notes late in this glossy documentary.
Resilient and resplendent as ever, Arena is still out there doing it at age 58 with the same professional tenacity she did as a prodigious 9-year-old on Young Talent Time.
Arguably its biggest alumna, she dazzled audiences as well as the TV phenomenon's late, legendary creator Johnny Young.
But Filippina Lydia Arena, or "Pina" as her Sicilian-Australian family lovingly call her, initially struggled to shake her girl-next-door image and transition to a solo career. Until, that is, she penned Chains, Sorrento Moon and Wasn't It Good. Hits too good to ignore.
Tina Arena: Unravel Me excels in chronicling this formative period, punctuated with input from the modern-day doyenne, an effortlessly glamorous, eternally impressive vocalist captured in photo shoots and to-camera narration.
A shame then that the film doesn't dig deeper past the curated image, regularly falling back on platitudes and gesturing to profound emotional stakes without really interrogating them.
We're told, rather than truly shown, the challenges of juggling motherhood and pop stardom, or navigating multiple international markets.
Nuance is often skated over in favour of melodrama or simply ticking the next box in Arena's trajectory.
Sometimes this surface-level approach is welcome. Arena's "winning partnership" with former manager, ex-husband, and now convicted rapist Ralph Carr is swiftly moved on from after being introduced to establish his part in shepherding Arena's 1994 commercial breakthrough.
Her best-selling Don't Ask album swept the ARIA Awards and made Arena the first female artist to win Album of the Year. Questioning how so many before her were overlooked, she begins poking at the bars of the gilded pop cage she found herself in.
Unravel Me bills her as a hard-working woman who overcame the fixed odds of a male-dominated industry. Why then is the doco's many talking head interviews commanded by a string of male, pale, stale record execs who dictate her highs and lows.
Several of whom, the film neglects to mention, operated under the toxic regime of disgraced Sony Australia boss Dennis Hadlin.
There's far more gained from the brief times we hear from Arena's peers. Archival footage of her palling about with Celine Dion is a delight, while her 2015 ARIA collaborators The Veronicas and Jessica Mauboy offer praise late in the piece.
Unravel Me falls short of its aim to be the kind of empowering, celebratory expose that made similar features on Celine Dion, Tina Turner and Kylie Minogue so rewarding.
Ultimately, Arena's grand half-century legacy is deserving of a more distinctive film.
Tina Arena: Unravel Me is in cinemas nationwide from August 27.
We Are The Shaggs (Dir. Ken Kwapis)
In 1960s small-town New Hampshire an obsessive father forced teenage sisters Dot, Helen and Betty Wiggins to take up instruments they clearly hadn't mastered.
The result was The Shaggs, the sisters writing bizarre songs that were out of tune and out of time.
The sibling trio became a cult rock music litmus test, variously dubbed as groundbreaking genus and, frankly, "the worst band ever".
Their crude curios 1969 album Philosophy of the World has prompted decades of disdain as well as delighted fascination.
It was hailed by Frank Zappa as "better than The Beatles" but also torn apart by Rolling Stone as "the worst album ever recorded".
Both extremes are valid in Ken Kwapis's ardent, highly entertaining doco We Are The Shaggs, which begins shrewdly with a montage of regular folks reacting to The Shaggs.
Their alien, amateurish songs provoke a mixture of laughter, pain, confusion, and the big question: "Is it music?"
A succession of experts and fans puzzle that out through various lenses. Are The Shaggs punk? Riot grrrl trailblazers? Accidental pioneers of DIY outsider music?
Then there's two absorbing tribute acts: a Brooklyn band recreating every bizarre tuning, phrasing and timing as gospel and violin duo String Noise, who re-arrange The Shaggs as a cerebral exercise.
Some cases are more convincing than others, but the film never sets a judgemental agenda, entertaining with animated sequences and interviews with surviving band members Dot and Betty.
They're charmingly down-to-earth and just as baffled as anyone by a cult legacy that includes being championed by Kurt Cobain and made the subject of a New Yorker profile and even an off-Broadway play.
The Shaggs songbook — odes to pets, fantasies about fast cars, desires for romance and rebellion — possesses an untarnished naivety, the product of being cloistered by their suffocatingly strict father, Austin Wiggin.
Kwapis triumphs in his mission to humanise the sisters, offering a perfect introduction to their extraordinary story in a dignifying portrait. We Are The Shaggs also poses bigger questions about art and how our perceptions can be shaped or subverted, even inadvertently.
To that end, legendary Prince engineer and academic Susan Rogers provides the most salient point: who gets to decide what is good and bad?
She compares The Shaggs to Picasso's cubist paintings, questions if they'd face the same ridicule were they brothers, and marvels at how they "invented their own music language and stuck to those rules, whatever they are" in unruly songs that disguise "pure universal truths … that's easier said than done".
We Are The Shaggs screens as part of the Sydney Underground Film Festival on September 12 and 13.
Broken English (Dir. Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard)
Named after Marianne Faithfull's 1979 comeback album, Broken English frames the British musician and screen star's life through the fictional Ministry of Not Forgetting, headed by a besuited Tilda Swinton and charged to "recalibrate her legacy".
This elaborate conceit shouldn't be a surprise coming from Iain Forstyth and Jane Pollard, the directing team behind the equally unorthodox Nick Cave doco 20,000 Days on Earth.
It certainly sets Broken English apart from the pack. But the framing device is also obtuse, sometimes distracting and, worse, at odds with a woman who regularly cut through bullshit.
Thrust into the industry at age 17, Faithfull was initially sold as an "angel-blonde" pop and folk chanteuse. She soon became an icon of swinging 60s London and a punching bag for the stuffy British press.
Broken English succeeds in reversing her dismissal as merely Mick Jagger's muse and girlfriend, damning her tabloid portrayal as a Rolling Stones groupie, demonised as the "nude girl" in a police raid on Keith Richards's estate.
An indomitable creative who overcame addiction, miscarriage, breast cancer, and a COVID-induced coma, Faithfull proved her growing artistry across multiple mediums. She was also a consistent target for merciless scrutiny and misogyny.
One powerful montage shows a series of sexist interviewers delightfully grilling her on celebrity romances and drug use.
Watching back at the sequence she remarks: "Despite all these stupid people and their stupid questions, I've actually had rather a lovely life, so f**k 'em!"
The film's beating heart is seeing the late-70s Faithfull, sharp-witted and radiant, making her oxygen tube look stylish, react to various younger versions of herself.
Whether revising or rattled by her own prior perspectives the emotion is written deeply, often wordlessly, on her face, beaming at kudos from Bob Dylan or long-time producer and confidante Hall Willner.
Faithfull was an artist's artist. Case in point: devotees like Beth Orton, Courtney Love and Sonic Youth's Thurston Moore show up to reinterpret her music.
Her role as a "destabilising influence" is debated by a roundtable of British personalities including broadcaster Edith Bowman, actor Sienna Guillory, and musician Bat For Lashes.
These many guests and fussy trimmings offer plenty of glowing praise but also reduce time with the main attraction, herself, who is unwaveringly honest about her mistakes and successes.
Despite her troubled persona, Faithfull doesn't buy into the notion of the tortured romantic. "F*** no! But it's a good hook to hang things on," she says.
Broken English is already historic for the fact Faithfull died during its production. Following a fourth-wall-breaking introduction by Swinton we're treated to what would be her final performance.
Reuniting with Nick Cave and Warren Ellis in the studio for a rendition of 2018's Misunderstanding, Faithfull's elegantly coarse voice gifts the wise lyrics heft even before the profound realisation that it's the last time anyone would hear her sing.
As the old showbiz mantra goes, always leave them wanting more.
Broken English is in cinemas nationwide from 17th September.
Hear My Eyes: Memento (Dir. Christopher Nolan; Score: Michael "Cavs" Cavanagh)
Pairing star director Christopher Nolan's structure-flaunting, daytime noir Memento with King Gizzard & The Lizard drummer Michael "Cavs" Cavanagh is exactly the kind of cool, unlikely pairing that Hear My Eyes specialise in.
For over a decade, the Melbourne collective has enlisted musicians to produce live scores for cult movie classics. And following the success of re-scoring Terminator 2 with synths (and lasers), Hear My Eyes scores another hit with Memento.
Released in 2000, Memento stars Guy Pearce as Leonard Shelby, a former insurance investigator who suffers from a form of amnesia where he can't make new memories. Instead, he relies for better or worse on notes, tattoos and intuition to track down his wife's murderer, aided and abetted by a cast including Carrie Ann-Moss and Joe Pantoliano, both fresh from The Matrix.
Just as the film makes the most from meagre ingredients, so too does Cavs, moving between two drum kits on-stage at the Melbourne Recital Hall.
On the right: he rolls out jazzy grooves familiar to classic hard-boiled detective flicks. On the left: a kit adorned with pads to trigger glassy synth notes, providing both moments of ambience and disquieting atmosphere that work beautifully with the protagonist's mixed-up memories.
Finding balance between augmenting the emotional beats and allowing space for them to breathe, Cavs syncs marvellously with the film's rhythmic pacing: cutting briefly to silence at the slam of a door, or building with nerve-shredding intensity to the hammering of a firearm.
It gels so well, there are times you forget he's there.
It may be a tad overwhelming for first-time viewers but this fresh score provides a vital new way to experience a film that, even once you learn its twists, retains its power to puzzle and satisfy.
It's a shame so much thought and care is put into something that, besides an additional Sydney screening, many will miss out on. Here's hoping Umbrella's upcoming 4K release includes Cavs's skin-thumping score as an alternative audio track.
Hear My Eyes: Memento plays at the Sydney Recital Hall on August 29.

An ancient &quot;shark graveyard&quot; tens of millions of years old was found in the Egyptian desert

An ancient "shark graveyard" tens of millions of years old was found in the Egyptian desert
Kyiv • UNN
Fourteen fossilized shark teeth from the Cretaceous period were discovered on the Abu Tartur Plateau. Two of the five identified species had not previously been found in Egypt.
Paleontologists discovered 14 fossilized shark teeth on the Abu Tartur Plateau in Egypt that belonged to five species of ancient predators. LRT reports this, citing ScienceAlert, UNN writes.
Details
The discovery was made in an area that was the seabed during the Cretaceous period, approximately 145–66 million years ago. At that time, Earth's climate was much warmer, sea levels were higher, and a significant part of North Africa was underwater.
Scientists had previously found the remains of two shark species in the area. The new studies made it possible to identify five more extinct species, two of which—Serratolamna cf. serrata and Squalicorax bassanii—had not previously been found in Egypt.
What ancient shark teeth revealed
The teeth found differ significantly in shape: some are long and thin, others are broad and serrated, while one has a sharply curved shape. According to the researchers, this may indicate that different shark species occupied separate ecological niches and hunted different prey.
Scientists suggest that the ancient sea in this region was rich in nutrients and could support a large number of marine predators. At the same time, the layer of phosphorus compounds in which the teeth were found does not allow them to state with certainty that all seven shark species known in the area lived there at the same time.

the art of the miniature staircases at cooper hewitt design museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
20:35:52 UTC
05:35:52 KST

In 2006, Cooper Hewitt put a collection of staircases on display that no one could climb. The exhibition was called Made to Scale: Staircase Masterpieces, The Eugene & Clare Thaw Gift, and it consisted of a collection of miniature model staircases, finely crafted from wood and metal, from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Looking at these tiny, swirling helixes and delicate balustrades, there’s a certain artisanship that makes them more than utilitarian tests of interior architecture.
spiral staircase model in English style, late 19th century | all images gift of Eugene V. and Clare E. Thaw
The Eugene & Clare Thaw Gift to the institution
The Thaw couple was introduced to the concept of a staircase model after seeing one, displayed like a statuette, in a friend’s home. In a 2006 interview, presented in the exhibition brochure, Eugene Thaw speaks to Sarah D. Coffin, former curator and head, Product Design and Decorative Arts, at Cooper Hewitt, about the beauty he saw in that first model. As he and his wife went on collecting—asking friends to be on the look out and obtaining them at auction—he mentioned that he learned more about why they were made and rendered so valuable. He says, ‘they were pièces de maîtrise, or masterworks, which were made as part of becoming a master and being accepted into a guild.’
staircase model with low curved double stringboard, mid–late 19th century
Artistic and architectural reference
In gifting their collection to Cooper Hewitt, they made available to the public the mastery that went behind each of these models. Not only are they a useful reference for architects looking to model a structure to scale, but they are also fascinating aesthetically. They are reminiscent of children’s dollhouses, albeit very luxurious ones crafted from oak and other fine woods instead of particle board. There’s a certain imagination that emerges from seeing things in miniature, as if they were extracted from another, much smaller world.
semi-circular staircase model, mid–late 19th century
The architectural precedent for modeled stairs
For those who went to architecture school, building a model staircase is a typical part of the curriculum, as it encapsulates, in many of its aspects, the intricacies of building space around the human form. Because a staircase is used as a tool, it must fit the proportions of the feet, its handrail must land at a comfortable height, and it should be angled in a way that efficiently brings someone from one floor to another. Hand-drafting one is a notoriously difficult task for similar reasons. At smaller scales, these models allow one to see a staircase in its entirety and appreciate all it is able to achieve technically while still providing a little aesthetic flair with a spiral, helix, or material innovation.
double staircase model in English style, 1850–75
Sarah D. Coffin’s history of model stairs
In approaching the staircase collection at Cooper Hewitt, Coffin’s text primes visitors with a history of staircases, saying they, ‘have been part of building design since about 6000 BC.’ She then goes into the history of why these models were made, bringing the reader into the world of France’s guild system, known as compagnonnage in French, that trained promising men in a specific trade or craft if they showed promise. It allowed young people to learn a professional skill outside of a traditional master-apprentice relationship or needing it to be passed on through familial knowledge systems. Drafting and then creating these models were thus signs of training and mastery. Coffin also mentions that, while they were being trained, these boys ‘lived and ate meals in monastic-style boarding houses,’ eager to prove their competence. This training would result in the emergence of masters who had competed over many years to perfect this craft.
curved staircase model on shaped base, ca. 1880
The small details in the tiny steps
When looking at the collection, there are models that show incredibly inventive forms. One is described as a ‘double staircase model in English style,’ where a series of stairs ascends to what looks like a raised, square walkway. To get there, four staircases converge at about half the height to a sub-platform. There, another four staircases, shifted 90 degrees with respect to the base, splay out to create the secondary climb upward. All the while, curving, spun details decorate this model made in walnut, mahogany, and satinwood. Another model, also in an ‘English style,’ is much more reserved, with a single spiral and simple geometric steps. Nevertheless, the restraint feels very contemporary, showing the aesthetic breadth these models achieved.
1/3
double staircase model joining at the top and base with opening at center, late 19th century
spiral and circular-section staircase model, mid-19th century
design for double curved staircase with blue balustrade, elevation at top and plan below, february 13, 1883
location: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York
curator: Sarah D. Coffin, former curator and head, Product Design and Decorative Arts, Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum

"We want to find out who those people are so it gives our search direction," she told the ABC.
Ms Raval said she had contacted the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade seeking clarification.
"I have called DFAT asking them. But they said due to privacy we can't release those details. I told them, 'I don't need to know anyone else's name, but tell me if my husband is on the list.' But they didn't tell me.
"The families deserve to know."
She said the uncertainty was preventing her family from making decisions about where to travel and how best to assist.
"Once I know which place my husband is in I will definitely go there and try to help the rescue team," she said.
"When they find the people, they are transferred in the hospital and they might need our support. We don't know what condition they will be found in.
"I have to be there when he is rescued. I need to be there."
Mrs Raval said she planned to travel in the coming days but first needed to know where to focus her efforts.
"I am extremely frustrated that the government has not provided any bit of information that can help us right now," she said.
"I am having nightmares every night of my loved ones stranded in the jungle or stuck in the mud.
"You have no idea the suffocation I am feeling. It is killing us."

📸 In pictures: Satellite images show extent of mudslides in Nepali valleys
Satellite images from Planet Labs PBC, an American Earth imaging company, reveal the extent to which mudslides have reshaped the landscape around Nepal's northern river systems.
Before-and-after images released by the company show a layer of thick mud many times the width of the rivers they are covering, including the Lhende River near Rasuwagadhi and small tributaries near the Langtang Lirung mountain.
The latter is the highest peak of the Langtang Himal, a sub-range of the Nepali Himalayas.
The glacier that caused Wednesday's flooding is believed to have fallen from the mountain's north face.
Survivors return to salvage possessions from flood-damaged homes
While the risk of further flooding in Nepal and Tibet remains real, some Nepali villagers forced to flee their homes are returning to see what posessions they can salvage.
Sometimes it can be as insignificant as a pair of muddy sandals, which one boy in a flood-devastated town was spotted carrying from his house.
On other occasions, the return trip has proven more than worthwhile.
Shoba Shretha returned to her home in Trishuli — from which some survivors are still being evacuated — to find Sweetie, her dog she was forced to leave behind when the floods hit.
She sat on the ground patting her and giving her water from a water bottle as others bustled around them.
Relief coordinators were forced to clear villagers, reporters and volunteers from one flood-damaged area to allow excavation equipment in to dig.
Reporting with AP
Aid beginning to arrive in Nepali communities, as survivors cluster at army base
In Nuwakot, one of the Nepali districts devastated by the floods, helicopters have begun to arrive loaded with boxes and bags of aid, including clothes, instant noodles, crackers and rice.
Others are carrying survivors from flood-hit areas to the Mathaili Barrack army base, which is now serving as the primary base for airlifted survivors.
An older man was carefully helped off one helicopter on Saturday, while a soldier carried an older woman on his back to a medical tent.
Most of those arriving landed with no possessions except the clothes they were wearing.
About a dozen people emerged from another helicopter. Soldiers carried several babies who were among the evacuees.
The evacuees had been brought from the nearby community of Trishuli.
Reporting with AP

Ontario premier slams Trump's order: "It's Lake Ontario now and forever"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
20:26:35 UTC
05:26:35 KST

Ontario premier slams Trump's executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Seneca Nation calls for reversal
Ontario's head of government on Saturday erected a sign by Lake Ontario that reads "Lake Ontario - Now and Always" and criticized President Trump after he signed an executive order to rename the body of water that connects the Canadian province and the state of New York.
"I'm here on the shores of beautiful Lake Ontario, a crown jewel of our province and our country," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said in a short video message posted on social media.
"You may have heard that President Trump is trying to rename this lake, all because he doesn't like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves," he said. "But let's be serious. Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario, and long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario."
Ford added that the province put the huge blue sign to remind Mr. Trump and everyone that "it's Lake Ontario now and forever."
The new sign, which also says in French "Lac Ontario - Aujourd'hui et pour toujours," is located at Fifty Point Conservation Area, a park in Hamilton, Ontario.
Amid an ongoing trade war between Canada and the United States, Mr. Trump last week sought to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" by an executive order. He also said the U.S. doesn't expect to be "doing much business with Ontario any longer."
The name Ontario came from the Iroquoian word "oniatarí:io," and means "lake of shining waters," according to the Center for Great Lakes Literacy.
The leader of the Seneca Nation, one of the Iroquoian-speaking nations in the region, on Friday also criticized Mr. Trump's decision to rename Lake Ontario and called for the executive order to be rescinded.
Seneca Nation President J. Conrad Seneca said the order violates a more than 225-year-old treaty and shows a "blatant disrespect" for the Indigenous people who gave it its name in the first place. He said the Lake Ontario name should remain as a reflection of the Indigenous people in the U.S. and Canada who lived in territory around and along the lake long before the creation of either nation.
"The President cannot assert ownership over our culture or erase it through irresponsible political action," he said in a statement.
Following failed trade talks between the two nations, the U.S. began imposing 50% tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods. Mr. Trump also announced that the U.S. will impose a 50% tariff on all Canadian automotive and steel imports beginning in January, while claiming that "Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years."
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney then announced new retaliatory tariffs against the U.S., saying that it would impose tariffs of up to 50% on about $20 billion of U.S. imports.
In recent days, Ford has openly pushed back against Mr. Trump's treatment of Canada.
"He's treating us like we're Communist China here," Ford told CBS News chief Washington correspondent Major Garrett last week. "We're the closest friends and allies that the U.S. has anywhere in the entire world, and I want to keep it that way."
Ford and Mr. Trump traded harsh words as the trade war escalates. The president called Ford "unimpressive" and a "flunky" of Carney, who belongs to a different political party but has drawn support from the Ontario premier.
Ford, for his part, has called the U.S. president a "dictator" and said: "I have a lot of real estate on my a**, so he has a lot of room to kiss my a**."

Skopje marks the 116th anniversary of Mother Teresa’s birth
“Days of Saint Mother Teresa” are being held in Skopje to mark the 116th anniversary of her birth and the 10th anniversary of her canonization, North Macedonia’s public broadcaster MRT reported. The events began on August 26 with the laying of flowers at a memorial plaque marking the site of the saint’s childhood home in central Skopje and will continue until September 5, the date of her death.
Mother Teresa (Agnes Gonxhe Bojaxhiu) was born on August 26, 1910, in Skopje, to a family of Albanian origin. At the age of 18, she left home and joined the Sisters of Loreto, later moving to India. From 1948 onward, she devoted her life to working among the poorest people of Calcutta. In 1950, she founded the Missionaries of Charity, an order that operates in many countries around the world, providing support to people who are rejected, abandoned, and marginalized. 
In 1979, she received the Nobel Peace Prize for her work helping people in need. She died in Calcutta on September 5, 1997. Pope John Paul II beatified her in 2003, and Pope Francis canonized her on September 4, 2016.
PHOTO Reuters
Former Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić dies in prison
Former commander of the Bosnian Serb Army, General Ratko Mladić, died in prison in The Hague, where he had spent the last 15 years of his life, BNR-Horizont reported, citing Reuters. Several hours earlier, the president of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Graciela Gatti Santana, had rejected his defense team’s request for early release on humanitarian grounds.
On August 18, Mladić’s defense team requested the release of the 84-year-old and his transfer to a hospital or palliative-care facility in Serbia, citing the likelihood of his death and the need for him to spend more time with his family.
Mladić was sentenced to life imprisonment for genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes committed during the 1992-1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 2021, the Appeals Chamber upheld his sentence, finding him guilty of the genocide of approximately 8,000 Bosniaks in Srebrenica in July 1995, the terrorization of civilians during the siege of Sarajevo, and the taking of UN personnel hostage. Mladić was arrested in Serbia in 2011 and has remained in custody under the supervision of the International Tribunal in The Hague ever since.
PHOTO visitgreece.gr
Drone base to be established on the island of Rhodes
Greece’s Ministry of Defence announced the launch of a procedure to establish a UAV base in the area of a military airfield on the island of Rhodes. This will be Greece’s second such base, following the one on the island of Skyros, BNR correspondent Katya Peeva reported. Until now, drones on Rhodes have been operated from temporary sites, making their use more difficult.
Greece already has a network of companies that design and manufacture their own unmanned aircraft. At the same time, Greece purchases drones from the United States and Israel because domestically produced systems cannot fully meet the needs of the Greek Armed Forces. 
This summer, at special military exercises, Greek manufacturers presented the technologies they are developing, including drones, counter-drone systems, and other types of UAVs. A facility for producing drones using Greek technology is currently under construction near Athens.

Drone fragment containing explosives destroyed on a beach in Romania
A drone fragment containing explosives was discovered on the morning of August 26 near sun loungers on the beach of the Romanian Black Sea resort of Olimp, approximately 38 km south of Constanța. Several people alerted authorities, who immediately cordoned off the area and restricted access for tourists, digi24.ro reported.
Specialists determined that the device contained explosives. It was moved to a hole that had been prepared in the sand and destroyed in a controlled explosion. A warning was sent to local residents and tourists via the RO-Alert system, observatornews.ro reported.
Romanian media reported that a second drone fragment was also discovered, but it posed no threat. The authorities have not provided information about the origin of the device.

Russia could have used nukes in Ukraine but chose restraint – top MP

Russia could have used nukes in Ukraine but chose restraint – top MP
Russia could have long ago used tactical nuclear weaponry to achieve victory against Ukraine, but it has always sought to minimize collateral damage, Leonid Slutsky, the head of Russia’s Liberal-Democratic Party (LDPR), has said.
The senior MP, who chairs the Russian State Duma International Affairs Committee, made the remarks in an interview with conservative American journalist and podcaster Tucker Carlson that aired on Saturday. Slutsky said Moscow would only opt for nuclear weaponry against Kiev if its Western sponsors supplied Ukraine with weapons of mass destruction. The politician expressed hope that the situation would not deteriorate to that point.
In any other scenario, use of nuclear weaponry against Ukraine would not fit Moscow’s approach and vision, the MP stated.
“We could have used them long ago and achieved victory, but we always rely on common sense and the principle of minimizing civilian casualties. Using such weapons as an instrument of terror, as was the case in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, if we recall World War II, is alien to us,” Slutsky stated.
Moscow could also have begun hitting Ukraine without any regard for collateral damage and civilian casualties, but still hopes that Kiev and its Western backers will show some “common sense” and come to the “position of peace, not war,” the politician believes.
“But for now they take an entirely different position, completely devoid of common sense,” Slutsky said.
Russia has so far avoided attacking bridges across the Dnieper River, the destruction of which would have deprived the Ukrainian military in Donbass of logistics, the politician explained. He said it has also refrained from striking the key airport of Borispol outside Kiev, which has been used to funnel weaponry from the West. Either option, however, would have drastically worsened the humanitarian situation in Ukraine and harmed civilians, according to Slutsky.

German establishment figures call for ban on country’s most popular party
Unknown

05:06:51 KST

German establishment figures call for ban on country’s most popular party
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Baden-Wurttemberg Governor Cem Ozdemir have called for the opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD) party to be banned. The two establishment politicians claim that the country’s most popular party poses a threat to Germany’s constitutional order and democracy.
The AfD is the largest opposition force in the Bundestag and enjoys the support of 28% of respondents, according to recent surveys.
The right-wing party advocates tougher immigration controls while also calling for an end to Germany’s green policies. It is also highly critical of Berlin’s support for Ukraine and sanctions against Russia.
In an opinion piece published by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung on Friday, Pistorius and Ozdemir drew parallels between the modern-day AfD and Adolf Hitler’s National Socialist party.
“Today, we are once again facing a threat to democracy from the extreme right,” the politicians, who represent the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the Green Party, respectively, claimed.
In making their case for outlawing the right-wing party, Pistorius and Ozdemir argued that a powerful faction within the AfD espouses the idea of ‘remigration’, thus calling into question the “inviolability of human dignity” enshrined in the German constitution.
“We cannot confront ethnic nationalist ideology through political debate. That would be naive,” the authors wrote.
“A legal review of the constitutionality of a political party is warranted when it calls into question and threatens the continued existence of our democracy,” Pistorius and Ozdemir stated.
The two also took issue with the AfD’s supposedly “pro-Russian stance,” describing it as a “security risk.” The opposition party’s calls for Germany to withdraw from the European Union, the Eurozone, and NATO are equally “dangerous,” according to the article.
While acknowledging the AfD’s rising popularity, Pistorius and Ozdemir argued that widespread public support for the party is another reason why it should be banned outright.
Voting for the opposition party out of dissatisfaction with the current state of affairs in Germany is no excuse, the authors argued.
“The undeniable radicalization of the AfD makes it impossible to claim ignorance of who one is voting for,” they wrote.
At present, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency classifies the AfD as a ‘suspected right-wing extremist’ entity – a designation that gives the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) powers to surveil the party and its members. In several regions, local AfD chapters have been subjected to even wider monitoring.
Meanwhile, an INSA poll published by Bild earlier this month showed that support for Germany’s governing Christian Democratic CDU/CSU bloc had fallen to 20%, with some 78% of respondents dissatisfied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government, which also includes the Social Democrats.

====================================================================================================

Adolescents report low regret and high satisfaction following gender-affirming chest surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
20:00:51 UTC
05:00:51 KST

Adolescents who undergo gender-affirming chest surgery report low levels of regret and high levels of satisfaction, experiencing outcomes similar to those of young adults. These findings suggest that age restrictions on these medical procedures lack support from actual patient experiences. The research was published in the International Journal of Transgender Health.
Gender-affirming care includes a range of medical and psychological services designed to help align a person’s body with their gender identity. For some transgender and nonbinary individuals, this involves surgical interventions. One common operation is gender-affirming chest surgery, which typically involves a mastectomy, or the surgical removal of breast tissue, to create a flat chest contour.
In recent years, policymakers in the United States have introduced legislation aiming to restrict youth access to these treatments. Proponents of these bans frequently point to the possibility that teenagers might eventually regret undergoing irreversible physical changes. Until now, most data showing low regret and high satisfaction rates following chest surgeries have come from adult populations.
Researchers Maya Younoszai, Caleb Haley, Cole V. Roblee, and their colleagues sought to fill this gap in the scientific literature. They designed a study to compare the postoperative experiences of adolescents and young adults. Their goal was to see if patients who had surgery before age 18 felt differently about their decisions than those who waited until adulthood.
The research team conducted a cross-sectional study, meaning they collected data from participants at a single point in time. They focused on patients who received chest surgeries at a pediatric hospital between January 2018 and April 2023. To be eligible, patients had to be at least one year out from their operation.
Prior to surgery, the hospital required patients to meet established medical protocols for gender-affirming care. This involved psychological evaluations by both a surgeon and a mental health provider. For patients under age 18, all legal guardians had to consent to the procedure. If any guardian was unsupportive, the surgery was not offered.
The researchers sent surveys to 183 eligible patients, and 77 completed the questionnaires. Of these respondents, 42 had their surgeries as adolescents under age 18, and 35 had their surgeries as young adults between the ages of 18 and 26. The surveys included standardized tools used widely in healthcare to measure how people feel about past medical choices.
One tool, the Decision Regret Scale, scores regret from zero to 100, with higher numbers indicating more regret. The other tool, the Satisfaction with Decision scale, rates satisfaction from one to five, with higher scores showing greater contentment. The researchers calculated the scores for both age groups and compared them.
The results showed high satisfaction and low regret across the board. The median regret score for both the adolescent and young adult groups was exactly zero. The median satisfaction score for both groups was five, the highest possible rating. The differences in average scores between the two age groups were not statistically significant.
The researchers also administered a third survey to evaluate family dynamics. This tool measures a person’s sense of belonging and support within their family environment. The researchers wanted to see if family support played a role in how patients felt after surgery.
When comparing the scores, the researchers found a positive correlation between family support and surgical satisfaction. Patients who felt more supported by their families tended to be more satisfied with their decision to have surgery. However, the connection between family support and decisional regret was not statistically significant.
The team also analyzed a smaller subset of participants who reported either higher regret scores or a mismatch between their regret and satisfaction scores. Out of the 77 participants, five fell into this category. The researchers looked at written responses and conducted interviews to understand what was driving these scores.
These patients reported dissatisfaction with specific aesthetic results rather than regretting the transition itself. Some expressed frustration with how their bodies healed, mentioning issues like keloids, which are raised, thickened scars. Others noted uneven chest contours.
Clinicians categorize regret into several types, distinguishing between medical regret over surgical outcomes and true gender-related regret. True gender-related regret involves a desire to return to the sex assigned at birth. None of the interviewed individuals reported true gender-related regret.
Even among the five patients with higher regret scores, those who provided qualitative feedback stated that the surgery improved their overall quality of life. They noted that the procedure allowed them to stop wearing restrictive chest binders. They also mentioned feeling more confident in their clothing and social interactions.
In addition, the researchers found that 13 participants had experienced a shift in their specific gender identity since the operation. For example, someone might have identified as a transgender man at the time of surgery but later identified as nonbinary. The regret and satisfaction scores for this group did not differ from the rest of the participants.
Most patients in the study were white, identified as male, and had a history of using testosterone. The researchers collected data on underlying health conditions, noting that high percentages of patients had documented diagnoses of depression and anxiety prior to surgery. Despite these mental health conditions, the patients navigated the surgical process with a very low complication rate.
Several factors limit the reach of these findings. First, the median time since surgery for participants was about 1.8 years. Because feelings about medical decisions can evolve, this timeframe might not capture long-term regret that could emerge many years later.
Another limitation is the 42 percent participation rate to the survey. This introduces the possibility of selection bias, a scenario where the people who chose to participate might differ fundamentally from those who did not. It is possible that individuals with higher levels of regret ignored the survey, which would result in an underestimation of regret in the overall group.
Patients might also experience social pressures that influence how they answer these types of surveys. Because access to gender-affirming care is a highly publicized political issue, some participants might minimize their dissatisfaction. They could fear that expressing regret might provide ammunition for policies that restrict healthcare access for themselves or others.
Despite these limitations, the data align with earlier studies conducted on older patients. The researchers note that adolescents seem to process their surgical decisions with outcomes comparable to young adults.
The findings add to a growing body of scientific literature regarding the physical and mental health outcomes of transgender youth. The study, “Regret and satisfaction after adolescent gender-affirming chest surgery,” was authored by Maya Younoszai, Caleb Haley, Cole V. Roblee, Alisha Nguyen, Tannon Tople, Anna V. Faino, Cyndy Snyder, Maya Gopalan, Danielle J. Eble, Russell E. Ettinger, and Shane D. Morrison.

Sprinter Ellie Beer reveals emotional toll of being elite athlete at 16
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
19:14:26 UTC
04:14:26 KST

Sprinter Ellie Beer reveals emotional toll of being elite athlete at 16
At age 16, 400 metre runner Ellie Beer was exceeding expectations.
She was the new kid on the block in Australian sprinting, smashing her personal best (PB) time and making history.
But maintaining that level of performance was all-consuming.
"It was just spotlight moment after spotlight moment," Beer tells ABC Sport.
"I remember feeling the pressure of what others were thinking.
"I felt like I had to rise to the occasion, like every race I had to run a PB and that it would be good enough."
It took another five agonising years for Beer to beat her 2019 PB of 52.53 seconds.
"There were moments where I was like, 'Will I ever get better?' I [felt] like maybe I peaked at 16," Beer says.
"I had thoughts of wanting to give up and not pursue it anymore."
The transition from a junior to a senior athlete, from about 17 to 19 years of age, was particularly hard.
"I had set my standards so high that I had to run consecutive 52 second runs, but I wasn't getting close to that time due to the pressure," Beer says.
She started overthinking her races, predicting what would happen before they had even begun.
"I would be worrying about the lactic [acid] hitting the last hundred. 'How am I going to run down that back straight?'
"I went out and pretty much just ran stressed and nervous."
Beer credits her coach and support team with getting her on the start line during that time.
"The back of my head [was saying] 'I don't want to give up the sport,' but the front of my head was telling me, 'No, [I] want to be done.'"
"I knew in my heart that I didn't want to give up," she says.
But moving forward wasn't easy.
When passion turns to pain
Beer stands out. She's more than 1.8m tall, with long, bouncy blonde locks and an infectious smile.
You can't miss her on the track thanks to her trademark arm sleeves, which help her to get in the zone.
"My coach always says, 'Wear your arm sleeves, Ellie, because you feel fierce,'" she says.
"[They] make me feel like I'm ready to go out there and perform."
Now 23, Beer is a different person to the 16-year-old who stormed onto the world stage. But it's only because of where she's been.
Beer's big break came at the Queensland Track Classic in 2019 when she won the 400m in a PB of 52.53.
It earned her a spot in the Australian 4 x 400m relay team for the 2019 IAAF World Athletics Championships, and the title of the youngest-ever Australian selected.
She then ran a flying time, which helped Australia qualify for the Tokyo Olympics.
Beer was selected for that 4x400m relay team for Tokyo, and at 18 her Olympic dream was realised.
After Tokyo, Beer won the 2022 national senior 400m title and placed seventh in the 400m final at the World Under 20 Championships. But still no breakthrough runs, no personal bests. That pressure to rise to every occasion was weighing heavily.
"I was just really worrying about trying to perform a perfect race, sometimes for others," Beer says.
"I used to be, after bad races, quite down on myself.
"And then [I] would kind of dwell into the rest of my season."
The power of pushing through
At 21 years old, already having graced the international stage for five years, Beer knew something had to change.
It was 2024, leading into the Paris Olympics, when her mindset switched thanks to a supportive team.
She now has a wellbeing coach, a psychologist, and Brett Robinson, who has been her running coach since she was 11.
"He [Robinson] has helped me so much along the way," Beer says.
"Particularly during times when I didn't believe in myself, he would always believe in me more.
"I don't even want to call him a coach; I want to call him family."
What they did together seems so simple, but it worked.
"Nerves, they never go away, [but] I've changed my mindset around them," Beer says.
"I channel them and [have learned to] embrace them.
"It's a word that Robbo and I have used quite often.
"Embrace the hurt, [because] the 400 [is] a very tactical event, but learning to embrace that lactic acid, embrace where you are and being grateful to go out there and perform."
With that, Beer stopped worrying about the uncontrollable and she wasn't so driven by the outcome.
She also stopped tying her identity to her race results.
"I'm learning, yes, I'm Ellie Beer the athlete, but I'm also Ellie Beer the daughter, coffee enthusiast, social girl, the friend," she says.
"I've just learned that you [might have] one bad race, [and] yes, it sucks at the time, but it's just one race. We move forward and we focus on the next."
Mind over matter
That change has seen results.
2024 was a good year for Beer. She broke the personal best drought at the Adelaide Invitational, took the national 400m title, the Oceania 400m title, and then produced another PB at the Paris Olympics.
In 2025, she won her third national title and got her PB down to its current form of 51.3 seconds. She also won a bronze relay medal at the World Indoor Championships.
This year, she secured her fourth national title, was crowned Oceania Champion again, and recently helped the mixed and women's relay teams qualify for the 2027 World Athletics Championships.
Her biggest goal now is running the 400m in under 51 seconds.
"I've had that goal for the last couple of years and we just haven't quite got it yet," Beer says.
"We've got PBs which I'm happy with, but our standard for Australia to get into most major teams is to run a 50.7.
"To run a sub-50, oh my gosh, I'm going to be ecstatic.
"But I've learned [that with] running, even just a PB is amazing [and] I'll be happy with that."
Beer stresses the nerves are still there and probably always will be.
When asked what her greatest challenge is in getting that sub-51 mark, her answer is not a surprise.
"Probably my own self," Beer says.
"I'm a different athlete compared to when I was a junior, [but I] still struggle with the self-doubt and the what if."
The Gold Coast local is now an ambassador for the Australian Institute of Sport's mental fitness program, and says she is happy to share her experiences of vulnerability to help other athletes.
"Having that experience of not running a PB for five years, that's the reason as to why at this age now I want to share better ways to deal with it," she says.
"As part of my training, I speak with my sports psychologist, I speak to my wellbeing officer, I speak with my coaches to help rewire my mindset leading into races.
"There's a major percentage physically, [but] mental plays a massive part as well."
It is possibly a contradiction, but mentally, Beer likes to switch off with coffee.
She just can't survive without her two iced long blacks a day, on top of an espresso shot with eggs on toast in the morning.
"I love coffee," Beer says.
"My favourite thing to do outside of training is search for the best cafes and try all of them."
The focus is just one part of rebuilding her identity outside of running.
In the long term, Beer has her sights set on being selected for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.
"I would love to perform in front of a home crowd," she says.
But for now, there's always coffee.

On August 29, 1897, Theodor Herzl convened the congress, where the "Basel Program" was adopted and the organizational foundations of the Zionist movement were established.
Herzl famously wrote in his diary, "In Basel, I founded the Jewish state."
The promotional posts for the planned protest, which circulated on social media, included the slogans "Free Palestine" and "Death to Zionism," along with an image of an Israeli tank featuring a red inverted triangle above it - a symbol associated with Hamas propaganda videos used to identify targets for attack.

Norway's new king remembers 'my dear father' in first speech
- Published
King Haakon VIII of Norway has paid warm tribute to his late father, Harald V, in his first speech to the nation since taking the throne.
"Thank you for being such a good dad," he said in an at-times emotional televised address, seated at a desk in Norway's royal palace, beside a picture of the late king, two lit candles and a bowl of white roses.
Harald, 89, who was seen as a moderniser and "people's king" during his 35-year reign, died in hospital on Friday morning after being treated for a rare blood condition.
"Now it is my turn," his 53-year-old son said, adding that a "major task" awaited him and that he wished to be "present and attentive" going forward.
- Who is Norway's new King Haakon VIII? 
  - Published1 day ago
- Norway mourns King Harald as Haakon VIII ascends throne 
  - Published1 day ago
- Oslo mayor calls off wedding ceremony after death of Norway's king 
  - Published1 day ago
Haakon stressed national unity in the speech, saying the royal family believed in a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal value".
He said Harald had been a good father to himself and his sister, Princess Märtha Louise, as well as a "warm and funny grandfather" to his six grandchildren and a "loving and caring husband" to his widow, Queen Sonja.
The new king appeared to choke back tears as he noted that Saturday would have been their 58th wedding anniversary.
Harald brought the family together "with a natural authority", of which he might not have been aware himself, his son recalled.
He had "always stayed true" to his "values and commitments", the new king stressed.
"He constantly reminded us in the family that each of us must do things in our own way. Find our own style. Be ourselves," Haakon said.
He also remarked on the "powerful and moving experience" of seeing thousands of Norwegians gather outside the royal palace in the capital Oslo with "flowers, tributes and candles".
"We are in mourning, yet at the same time it brings comfort and strength that so many are grieving together with us," he said.
Norwegians have been laying flowers outside the royal palace in Oslo since news broke that Harald had died on Friday. A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet given for his funeral.
Among them was Norway's Prime Minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".
Haakon will swear an oath of allegiance in parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service with his wife, Queen Mette-Marit - a stripped-down version of a coronation, which Norway no longer holds.
He assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.
Mette-Marit came under scrutiny when it was revealed that she had had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she publicly apologised.
She later received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.
Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.
Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when Haakon married his mother.
Haakon's sister, Märtha Louise, has also courted controversy for remarrying an American self-styled shaman in 2024, their business activities ultimately leading her to step back from royal duties.
Without directly referencing these controversies, Haakon said during his speech: "Our family has experienced the importance of standing together in order to remain steadfast both within ourselves and for one another even during difficult times."
He said he, along with Mette-Marit and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, would "always strive to understand the life situations of different people".
He added: "No one who lives in this country knows what we will face together, but what we do know is that we will stand by one another through both good days and difficult ones."
Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year suggested that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.
However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges.

Indian Standard Time to become mandatory for all entities from March 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
19:02:32 UTC
04:02:32 KST

Govt notifies Legal Metrology (IST) Rules, 2026, making IST mandatory for all legal, commercial and administrative activities from March 2027.
NEW DELHI: From March next year, all entities in India will be required to use Indian Standard Time (IST) for legal, commercial, digital and administrative activities, with govt on Saturday notifying the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026.The rules, notified under the Legal Metrology Act, will come into force 180 days after their publication in Gazette, making IST mandatory from around March 2027. Violations of the rules will attract penalties under the Act.The notification makes IST the mandatory time reference for all legal, administrative and official documents unless specifically exempted. It also makes IST the standard time reference across commerce, transport, public administration, legal contracts and financial operations.Entities will not be allowed to use, display or record any time reference other than IST for official purposes, except where foreign time zones are clearly labelled or where alternative time sources are permitted for scientific research, navigation or astronomy.The rules are significant as modern digital infrastructure depends on microsecond-level timing accuracy. Payment systems, stock exchanges, telecom networks, 5G services, digital navigation, power grids and data centres require synchronised clocks to authenticate transactions, coordinate operations and maintain network reliability.
The notification establishes a nationwide system for time synchronisation, traceability and cybersecurity, recognising accurate time as critical digital infrastructure. Under the rules, CSIR-National Physical Laboratory (NPL) will continue to maintain India’s primary time scale, UTC(NPLI), from which IST is derived, while Regional Reference Standards Laboratories (RRSLs), ISRO’s NavIC and other authorised timing sources will disseminate official time.
Another major feature of the rules is the focus on cyber resilience. Organisations must deploy proper time-synchronisation systems, protect networks against spoofing, jamming and cyberattacks, integrate multiple authorised timing sources and maintain contingency mechanisms, including atomic clocks where necessary, to ensure uninterrupted operations.

As the housing crisis changes way we live, is multi-generational the answer?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
19:02:21 UTC
04:02:21 KST

Modular solution for multi-generational living as housing crisis changes way we live
If Sheena Carter wants to talk to her daughter or grandchildren, she doesn't pick up the phone or get on Facebook.
She opens the back door, walks down a short garden path, and knocks on the door of the home next door.
But it hasn't always been that easy.
Eight years ago, she and her husband Barry Flentjar sold their home in Central Victoria and had a prefabricated modular house assembled on her daughter's 8-hectare block at the foot of Hanging Rock in Newham, about an hour north-west of Melbourne.
"We had looked at building, but it was just too expensive,"
"Then we bought [a modular home], and it's been the best thing we've ever done. It came in on the back of a truck, delivered like a pizza, and was fantastic for us."
The move has allowed them to be much closer to family without crowding each other out, while also giving her daughter, Jacqui Carter, some much-needed help. Carter works full-time and has four children with her husband, Cameron Creer, a firefighter on rotating shifts.
Selling their house released financial equity and gave Sheena Carter and her husband the freedom to travel.
As for the grandchildren, the move has given them somewhere to escape, be it for a snack, a chat or a board game.
"We're very close, Mum and I," Jacqui Carter said. "But we're not living in each other's pockets; she doesn't come and poke her nose in when she's not welcome."
On the move
The Carters' unique living arrangement is part of a push towards more multi-generational living.
The number of multi-generation households jumped from 275,000 to 335,000 in the 2021 census, a 22 per cent increase.
About one in five people in Australia live in multi-generational households, a figure demographer Simon Kuestenmacher expects to keep climbing amid rising housing and living costs.
"We would expect the trend to go up simply because the cost-of-living pressures have increased so starkly, and this is how people react to it,"
While the Carters' approach was to add another dwelling, some like Michael St Vincent in Newcastle have kept things under one roof.
He's reconfiguring his family home of 56 years so his adult grandchildren, who are struggling to get into the housing market, can move in if they want.
"It's our duty as oldies to help out where we can,"
Mr Kuestenmacher said while multi-generational living was ingrained in some cultures, the broader increase was predominantly a story of necessity.
"Some of this will be out of a choice, out of providing a wonderful intergenerational set-up where the grandparents can help with the grandchildren, and it's all just a wonderful, helpful environment," he said.
"But we have to suspect … that the majority of intergenerational households have at least some element of financial necessity built into it."
No more quiet
There was a quiet that settled over Ellen McNeice's Toorak home after her husband died six years ago. For years, it stayed that way.
Then, two of her adult sons moved back in while they saved for a deposit. The house, she said, was full again.
Her home needed very little modification to welcome back her new tenants.
"It's wonderful for them because they're not wasting money on rent," Ms McNeice said.
"And it's good for me because as I'm getting older, it's nice to have somebody home at night."
The two generations keep everything separate: individual food, cleaning and living schedules.
They'll share meals when it suits, but otherwise, they live quite independently.
"We decided when they moved in they would move in not as a mother and children, but as a housemate arrangement," Ms McNeice said.
Last year, Ms McNeice was diagnosed with motor neurone disease.
She is matter-of-fact about what it means, knowing she'll have to move out of home one day.
"With a bit of luck I'll have another year or two in my own home before I have to move into care," she said.
Building for the future
The housing industry is responding to the changing ways Australians are living.
While the Carters had space on a generous-sized regional block, the number of suburban plots taking on additional buildings is also increasing.
In New South Wales, the number of secondary dwellings approved jumped by 24 per cent in one year, in part to a relaxation of planning laws.
Housing Industry Australia has called for a national approach to planning laws, allowing granny flats of up to 90 square metres to be allowed to bypass lengthy planning queues.
Hugh Hartigan, former head of research at Housing Australia, said modular homes, like the Carters', are a speedy solution that has yet to completely take-off.
"The main issue is really demand," he said. "People don't necessarily trust the product yet."
Modular or pre-built housing makes up between 3 and 5 per cent of Australia's construction industry, a fraction of what is achieved in countries such as Japan (about 20 per cent) and Sweden (nearly 50 per cent).
University of NSW construction researcher Riza Yosia Sunindijo said the housing industry faces a structural problem; without a steady pipeline of projects, pre-modular building manufacturers could not achieve the economies of scale needed to bring costs down.
He said a commitment to modular could be a boon for regional areas struggling to fill housing and workforce shortages.
"Modular construction can address both issues by reducing the amount of labour required onsite, while also improving productivity for housing delivery," Professor Sunindijo said.
Mr Hartigan said modular's biggest selling point was speed, with homes built in roughly half the time of a traditional build
Modelling by his firm found that with coordinated industry and government action, modular construction could deliver an additional 192,000 homes over the next 20 years.
"To put that in perspective, by about the 20th year, you'd be getting about 20–25,000 additional homes on top of business as usual in the residential construction industry," he said.
"If you think about the fact we generally get 160–180,000 homes built a year, that would be a huge boost to the overarching residential housing industry."
A best friend
Back at Hanging Rock, Sheena Carter is thinking about the future.
She and her husband are in their mid-70s, fit enough to play golf, hike and travel — to Darwin, most recently, for a family birthday.
For now, they help with school runs, pantry raids and family time. Her daughter provides the land, the Sunday dinners, and the grandkids.
"My grandson said last night that Papa is his best friend," Sheena Carter said with obvious pride. "We're very, very lucky".
But one day, the tables will turn. Then it will be her daughter traversing the garden path to check in, rather than the other way around.
"I know there'll be a time when she'll need to do more for us, or me, or Barry, whoever's still living there," Sheena Carter said.
But for now, they're enjoying the memories made, and the ones still to come.
"I just wish more people realised that sort of building and opportunity was out there," she said.
"I cannot believe more people aren't doing it."
Who asked the question?
Sheena Carter reached out to the ABC to share the joy she's found since purchasing a modular home.
"We bought a modular home that was built in a factory and arrived on a truck. Three months from contract sign to delivery. It's a fantastic home," she wrote.
"We were able to 'build' it on our daughters's property and there are 8 of us over 3 generations helping each other and enjoying intergenerational support. We are very lucky!"
Ellen McNeice and Michael St Vincent also reached out to the ABC via Your Say.
Want to have your say? Go to www.abc.net.au/yoursay

New threats testing Australia's plan to end violence against women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
Algorithms, 'pervert glasses' and the scourge governments are struggling to end
Australia has again reached a moment where the safety of women is dominating the national conversation.
A horrific period of violence and sexual assault allegations has governments promising to accelerate action.
Their commitment to the cause is not in doubt, but after hundreds of recommendations and billions of dollars, it is time to ask if Australia's problem is now less about what to do, and more about getting it done.
At the same time, new forms of harm are clearly emerging faster than governments and laws can respond.
This week, national cabinet acknowledged rates of intimate-partner homicide and sexual violence remained "unacceptably high" and it agreed to priorities for the next five-year plan to tackle the issues.
States and territories will give progress reports later this year on work related to sexual violence and judicial responses, respectful relationships education, men's behaviour-change standards, emergency accommodation and alcohol reforms.
They have also signed off on a new national family and domestic violence risk-assessment framework.
The idea there is that whether someone presents to police, a GP or hospital, they should have any warning signs recognised consistently across jurisdictions.
But states will get two years to align their systems, which is frankly a peculiar interpretation of acceleration.
Crossbenchers want to give commission more teeth
Australia is at the halfway point of the current 10-year national plan to end violence against women and children, which came with the explicit ambition to end gender-based violence "in one generation".
It is a logical point to assess what the first five years have achieved and what needs to change for the next five.
That is certainly the view of the more than a dozen crossbenchers who wrote to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese this week.
They argued that despite all the inquiries and spending, governments still cannot adequately demonstrate where all the money goes and whether interventions are reducing harm.
The crossbenchers, which include MPs such as Allegra Spender, Dai Le, Helen Haines and Andrew Wilkie, want the Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commission to be given more teeth.
By making it a statutory body able to compel information, track implementation of recommendations and audit spending, they argue Australia will get a better understanding of what is working.
From there comes holding the nine governments charged with ending this scourge to account.
"Giving the commission the power to measure and assess the effectiveness of our policies is the key that could unlock the real change our communities want to see," Spender says.
'Young boys and men are prime targets'
Implementation is a major factor in Australia's efforts to tackle family, domestic and sexual violence, but at the same time the very nature of the threat is changing.
The current plan was only designed a few years ago, but the online environment is changing extremely fast.
Founder of the Teach Us Consent advocacy group Chanel Contos has launched a campaign calling on the federal government to "fix our feeds" by making social media algorithms "opt-in" for everyone.
She warns content is increasingly being served to young boys and men that labels women and minorities as the "grievance" for their issues.
"Social media algorithms, it may not be clear the link of that to violence against women and children, but if you peel back some layers, you can imagine that we have this profit model that is based on promising outrage, fear, insecurity, desire, arousal, any strong emotions," Contos told David Speers on the Insiders podcast this week.
"And young boys and men are prime targets for that."
Contos is appreciative of the government's efforts broadly, but says if it doesn't act on algorithms, it isn't being "serious" about the problem most impacting young people.
"I think it's quite obvious the harm that algorithms are doing to everyone, but particularly young people, and women are largely on the receiving end of that," she says.
Loading
Surveillance glasses sell
Another clear example of technology outrunning policy is the recent proliferation of wearable smart devices, such as glasses, able to surreptitiously record their surroundings.
Variously (and understandably) dubbed "creepy" or even "pervert glasses", they have already been used to create endless online videos in which men have covertly filmed women in workplaces, at gyms and beaches or on the street.
Gina Martin, who successfully campaigned to criminalise upskirting in England, is now in Australia campaigning against Kmart's Anko brand "surveillance glasses" that retail for just $89.
Her petition to have the technology removed from sale has already racked up more than 56,000 signatures.
Martin says Kmart "shouldn't be selling" these glasses "especially when the law hasn't caught up to protect people from them".
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has asked the privacy commissioner to consider the issue of smart glasses as a priority due to the risks for women and children.
"The government is continuing to work on the next phase of privacy reforms to ensure our … laws are fit for purpose in the digital age," she says.
But as each day passes, more pairs are sold.
Extra immediate political pressure
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek this week said she was "super concerned" by the "explosion of sexual violence" where both victim and perpetrator were under the age of 18.
She knows the next five-year national action plan on violence against women and children doesn't just have to deal with longstanding failures in policing, housing, courts and services.
It must address forms of gendered harm that barely existed when the last one was written.
Recent unrelated allegations involving young people and prominent institutions such as the Sydney Swans AFL club have intensified the immediate political pressure.
The next five-year plan will have to do more than accelerate existing efforts; it will have to prove governments can keep pace with a problem that itself is changing.

US judge rules against Trump’s effort to deport pro-Palestinian students

US judge rules against Trump’s effort to deport pro-Palestinian students
A federal judge criticised the Trump government for attempting to infringe upon foreign students’ rights to free speech.
A United States federal judge has ruled that President Donald Trump’s administration violated the constitutional rights of international students when it sought to punish them for criticising Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
In California on Friday, District Judge Noel Wise heaped criticism on the US Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) after the agencies attempted to deport noncitizens over protected speech.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Mahmoud Khalil alleges conspiracy in lawsuit against Trump officials
- list 2 of 3US court affirms release of pro-Palestine scholar as legal battle continues
- list 3 of 3Judge nixes Trump lawsuit alleging Harvard did not protect Jewish students
“Stated plainly, in the United States, freedom of speech belongs to the people,” Wise said in her 90-page decision. “It is not the government’s to take.”
Wise, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, added that, in the US, speaking out about the government and its leaders was a testament to the health of the country’s democracy.
“That strength is diminished when members of our society — citizens and noncitizens alike — must self-censor and ‘behave’ or suffer the government’s retaliation,” she said.
The ruling centred on how the second Trump administration revoked visas and detained international students studying in the US after they engaged in pro-Palestinian advocacy.
The detentions began with Columbia University graduate Mahmoud Khalil in March 2025.
Columbia had been an epicentre for the student protest movement, and Khalil, a graduate student and permanent US resident, had emerged as a key negotiator for the student groups.
Khalil, who is fighting his deportation in a separate case, praised the ruling on Saturday in a post on social media.
“No one should fear speaking up for Palestine,” Khalil wrote on X.
Arrests like Khalil’s formed the basis for the lawsuit against US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, one of the defendants in the case. In August 2025, Stanford University’s independent student newspaper, the Stanford Daily, filed a complaint claiming that some of its noncitizen writers had chosen not to cover pro-Palestinian protests due to the administration’s actions.
Two anonymous plaintiffs also joined the suit, identifying as foreign nationals with no criminal record. They said they too felt the need to self-censor, for fear of losing their student visas.
The Trump administration, however, has pointed to the Immigration and Nationality Act as justification for its deportation efforts.
Part of that law asserts that the secretary of state can “exclude” foreign nationals from the country if their presence could cause “potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States”.
But critics have argued that the standard is largely untested in court and does not supersede the First Amendment of the Constitution, which protects free speech.
In her ruling, Wise chastised Rubio for what she described as a “standardless” enforcement of his visa revocation policy.
“The record does reveal one clear pattern in the enforcement actions the government has taken to revoke noncitizens’ visas since March of 2025,” the judge wrote. “The secretary revokes visas when noncitizens are critical of the government or the causes or people it favors. This exemplifies ‘seriously discriminatory enforcement.’”
Conor Fitzpatrick, a lawyer at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Free Expression (FIRE), the nonprofit that filed the lawsuit, hailed the ruling as a win for First Amendment rights.
“Today’s ruling proves that free speech isn’t a privilege, but the inalienable right of every man, woman, and child,” Fitzpatrick said in a statement.
The Trump administration has faced other setbacks in its student deportation campaign as well.
In September 2025, for instance, a federal judge in Massachusetts ruled that US officials had violated the First Amendment when they attempted to detain and deport noncitizen students and academics for pro-Palestinian advocacy.
The case had been brought by a coalition of education groups, which argued that the deportation policy had created “a climate of repression and fear on university campuses”.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the State Department and DHS for comment.

The Oligarch Part 3: How Ukraine’s richest man rose as bodies fell – and became too powerful to touch
Unknown
