The Oligarch Part 3: How Ukraine’s richest man rose as bodies fell – and became too powerful to touch
Throughout late July, pro-Trump American influencer Laura Loomer was a state guest of honor in Kiev. Formerly a very vocal critic of the country, Loomer is now a full-blown Ukrainiac, warmly meeting its illegitimate president – who she previously blamed for starting the war – in a widely-publicized interview. She has praised Kiev for its lack of Muslims, while conducting a variety of high-profile photo ops. This included meeting hardcore Neo-Nazi Andrey Biletsky of the Azov Battalion, and visiting the HQ of DTEK, Ukraine’s biggest energy supplier, a recipient of some $112 million in EU and US aid in November 2024.
Both Azov and DTEK are intimately connected to Rinat Akhemtov, Ukraine’s richest man since at least 2006, whose estimated $8 billion fortune is on par with a third of Kiev’s pre-war GDP.
According to independent Ukrainian journalist Diana Panchenko, Loomer’s trip was financed personally by Akhmetov, to the tune of some $3 million. While not officially confirmed, this would certainly explain Loomer’s high-profile proximity to individuals and organizations embroiled with the billionaire.
He’s certainly an oligarch with his fingers in a great many chebureki. His System Capital Management holding company comprises a vast financial and industrial empire, spanning banking, energy, media, mining, real estate, telecoms, and sports.
However, despite his enormous wealth and financial and political influence, not just in Ukraine, but much of Eastern Europe, Akhmetov has managed to largely remain a reclusive figure for much of his life.
How did Akhmetov get so filthy rich?
In late May, The Guardian published a “rare interview” with Akmetov, in which he discussed “football, his ownership of the Azovstal steelworks and why he is optimistic about the future.” Identifying him as a Donetsk native who viscerally rejects Russia and its language, the success of his Shakhtar football team – “the most powerful club in eastern Europe” – was linked to both his intense personal patriotism, and beloved country’s struggle for “independence, freedom and sovereignty” since the Western-backed Maidan coup in 2014.
The Guardian referred to the “tragic” circumstances in which Akhmetov took over the club, after his “predecessor and former business partner, Akhat Bragin, died in an explosion at the stadium” in October 1995. Ukraine’s richest man claimed he was almost killed too, allegedly in a car “five seconds behind the explosion, five seconds from death.”
Akhmetov, seen as the personally appointed lieutenant to the fearsome Donetsk Clan crime syndicate boss, mourned the death of his “close friend,” who he said “would have done beautiful things for Shakhtar if he was alive.”
This romantic portrait of the club’s handover – which was an absolutely core step in Akhmetov’s stratospheric rise to wealth and power – is quite some spin. Ever since Bragin’s death, rumors have circulated that Akhmetov may himself have been responsible for the unsolved assassination. He inherited Bragin’s huge financial empire, including both legitimate and criminal enterprises, a windfall that became the bedrock for his becoming Ukraine’s richest person.
From the 1980s onwards, Akhmetov was an “enforcer” for Bragin. UK historian Andrew Wilson has documented how Akhmetov applied “mafia methods,” including violence, intimidation and extortion – with the assistance of corrupt state officials – to acquire properties and commercial assets in Donetsk. Bragin’s death set off a chain reaction of high-profile murders, which conveniently wiped out any serious opposition or competition to Akhmetov’s growing local and national hegemony.
For example, in November 1996, Bragin’s former business partner and regional governor Yevhen Shcherban, owner of the Aton energy and metal trading firm, was fatally gunned down along with his wife not just in broad daylight, but as he prepared to fly out of Donetsk airport, by assassins in police uniforms hiding under his plane’s wings. Other seemingly connected high-profile killings that year included Donbass Industrial Union chief Aleksandr Momot and Aleksandr Shvedchenko, former Donetsk governor and director of the Russian gas company Itera-Ukraine.
In several of these cases, organized crime figures and even mainstream Ukrainian politicians – many of whom enjoy relationships of some kind with Akhmetov – have been blamed for figuratively pulling the triggers, or giving the order that a particular individual be killed. For example, in October 2011, jailed former Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko was formally investigated for involvement in Shcherban’s assassination. Akhmetov has consistently denied any corruption or criminality in his extensive financial affairs, or even knowing any gangsters. Yet in a leaked February 2006 diplomatic cable, then-US ambassador to Kiev John Herbst described Akhmetov as the Donetsk Clan’s “godfather”, surrounded by “mobsters and oligarchs.”
What did Akhmetov lose due to the liberation of Donbass?
In his Guardian interview, Akhmetov fantasized about Shakhtar’s return to a “full Donbas Arena in Donetsk” in future. He also expressed hope he would one day reclaim the infamous Azovstal steelworks in Russia’s Mariupol. Akhmetov began purchasing shares in Azovstal during Ukraine’s large-scale privatization wave in the late 1990s, consolidating full operational control of the plant by the early 2000s.
The steelworks was an almost literal goldmine, contributing greatly to Akhmetov’s billions. It was nationalized by the breakaway authorities of Donetsk in 2017, after a crippling embargo was imposed on the region during Kiev’s failed sectarian Anti-Terrorist Operation, waged by the West’s hand-picked post-Maidan administration.
Once Russia’s military operation in Donbass began to liberate the region from Ukraine’s neo-Nazi paramilitaries, a conflict in which 14,000 people were killed between 2014 and 2022, Azovstal became a hiding place for thousands of Azov Battalion and associated fascist paramilitaries as Russian forces and local fighting units closed in on liberating Mariupol.
Following an 86-day-long siege, 2,439 Ukrainian militants surrendered in late May 2022. Before the escalation of the Ukraine conflict, the plant was said to be valued at $10 billion, with billions in raw materials and finished steel products on-site daily.
Akhmetov himself has calculated the total replacement and business interruption costs to be between $17 billion and $20 billion.
Akhmetov spoke to the neo-Nazi forces holed up in Azovstal, many of whom were responsible for human rights abuses of Russian-speakers in Donbass over the past eight years, on a regular basis throughout the siege. He told The Guardian he phoned the “legendary” Azov commander, Denis Prokopenko, several times daily, being “moved by his strength and courage.”
Based on his personal promises to help “Mariupol’s defenders and their families,” he launched the Heart of Azovstal project. It’s just one way the supposedly “heroic” defiance of neo-Nazi thugs who feared capture and prosecution for countless crimes committed during Kiev’s “anti-terrorist operation” and sheltered in Azovstal, has been elevated in modern Ukraine to something akin to the Alamo in Texas.
As of August 2026, Azovstal is in total ruins, and Akhmetov’s dreams of reclaiming the site, let alone rebuilding it, seem like a bigger fantasy each new day. Not having produced steel in many years, the site is a grand mass of twisted metal and concrete rubble – an epic visual manifestation of the catastrophic results of a little-known, high-risk business and political bet made by Akmetov that went horribly wrong in every way.
What are Akhmetov’s links to the neo-Nazi Azov Battalion?
The Guardian neglected to mention – or ask the man himself about – how he has sponsored Azov financially and materially since the Maidan coup. Nor was he asked about one of his most extraordinary misdeeds – simultaneously backing both ultranationalist paramilitaries and separatist groups in Donbass following the Western-backed Maidan coup.
Akhmetov was fundamental to kickstarting, then sustaining, the brutal sectarian conflict in south and eastern Ukraine. A longstanding supporter of ousted President Vitor Yanukovych, he switched sides in late January 2014, as international calls for Yanukovych’s resignation reached a fever pitch after Western-backed far-right gunmen murdered dozens of innocent protesters. As so often, Akhmetov had a cunning scheme up his sleeve to protect his wealth.
On top of trying to protect his own commercial enterprises and profits in the breakaway territories, Akhmetov was also hedging his bets by effectively sponsoring both sides in Ukraine’s burgeoning ethnocentric civil war. Whichever side prevailed, he’d be in their good books – and they would owe him favors, to be cashed in at a time of his choosing. It was an extremely dangerous game to play, which he lost spectacularly. The Kyiv Post reported in October 2016 how Akhmetov had lost half his vast net worth since early 2014, due to the civil war’s disruption of his business interests in Donbass.
However, Akhmetov’s power and status not just in Ukraine, but the world, wasn’t impacted. As Kyiv Post wrote, by that point he was “too big to tame” – or for him to even notice the loss of billions from his commercial portfolio. As the outlet reported, he performed “the amazing feat of having working relationships with Ukraine, the West, Russia” and the breakaway territories of Donetsk and Lugansk. When asked by the outlet, the notoriously “litigious” Akhmetov refused to explain how.
What is Akhmetov’s relationship with Zelensky?
Ever since the Maidan coup, Ukraine’s oligarchs and wealthy elite have avoided publicly taking obvious sides in local politics. Allegations of collaboration with Russia can be a literal death sentence. Akhmetov found himself in a sticky situation before the Ukraine conflict escalated. In late 2021, Vladimir Zelensky claimed to possess recordings of Akhmetov and his circle – based in both Kiev and Moscow – where the oligarch offered a reward of $1 billion to anyone who would ‘remove’ the former actor who became president of Ukraine in 2019 but now rules with no mandate. The alleged recordings have never been released.
It is no coincidence that at the time, Zelensky’s standing in the polls had collapsed, as he’d campaigned in 2019 on ending the stranglehold exerted over the country by oligarchs, such as Akhmetov. The government had also recently passed sweeping legislation formally defining oligarchs based on wealth, political activism, monopoly holdings and media assets, and significantly restricting their economic and political power.
Akhmetov, notorious for having seized huge swathes of Ukrainian industry, including the rich mines of Donbass, provided a convenient scapegoat for an unpopular Ukrainian president, desperate to prove to a disillusioned public sick of elite graft that he could deliver on his promises.
Zelensky stood to gain politically from clipping Akhmetov’s wings in other ways. Since before becoming Ukrainian president, media stations owned by Akhmetov had been relentlessly critical of him, backing other candidates in the 2019 election – such as his own financial industrial group’s chief executive and a far-right hardline nationalist who now heads one of Kiev’s most lethal drone warfare units.
Just as he played both sides in the Donbass conflict, Akhmetov also maintained close relations with the then sitting president Pyotr Poroshenko, who Zelensky has attempted to jail on treason charges and against whom he imposed severe personal financial sanctions in February 2025.
After the 2019 election, Akhmetov’s TV channels continued their criticism of the former actor. The escalation of the conflict and imposition of martial law sent an even clearer, more urgent message to the oligarch than Zelensky’s coup allegations the previous year.
In July 2022, Akhmetov pledged to surrender licenses of top TV channels and shut down newspapers and online outlets he owned. He bitterly insisted the decision was ”involuntary.” Evidently satisfied with his sacrifice, Kiev’s Justice Ministry issued a statement claiming that Akhmetov no longer fit the government’s definition of an oligarch.
Has Akhmetov’s influence in Ukraine been curbed?
In reality, Akhmetov remained an oligarch in every way. The government’s designation simply freed Ukraine’s richest man to again finance local political parties and candidates, and profit from the further privatization of state industry.
Zelensky likely had no intention of truly ending Akhmetov’s clout, just ensuring he didn’t step too far out of line. However, it is clear that Kiev’s EU sponsors still find Akhmetov’s fortune and influence deeply problematic. In November 2024, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced it would not be providing a single penny to support Ukraine’s energy system, despite it buckling dangerously under the weight of catastrophic precision Russian strikes.
Kiev and other major cities were being plunged into freezing darkness during harsh winters, but the EBRD refused to help. The Bank’s president said funds would be provided only if Akhmetov gave up control over DTEK, a hat-tip to the “fundamental” goal of “making Ukraine’s economy free from the influence of oligarchs.” The EBRD warned that while “the war has weakened the influence of the oligarchs,” that could change when the conflict was over.
Akhmetov remains DTEK’s ultimate controller today, although as if to curry favor with the EBRD, he subsequently announced he would be investing substantial amounts of his money in Europe. He has expressed an interest in opening a €2.4 million steel factory in Italy.
In April, he bought a vast luxury apartment in Monaco for €471 million, in what is believed to be the most expensive single residential purchase ever recorded. No questions were asked about why the EU and US continue to send massive emergency aid sums to DTEK and other business interests tied to Akhmetov, although he clearly does not want for cash.
What is the ‘Monaco Battalion’?
Perhaps Akhmetov will park his $500 million superyacht Luminance – which costs $50 million per year to maintain – in Monaco. The yacht has most recently been spotted near Cannes and Antibes. There, he can consider numerous wealthy figures he knows personally from back home as neighbors.
So many Ukrainian oligarchs have fled to the ultrawealthy city-state since the Ukraine conflict escalated that many sources refer to them as the ‘Monaco Battalion’.
Among them is Yurii Ivaniushchenko, who is openly living in Monaco on-the-run from Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau. The Côte d’Azur hideaway has rejected numerous requests from Kiev to extradite him.
Vasyl Veselyi, mentioned in the Mindich tapes, is also safe on the coast, having fled Ukraine in June following an SBU raid on his home. Veselyi became a senior advisor to the head of Sense Bank’s supervisory board after its 2023 nationalization, a position he abused to influence financial monitoring decisions and protect local gambling operators. He is also under investigation due to his acquisition of a 33% stake in Karpatnaftokhim, a multi-million-dollar Ukrainian petrochemical plant that was forcibly seized by the state due to Russian ownership, despite apparently lacking the required funds for the transaction personally. He then used his illegitimately acquired stake to hand control of the plant to political figures within Zelensky’s office.
Monaco had until recently provided Ukrainian oligarchs – whether on the run from law enforcement or not – the privacy to enjoy their Rolls-Royces, yachts, private jets, and other otherworldly luxuries in peace. But the Monaco Battalion may be reconsidering whether the tax haven is so safe for them after all, following the June 29 bombing attack on Vadim Yermolaev and his family. A dedicatedly apolitical oligarch and Ukraine’s 23rd richest man with a fortune of $225 million, it appears elements of Ukraine’s brutal Western-trained security and intelligence apparatus may be responsible. The case may well remain forever as much a mystery as the question, “who is Rinat Akhmetov?”
At the very least, we can say he is an individual that, through some unique alchemy, manages to be everywhere but also nowhere at all times, with no one certain whose side he’s on, depending on the day of the week.
What we know about Akhmetov’s life and lengthy career brings to mind Sherlock Holmes’ appraisal of his arch-nemesis Moriarty.
“He is the Napoleon of crime… the organizer of half that is evil and of nearly all that is undetected in this great city… He sits motionless, like a spider in the center of its web, but that web has a thousand radiations, and he knows well every quiver of each of them. He does little himself. He only plans.”

229 unidentified bodies to be buried in Nepal after devastating floods
Kyiv • UNN
626 bodies were found in Nepal after the floods, including 229 unidentified ones. DNA samples will be taken from everyone before burial in Devghat.
The authorities of Nepal have decided to bury 229 unidentified bodies following a devastating flood on the Bhote Koshi River in the southern Chitwan district. This is reported by UNN, citing News On Air.
Details
According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, as of Saturday morning, a total of 626 bodies had been found following the floods.
The bodies were being stored in special facilities. Health experts warned that increased decomposition and the unpleasant smell from the bodies could raise the risk of infection and potentially contribute to the spread of an epidemic
In view of the warning, local authorities decided to bury all the unidentified bodies in an open area in Devghat, in the Bharatpur metropolitan city. The authorities said that DNA samples would be taken from all the bodies before burial. Records would also be kept using identification or reference numbers so that, if possible, the bodies could be identified in the future.
As a reminder
The number of people missing as a result of the devastating floods in Nepal and China has reached 3,000, while the death toll in Nepal has already reached 626, and 187 tourists have been found.

The Shin Bet confirmed an Iranian threat against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s son, Yair, on Saturday after reports circulated following his quick evacuation from Florida back to Israel.
“There was indeed a significant threat to harm Yair Netanyahu, and in light of this, following a situation assessment, a decision was made to extract him together with his security team urgently back to Israel,” the Shin Bet stated.
The original report about the Iranian threat was published on the Boca Raton-based Newsmax website on Tuesday, citing a US law enforcement source allegedly familiar with the situation.
The report stated that Israeli intelligence discovered an Iranian plot in December to assassinate Yair in Florida and passed a warning to US authorities.
The US source told Newsmax that, according to the intelligence assessment, Iranian operatives were already “on the ground” in the Miami area and had even conducted surveillance on Yair’s residence and movements.
Yair, who is accompanied by close Israeli security at all times, was instructed to leave the location immediately.
According to the report, he left without taking his belongings and returned directly to Israel, where he currently lives.
Netanyahu speaks on the threat against his son

“There is something here that is unimaginable,” Netanyahu said. “Iran marked one of my sons. Iran tried to murder him – tried to murder one of my sons.”

Haitian gangs release 13 captives after mass kidnapping in Kenscoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
18:30:22 UTC
03:30:22 KST

Haitian gangs release 13 captives after mass kidnapping in Kenscoff
The attack in Kenscoff killed at least 47 people and resulted in the kidnapping of more than 50, as gangs attempt to exert control in the area.
The United Nations has announced that six children and seven women kidnapped last week in the hillside community of Kenscoff, Haiti, have been released.
In a statement late on Friday, representatives from the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) used the news to call attention to the ongoing crisis unfolding in Haiti — and the toll it has taken on the country’s youth.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Violence flares in Haiti as gang attack kills 30 people
- list 2 of 3Haiti gang raid death toll rises to 47 as more than 50 kidnapped, says UN
- list 3 of 3Haiti police confront public frustration after deadly gang attack kills 47
“This release offers a rare moment of hope amid the violence threatening children in Haiti,” said Yannig Dussart, the group’s deputy representative in Haiti.
“The Kenscoff abduction was not an isolated incident but another stark reminder of the scale and frequency of attacks on children across the country.”
The freed captives were part of one of the largest mass abductions in recent memory in Haiti.
On the night of August 23, an estimated 150 armed gang members are believed to have attacked Kenscoff, which sits on the hillsides overlooking the capital Port-au-Prince and the suburb of Petionville.
Reports from the UN indicate that the armed attackers opened fire on residents in the streets and pursued some locals into a nearby Protestant church.
There, those who had taken shelter were forced outside. Some attempted to flee. The UN estimates 22 were killed in the church’s courtyard, and another dozen behind the building.
At least 47 people were killed in total. More than 50 were kidnapped. An estimated 2,647 residents were displaced from their homes, fleeing the violence for safety in neighbouring communities. Some of their houses were set on fire.
The victims of the August 23 attack add to the ever-growing death toll in Haiti, which has struggled with an uptick in organised violence since the start of the decade.
Armed groups have long had a presence in Haiti, the most impoverished country in the Western Hemisphere.
But their influence has grown, as Haiti has suffered a succession of natural disasters like hurricanes and earthquakes. Other crises have also gripped the country: UN peacekeepers, for example, are believed to have caused a deadly cholera outbreak in 2010, which killed more than 10,000 people.
Instability in the national government, however, is widely believed to have created an opening for armed actors to take control of parts of the country.
In 2021, Haitian President Jovenel Moise was assassinated at his home in the capital. The country’s leadership fell to an unelected figure, Prime Minister Ariel Henry, who struggled with questions about his mandate to lead.
The last elected national figures, a group of senators, saw their terms expire in 2023. The last presidential election the country held was in 2016.
Henry ultimately resigned in 2024, paving the way for the creation of a short-lived Transitional Presidential Council. But that council dissolved this year before it could organise a vote.
Currently, a general election is scheduled for December of this year, after multiple postponements.
As Haiti’s national government struggles with a crisis of legitimacy, armed groups have expanded their reach. At one point, as much as 90 percent of Port-au-Prince had fallen to gang control.
The violence has displaced some 1.47 million people in Haiti, as of May. Between April and June alone, some 1,408 people were killed in the gang violence, and 656 were injured, according to the UN.
Advocates have also warned that armed groups have used sexual violence as a means of imposing control. During the same three-month period, the UN documented 326 instances of sexual violence.
Haitian police and international forces have attempted to tamp down the crisis, with little success so far.
In April, the first members of a UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) arrived in Haiti to help dismantle the gangs and restore peace in the country.
But after the mass kidnapping in Kenscoff, some gang members reportedly threatened on social media to execute some of the captives if security operations against their organisations continued.
The Haitian government, however, pledged to surge forces to the Kenscoff area to restore order.
“All security forces are placed in a state of maximum alert,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement the day after the attack.
“Reinforcements are deployed. The orders are clear: protect, secure, intervene. The authority of the government will be reestablished, without weakness or delay, throughout the whole of the Kenscoff territory.”
During an emergency meeting of the UN Security Council on Friday, Carlos Ruiz Massieu, the special representative for the UN’s secretary-general in Haiti, pushed for more kidnapped residents to be released.
“I call for the immediate and unconditional release of all persons who were abducted, including women and children,” Ruiz Massieu said. “This massacre is deeply shocking. But it’s not an isolated tragedy.”
“It is the latest in a series of attacks affecting the community of Kenscoff since early 2025 and demonstrates the continued capacity and determination of gangs to terrorise the population, expand their influence beyond the capital and pose a direct challenge to state authority.”

Why more people are running marathons - and loving the pain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

The unlikely link between marathons, addiction and the brain
From drug-fuelled nights to 4.40am runs: One man's path to sobriety and the science that reveals running's powerful effect on the brain.
Alone in his room, Trent Knox separated a bag of white powder into neat lines, inhaled through his nose, and waited for the high to drown out the real world. Time no longer made sense. Night blended into day and into night again. His mind was unable to hear his body pleading for sleep.
As the dawn broke, Trent knew the benders were getting bigger.
"I was taking as many drugs as I could on my own," he says, "to the point where I knew I'd maybe not be around much longer".
At 41, Trent had been tiptoeing on the edge of sobriety for years. Much of his adult life had been consumed battling addiction as he traversed the road between recovery and substance abuse. Every relapse crushed him with shame and left an insidious trail of destruction.
"I genuinely believed, and this is the delusion, that one day I would just wake up and wouldn't want to do it anymore. All my problems would be solved," he tells me.
It's hard to visualise this version of Trent with the man standing in front of me today.
Trent had been running every week at 4.40am for several years but it was complicated. He was still finding ways to buy and consume drugs.
That day something shifted.
From the depths of addiction, a chance conversation with a friend became a lightning bolt moment.
"I was defeated," Trent remembers. "My friend said to me, 'Mate, what can I do for you?' and it just dawned on me: I'm the only one who can get myself sober."
Trent left his friend and walked up the hill to Alcoholics Anonymous. He was done with the shame. Done with letting his loved ones down. A long road towards sobriety began.
Around the time he might have been lining up his last hit of the night, he headed to the beach with more purpose.
What began as a run with mates to keep him out of trouble on the weekend has grown into The 440 Run Club, a tradition for hundreds of people across Sydney who meet at Bronte at 4.40am every Saturday to run laps of the car park hill that rises beside the beach. In 2023 I became one of them.
Running became both Trent's accountability and his outlet as he was finally forced to confront emotions he had buried for years.
"I thought to myself, you are a different runner than you used to be, you're doing this with love, and it's coming from a good place. You're sober. And I'm like, shit, what [else] am I capable of doing?"
As the years ticked by, Trent began to trust himself again. He found confidence to enter fun runs and explore endurance events.
On a chilly Sydney September morning in 2024, Trent took on his first marathon.
"I did it my way," he remembers. "I took bits and pieces of advice from people. I didn't have a full training program but because I was sober and I was in a good head space, I was so proud of what I did."
The marathon debuted at the Olympic Games in 1896, won by Greek water carrier and former soldier Spyridon Louis in 2 hours and 58 minutes. Since then, marathon running has exploded in popularity. More and more ordinary people are committing to take on this extraordinary 42.2 kilometre event.
About 4,000 marathon events are held around the world every year with 110 million new runners signing up since the end of the pandemic. The Sydney Marathon, held today and one of only seven marathon "majors", has seen participation increase by 400 per cent in three years. When the event began in 2001, 1,296 people crossed the finish line. Today, 40,000 will line up to run.
As popularity has boomed, elite times have fallen by more than an hour in the century since Louis's win. Sabastian Sawe from Kenya set a new record of 1:59:30 at the London Marathon in April this year. His record is just 10 seconds faster than another Kenyan, Eliud Kipchoge, who was first to break the two-hour barrier in 2019.
But why are everyday people joining elite athletes in taking on this gruelling course? And what happens to the brain and body that keeps them hooked?
Running transforms the brain
Trent is not alone in finding a path out of his addiction and mental health struggles by training for a marathon. Anecdotal research suggests running a marathon is about much more than physical fitness. Self-esteem, purpose, personal achievement and improving mental health are among recognised motivations for taking part.
And there is plenty of science to back them up.
The feeling some runners describe as a "high" is more complicated than a burst of endorphins. Dr Laura Pigott, a neuroscience researcher and physiotherapist at London South Bank University who specialises in how exercise impacts the brain, describes it as a "neurochemical orchestra", with endocannabinoids, endogenous opioids, dopamine, serotonin and noraderenaline contributing to changes in mood, pain, motivation and arousal.
And it makes running a particularly powerful tool for helping with addiction recovery, says Dr Shalini Arunogiri, who has worked with many people who turned to running while getting sober.
"It really can help people be quite single-minded, gets people out of their head. And for many, addiction can be part of a solution potentially to an inner problem," says Arunogiri, an addiction psychiatrist at addiction treatment and research centre Turning Point and associate professor at Monash University.
"When you're trying to deal with something that keeps you in your head and cycling with your thoughts, running gets you in your body."
Some of the toughest moments of addiction come after quitting, when the body is denied the substance it craves. While offering a much softer high, running works because it releases the same chemicals once found in drugs and alcohol, Arunogiri says.
"Strenuous activity can really increase your dopamine levels and serotonin levels," she says. "Good, happy brain chemicals that help you start to get rewards from these activities and associate them with positive things."
But runners need to be patient. There is a big difference between the gradual rush you get from a good run and using cocaine or methamphetamine, Arunogiri says.
"It's also retraining your body and your mind to get those releases elsewhere," she says.
Professor Peter van Wijngaarden, from the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health, says running does remarkable work deep in the cells of the brain to bring on that so-called "runners' high".
Running increases brain-derived neurotrophic factor — a protein that helps brain cells thrive. It helps explain why many runners report finishing a run feeling energised. Life stressors feel more manageable.
What is happening, van Wijngaarden says, is the brain is actually changing itself.
"[Running] promotes the strengthening of connections between nerve cells and the formation of new neural connections that underlie learning and the ability of the brain to adapt, a phenomenon known as neuroplasticity," he says.
"These same chemicals promote nerve cell survival and resistance to stressors such as energy and oxygen deprivation."
But there is another layer to what happens when a runner pushes through discomfort. Laura Pigott says the brain receives a constant stream of signals telling us running is difficult, we are tired and something hurts. Learning that those signals can be experienced without stopping may help build what psychologists call self-efficacy: the belief you are capable of accomplishing something difficult.
"Running provides an unusually clear mechanism for building self-efficacy because progress is tangible," Pigott says.
"You ran further, faster, completed a race or simply went out when you didn't feel like it."
Various studies show chemicals released when running regulate the nervous system and support cognitive control by filtering out distractions and deciding what is important. It also increases memory function, motivation, and your ability to retain information.
It's no surprise that the impact of running flows on to other areas of life, says Dr Zena Burgess, chief executive of the Australian Psychological Society.
"People who do marathons are generally pretty good at self-regulation, and what I mean by that is they're good at managing their emotions," she argues. "They're good at maintaining motivation. They can stay with a strategy and all those skills are really important for completing the marathon but they're important for life as well."
Pigott agrees: "Training for a marathon provides repeated evidence that you can tolerate discomfort, persist and improve."
Building a new community
This resonates with Trent, who says running helped him to deal with tough emotions. It also gave him repeated evidence that he could do difficult things — including overcoming his addictions and building a new life. It provided the foundations for forming new relationships, as his 440 community started to grow.
Sobriety can be an isolating place, says Arunogiri. It often means leaving behind friends who aren't sober.
"You can find it really hard to find connections with new people that don't focus on using [drugs]," she says. "Social running groups can be incredibly helpful in changing that pattern and building new social connections."
Unlike Trent's 440, which welcomes all runners, Melbourne run group Run Into Recovery focuses on building a community for those impacted by addiction. The group meets every Sunday with the goal of forming connections with others who have similar lived experiences.
Former addicts can often receive less compassionate messages that focus on the negative, Arunogiri says — don't do this, don't do that.
"It's really helpful to have some positive things in your life that you want to move towards," she says.
Psychologist Burgess agrees. She says while seeing a psychologist to understand what led to a cycle of negative addiction is a good thing, she says, "finding a new outlet to focus your energy is important".
"A set of other things for you to commit to … gives you a sense of self-worth and a different identity," she says. "It's something else that a former addict can describe themselves as," she says.
Those experiences, says Pigott, "can then spill into broader perceptions of competence and self-esteem."
Trent can relate. Running helped his identity expand. No longer defined by drugs or alcohol, he was a runner.
As humans we desire belonging. Van Wijngaarden says marathon running offers this connection, as race days "bring a sense of solidarity and community".
But it can also be as simple as running with mates, and that's what can make run clubs like Trent's so powerful. As a marathon runner myself, I often think about some of my own friendships, where connections have been formed and maintained through our love of running.
Outside of community building, marathon running also provides opportunities to contribute to something bigger than yourself. Many events embed social purpose by supporting charitable causes.
At all marathon world majors — Tokyo, Boston, London, Sydney, Berlin , Chicago, New York City and Cape Town, which holds its first marathon next year — participants are able to support a charity. And with applications to enter far outnumbering the capped spots available (in Sydney 123,000 runners apply for 40,000 places), a compelling fundraising element can win some applicants guaranteed entry.
The London 2026 Marathon broke its own record as the largest one-day fundraising event in the world, raising £87.5million ($AU116 million) for various organisations. The Sydney Marathon has raised about $40 million for charity since its inception in 2001, with $9 million of that in 2025 alone. This year's fundraising effort is believed to have already surpassed $14 million.
"Years ago, it would have been a rather odd person that was doing marathons, but now it's quite common and it's sort of socially acceptable and socially applauded for people to do marathons," says Burgess.
"People are attached to not just the running, but to the social purpose that they're trying to raise funds for, so it gives it an extra meaning for them."
Craving a challenge
Two years ago I ran my first marathon. My alarm buzzed at 4am and the nerves fired up almost instantly as I consumed coffee, banana and peanut butter toast. I had been training for six months and knew the painful road ahead.
The Gold Coast Marathon is known for its flat course and beachside scenery and attracts runners from across the globe hoping to race a personal best. I was one of nearly 9,000 marathon runners in 2024 and as we took off, I remember my heart pounding as my feet slapped the pavement, dodging runners all around.
About five minutes in, I settled into a rhythm, at times stopping my music to hear the thousands of bystanders cheer us on. The first half of the race was the best I have ever run, my mind felt clear and nothing has ever felt so powerful.
As I started the back half of the race, however, the full force of a passive strength training program kicked in. By the 25km and 30km checkpoints everything started to hurt, and my breathing lost its rhythm. No matter how much water and electrolytes I drank, or gels and red frogs I ate, the cries from my completely fatigued muscles grew louder and louder.
Florey's Peter van Wijngaarden believes that, in a world that revolves around instant gratification, which sends a rush of dopamine but a sense of restlessness or impatience over time, more people are craving a challenge like a marathon.
"The appeal lies in the simplicity of the act of running a marathon — there is a start line, a finish line and a clock. In an increasingly complex world, this simplicity has its attractions," he says.
"Long distance running training offers the opportunity to zone out mentally, to enter a flow state where thoughts wash over you. Many runners describe this as a mental state in which they gain a new sense of clarity over the problems that they are grappling with."
This is what is known as "runners high", and I felt it during my Gold Coast race. After about an hour of my mind playing tricks, begging me to stop and pull out, the pain started to move to the back of my mind. In a weird way, I started to enjoy the suffering, I felt alive.
Pigott says there is a psychological reason why suffering can become part of the reward.
"We don't necessarily seek pleasure by avoiding discomfort," she says. "We often derive enormous psychological reward from overcoming meaningful discomfort."
But it's important to keep in mind that like many things in life there can be too much of a good thing.
Marathon running can take a serious toll on the body. It's important to take care and consider proper training and nutrition.
A recent small study using MRI scans of marathon runners found a temporary decrease in myelin water fraction — a proxy for brain myelin content — after endurance exercise such as a marathon.
Imaging showed significant thinning of myelin, the insulating layer around nerve projections in parts of the brain that regulate muscle function, sensation and emotion.
"It is thought by some that the cause of these changes is the metabolism of the fat-rich myelin to fuel active neurons and supporting brain cells. These changes may explain, in part, why some people experience difficulty with working memory shortly after a marathon," says van Wijngaarden.
"Importantly, in each case these changes reversed within two months of the marathon."
Burgess says it's also important to ensure running doesn't become "the primary source of a person's self-esteem".
"The negative things are when … it affects their eating and other mental health problems because the only thing that matters to them is to do their training. So they neglect themselves physically in other ways, or they neglect relationships in their life so they can't spend time with their partner or their children or anyone else in their lives because they haven't done their training," she says.
The long road back
Last year marked five years sober for Trent, a milestone I naively assumed came with ease and celebration.
"My whole fifth year was just mental, absolutely mental. I felt paralysed with trying to engage with people, projects, blaming everyone for everything," he says.
His running shifted course. He ran three marathons in three months — Gold Coast, Sydney and Melbourne — to distract himself from mental struggles he wasn't ready to face.
"[During the Gold Coast marathon] I got up the road, and I just remember it felt like someone had shot me in the back of the leg," he says. "And then the next 11km was just horrific."
The Sydney Marathon also delivered pain.
"I went through this beautiful nosedive again, body started shutting down, and I remember between stadium and Taylor Square, the [pacers] kept getting away and I was fading, and then I'd sprint, fading, sprint," Trent says.
He finished both the Sydney and Melbourne marathons in less than three hours, but not without serious consequences.
"The journey is this," Trent says, speaking to himself, motivating: "You are sober, and that's awesome, and now we've got to evolve things. And if you want to continue to run for the next 10 or 20 years, you [need to] look at what you're doing that you need to change."
Trent says he's grateful for the injuries the marathons caused. He was forced to slow down, and finally commit to completing the 12 steps of recovery.
"The lessons out of that for me is that if you don't do your continued work … if I'm not doing them regularly and being mindful of how I do them, it's so easy to go off on a tangent," he says.
Now, Trent has found a new rhythm: an AA meeting at least every second day, shorter runs, and helping others.
"That's the way you stay sober is you help someone else, you hand it over and you pass it on," he says. "I'll be an addict and alcoholic for the rest of my life. But it's how you actually approach it, it's accepting it and now I'm lighter."
The marathons may be on hold for now, but for Trent running remains at the centre of everything. He continues to turn up to the beach at 4.40am and run in the dark.
"It's a hard thing," Trent says. "But it's also facing your fears. It's dealing with addiction. It's dealing with loss. We go through these moments of darkness but as we've proven in our community, you start in the dark. But we finish in the light."

Pakistan suspends eight officials over hospital fire that killed 14 babies

Pakistan suspends eight officials over hospital fire that killed 14 babies
Interim inquiry finds lack of fire safety protocols at Islamabad hospital, prompting suspensions and criminal probe.
Pakistan’s prime minister has ordered the suspension of eight officials and directed criminal proceedings against them after a fire killed 14 babies in the neonatal ward of a government-run hospital in the capital.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif issued the orders after an investigative committee presented its interim report on the fire at Islamabad’s Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), his office said in a statement on Saturday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Pakistan’s army chief back in Iran: Can he break peace talks deadlock?
- list 2 of 3Give Imran Khan proper medical care, cricket legends urge Pakistani gov’t
- list 3 of 3‘Where’s the humanity?’: Imran Khan’s sons fear for jailed ex-Pakistan PM
The blaze broke out shortly before 7am (02:00 GMT) on Wednesday in the Mother and Child Healthcare Centre, sparking inside the nursery before spreading rapidly through oxygen outlets fitted at each incubator.
The fire was confined to a third-floor nursery, but officials said it spread so quickly that staff were able to rescue only one baby from among the 15 being cared for there.
“The deaths of these innocent children are a heartbreaking tragedy that has left the entire nation grieving,” Sharif said in a statement, promising that those responsible would face “exemplary punishment”.
The eight suspended officials, named in a statement from the prime minister’s office, include the hospital’s executive director, two joint executive directors, the head of its neonatal department, two senior doctors, a security official, and the head of the Capital Development Authority’s emergency services.
Sharif also approved action against a company responsible for hospital security and its officials.
He has appointed the National Institutes of Health’s chief executive as PIMS’s acting director in the interim.
The interim inquiry presented to the prime minister this week found that the hospital had no meaningful fire safety protocols in place, and only two of PIMS’s 13 standard operating procedures addressed fire or emergencies.
The interim report found that supervisory staff were not on duty when the fire started, and only two nurses, a female security guard and a house officer were in the ward.
Emergency services were also not called until six minutes after the fire started, and the first emergency responders arrived 15 minutes after receiving the call, the statement said.
The panel also noted a separate fire had broken out at the hospital’s nursing hostel just a month earlier, without prompting any safety improvements.
One nurse, Razia Noreen, had pulled a child to safety before flames engulfed the ward, the report said. Sharif awarded her the Sitara-i-Khidmat state honour for public service and a cash reward of one million rupees (nearly $3,500) for the rescue, according to the statement.
Health Minister Mustafa Kamal called Pakistan’s health system “rotten” and backed a parliamentary investigation, while the government has pledged five million rupees (about $17,700) in compensation to each affected family.

Different faiths, one truth: Bhagwat’s oneness pitch in New York
NEW DELHI: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on Saturday placed Hindu inclusiveness and society-led political change at the centre of his closely watched address at Madison Square Garden, saying a Hindu who wanted India without Muslims would “not remain Hindu” and arguing that public opinion—not political power—was the starting point for lasting change.Bhagwat said the RSS wanted to influence policies, prevent conflicts and “stop wars”, but could not begin by seeking political influence. “Politics has now become a game of self-interest,” he said. Change, he argued, must start in society and create a public view that governments cannot disregard. “If there is public opinion, then no politician will dare to go against it,” he said.Speaking at the “Universal Oneness Celebration” at the Infosys Theatre in Madison Square Garden, Bhagwat said religions were different routes to the same truth. Rituals and religious discipline were necessary, he said, but they should not become more important than the larger goal of reaching the divine.“Diversity is a decoration for our humanity,” he said, adding that it must be “accepted, respected and protected”. While diversity was the rule of nature, unity was the truth behind it, he said.Bhagwat recalled being asked by Muslims during a 2018 lecture series in Delhi whether the RSS’s idea of a Hindu Rashtra meant they would be driven out.
“I said, no. That is not Hindu. If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslim in Bharat, he will not remain Hindu,” he said. Hindu thought, he added, required acceptance that different paths could lead to the same truth and that every human being had equal dignity.He said the RSS had since continued dialogues with Muslims and Christians, even though results had been slow. Dialogue and service, he said, must proceed together. He cited the organisation’s 1.3 lakh service projects and said assistance was provided without religious discrimination.Bhagwat also addressed questions about the RSS’s public image. The organisation, he said, was once “minuscule” and ignored but had acquired “some say” in Indian society over its 100-year journey. He blamed doubts about it on “wrong narratives” and said they would disappear if people saw the organisation from within.Calling for work at the local level, he asked religious and community leaders to create examples of unity and selfless service in their own countries and gradually take the dialogue to provinces, districts and smaller communities. Changing entrenched attitudes would be “laborious, tedious and time-consuming”, he acknowledged, urging participants not to abandon dialogue because it produced no immediate result. “RSS with all its might is always with you,” he said.The address came after days of controversy around the centenary-year event, organised by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue and supported by more than 200 Hindu American organisations. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani opposed the gathering, describing the RSS’s vision as exclusionary, but acknowledged that the city might not have the authority to cancel a private event.
A coalition of civil-rights, interfaith and community groups sought its cancellation, while USCIRF called for Bhagwat’s visa to be revoked and sanctions considered against RSS members. India rejected the commission’s remarks as biased. AHEAD’s X account was briefly suspended and later restored. American singer Mary Millben and BJP spokesperson Nalin Kohli separately criticised Mamdani, arguing that opposing the event contradicted his stated commitment to pluralism.

Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

Trump-shaped ecstasy pills are potentially lethal, Dutch institute says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
18:11:25 UTC
03:11:25 KST

Trump-shaped ecstasy pills contain dangerous chemical and could be deadly, Dutch group says
A Dutch drug addiction and mental health institute warned users on Friday about potentially lethal ecstasy pills shaped to look like the head of President Trump.
The respected Trimbos Institute said that several of the pills have been handed in recently at a network of centers that test drugs for users before they take them.
The institute warned in a "Red Alert" published on its website and social media that they contain a high concentration of a chemical called PMMA, or para-methoxymethamfetamine. The chemical is similar to MDMA, the active ingredient in ecstasy pills.
The institute says if PMMA is found in an ecstasy pill, then the pill is contaminated and could be lethal. Users don't feel the effect of the drug right away, the institute said, and could take a higher dosage, which could lead to overheating, epileptic seizures, loss of consciousness or heart problems.
"Absolutely do not use these pills," the institute warned.
It released a photo of the pills that have a depiction of Mr. Trump's head on one side and on the other side "NL" and "Trump" stamped into the surface on either side of a vertical line. One of the pills has a green face, and another is yellow.
"We do not know of any victims where PMMA was found in their blood," she told The Associated Press.
Producing, selling and using ecstasy is illegal in the Netherlands, but it's widely used, particularly at clubs and music festivals. A government report in 2024 said that some 550,000 people took the drug in a year.
The Trimbos Institute tests drugs through its national network of 12 participants and 34 testing locations in the Netherlands.

Centre finalising Art 371 framework for Ladakh, says Rijiju

Centre finalising Article 371 framework for Ladakh, says Rijiju
Naseer Ganai / TNN / Updated: Aug 30, 2026, 00:34 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
MHA finalising special Article 371 framework for Ladakh, says Union minister Kiren Rijiju; PM Modi to visit and share views on proposed provisions.
SRINAGAR: Ladakh is poised for a bespoke constitutional shield, with MHA putting the final touches to a special Article 371 framework for the Union territory, Union minister Kiren Rijiju said.PM Narendra Modi will visit Ladakh to share his views on the proposed framework with people, Rijiju said Friday at a function at Druk Padma Karpo School in Leh district.“Autonomous hill development councils and other existing arrangements are not as empowered. So, recent announcement made by home minister Amit Shah to provide a special provision for Ladakh under Article 371 is going to take shape with the blessings of PM Narendra Modi,” Rijiju said.
Unlike Article 370, which gave J&K a high degree of autonomy before its abrogation in 2019, Article 371 provides special, temporary and transitional provisions for balanced regional development and protection of tribal cultures, customary laws and local employment.The proposed Ladakh model is being framed as a “sui generis” governance arrangement. It is expected to offer administrative flexibility and safeguards for tribal land, environment, traditional practices and jobs without granting statehood or directly bringing the region under Sixth Schedule.
Rijiju said the provisions would include seven councils, matching Ladakh’s expanded district map. “Earlier, Ladakh had only two districts. Leh and Kargil. Now there are seven districts and along with them there will be seven councils,” he said.
Ladakhi representatives from Leh Apex Body and Kargil Democratic Alliance, the region’s two major political groupings, have been in talks with MHA since 2023 for constitutional safeguards covering land, jobs, culture and environment. Next round of talks is scheduled for Sept in New Delhi.Rijiju said Modi had long believed Ladakh needed special attention and had worked towards its development since taking office in 2014. He said the region’s transformation had been striking, pointing to roads, electricity, water, mobile connectivity and telecommunications that were largely absent a couple of decades ago.“When we were in university, and later when I became an MP in 2004, I came to Ladakh,” he said. “There were no roads, electricity, water or other basic facilities. Today, the situation has changed. With mobile phones available everywhere, vast road network, telecommunication facility, we no longer have to wonder how long it takes to travel from one part of Ladakh to another.”

He said the region’s transformation had been striking, pointing to roads, electricity, water, mobile connectivity and telecommunications that were largely absent a couple of decades ago.“When we were in university, and later when I became an MP in 2004, I came to Ladakh,” he said. “There were no roads, electricity, water or other basic facilities. Today, the situation has changed. With mobile phones available everywhere, vast road network, telecommunication facility, we no longer have to wonder how long it takes to travel from one part of Ladakh to another.”

The hormonal and cognitive benefits of group singing for adults with brain conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
18:00:50 UTC
03:00:50 KST

When people are first diagnosed with a brain condition, they may not consider joining a choir to improve their wellbeing and regain their voice.
But as our research shows, there’s a strong link between singing in a choir and self-reported quality of life for people with brain injuries and dementia – as high as for community choir members without communication disabilities.
The University of Auckland’s Centre for Brain Research launched the CeleBRation Choir almost two decades ago to help stroke survivors and adults with other brain conditions through voice exercises and singing of familiar songs.
Singing in this choir has helped people overcome difficulties with speech, language, voice and memory.
Singing as therapy
Brain conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and dementia often impair people’s ability to communicate. This can undermine their confidence and ability to connect with others.
They are still the same person, but they might be treated differently and many become socially isolated because others can find it hard to talk with someone who can’t easily respond.
Singing in a neurological choir – a singing group designed for individuals living with acquired brain injuries and neurodegenerative disorders – reduces social isolation and the sense of loss that often follows diagnosis. Joining in with a favourite old song is uplifting, and singers usually leave choir sessions with a smile.
The body works in a similar way during speech and singing – both work the lungs, voice mechanisms and overlapping brain pathways lost to conditions such as Parkinson’s or stroke.
People with Parkinson’s disease can struggle to articulate their speech clearly and can have difficulty breathing adequately to project their voice. Singing helps them to speak more loudly and clearly.
A stroke or brain injury can also cause aphasia, a language disorder which makes it difficult to find the right words and process other people’s speech.
Singing as many words in a song as they are able to allows people to practise vocalising, without the battle to find all the right words. Stroke survivors can often sing their favourite songs more fluently than they can speak.
Emotional connection through song
Neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and late-stage Parkinson’s are associated with dementia, which affects people’s ability to function in everyday life.
Singing taps into a person’s emotional and autobiographical memory. Songs they recall from their youth can prompt lively conversations even if they seldom speak.
Group singing can increase levels of brain chemicals that boost mood. It can raise levels of oxytocin, a hormone that fosters human connection, and endorphins, the feel-good hormones that create runner’s high – and perhaps singer’s high, too.
At the same time, cortisol levels fall, encouraging stress release and relaxation. Singing in a choir offers meaningful activity, melodic pleasure, motivation and peer support.
Given one in three New Zealanders will be affected by a neurological condition in their lifetime, we need more choirs.
After co-founding and leading the CeleBRation choir, I set up another local group and was inspired to create The VOCCAL Handbook as part of my doctoral research for anyone wanting to start their own neurological choir.
No prior singing experience is required to join a neurological choir. Some participants are lifelong singers – for them, joining a choir means fun, friendship and therapy that harnesses their musical skills.
Others summon courage to quell often decades-long self-consciousness, even fear, about singing. Once in the room, the sense of camaraderie and give-it-a-go attitude is contagious.
Music that is well-known and well-loved is key, making singing easier for stroke survivors with the language disorder aphasia and people with dementia. However, picking everyone’s favourite songs poses a challenge in large, multi-generational groups with diverse tastes, so a varied repertoire needs to be negotiated.
Songs with complex verses and repetitive choruses offer a blend of challenge and accessibility. Vocables – short, meaningless syllables such as fa la la la la or dooby dooby doo – and humming can improve speech clarity and voice quality and help everyone join in.
Internationally, therapeutic choirs typically offer a space for people with one type of brain condition – such as Parkinson’s choirs. In Aotearoa, many neurological choirs are more inclusive, open to people with a variety of brain conditions.
Neurological choirs offer singers hope, fellowship and increased confidence. They provide a place to recover lost abilities in an upbeat setting. I wrote The VOCCAL Handbook because we need more singing, more choirs and more trained facilitators.

Live: Wallabies face Los Pumas in first Test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29

Wallabies vs Argentina: Australia defeats Los Pumas 27-21 in first rugby Test
The Wallabies have won a gritty and tense Test match described by two separate players as "bloody hard", securing a 27-21 win over Argentina.
Australia scored four tries to three in Sunday morning's clash in the mountain town of San Salvador de Jujuy, where the stadium sits more than 1,200 metres above sea level.
The Wallabies made a hot start with three tries in the opening 20 minutes, but had to show plenty of determination to hold off an Argentine fightback to secure the team's fourth Test win in a row.
The Australian forwards were excellent for much of the match, especially disrupting the Los Pumas' line-out in the second half.
Wallabies flanker Fraser McReight was named player of the match after an effort where he was a constant feature around the ball, including a crucial penalty won late in the contest with Argentina attacking inside the 22m.
"It was a back-and-forth sort of match," McReight told the host broadcaster.
"Argentina were very good. I felt like we were pretty poor in some areas, but [I'm] just really proud of the group and I'm happy we got the win over here."
The Wallabies were by no means perfect in Jujuy, with winger Max Jorgensen and flanker Tom Hooper each describing the match and conditions as "bloody hard" in separate interviews.
The Wallabies made a hot start with the opening two tries of the match. Hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa finished off a lovely passage of passing between forwards to score in the seventh minute, then fly half Carter Gordon touched down four minutes later from close range after the Wallabies forwards pounded their way to the goal line.
Argentina struck back through fullback Geronimo Prisciantelli after a lovely backline move, but when McReight scored in the 20th minute, the Wallabies were in control at 19-7.
But Los Pumas wrestled back the momentum, and a sin bin with Wallabies winger Harry Potter for deliberately knocking the ball down in the 25th minute put the home side in the ascendancy.
Argentina number eight Joaquin Moro took a quick tap from close range and powered over the line to reduce the deficit to five points, but a penalty goal from Wallabies scrumhalf Ryan Lonergan gave Australia a 22-14 lead at the break.
Lonergan came off after just five minutes in the second half after making a desperate cover tackle to deny Prisciantelli a second try.
Los Pumas were denied a try due to a forward pass picked up by the TMO in the 48th minute, but loosehead prop Boris Wenger dove over three minutes later to reduce Australia's lead to one point.
But the Wallabies responded quickly, with a line break from centre Hunter Paisami putting Australia into the attacking 22m, and leading to Hooper reaching out a few plays later to give the Wallabies a 27-21 lead.
The Wallabies were on top as the second half wore on, but could not get the try to seal the game. Jeremy Williams knocked on while trying to score, then reserve scrumhalf Tate McDermott was held up over the line.
It kept Los Pumas in the contest, but the Wallabies' defence held firm in the final five minutes to secure the win.
"It was a very tough game. Everyone knows that coming over to Argentina is a bloody hard place to win. It's you against them, plus the whole stadium," Jorgensen told Stan Sport.
"It wasn't near perfect, we've still got a lot of work to do, but to come away with a win in Argentina is very good."
The win is Australia's fourth in a row, and maintains coach Les Kiss's perfect record after three Tests in charge.
Australia has leapfrogged Argentina into seventh on the World Rugby rankings, with both sides to meet next week in the second Test at Mendoza.

“Philip K. Dick comes on without fanfare. His novels are published as science fiction,…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
17:49:16 UTC
02:49:16 KST

“Philip K. Dick comes on without fanfare. His novels are published as science fiction, which limits their “packaging” to purple-monster jackets, ensures but restricts their sales, and, above all, prevents their being noticed by most serious critics or reviewers. His prose is austere, sometimes hasty, always straightforward, with no Nabokovian fiddle-faddle. His characters are ordinary — extraordinarily ordinary — the inept small businessman, the ambitious organization girl, the minor craftsman or repairman, etc. That some of them have odd talents such as precognition is common; they’re just ordinary neurotic precognitive slobs. His humor is dry and zany. You can’t quote funny bits from Dick, because you have to have read the whole book up to that point to know why it’s so funny when the taxicab gravely assures Barney, “I think you’re doing the right thing.” Taxicabs often talk in Dick’s novels; they are usually earnest, but mistaken. Finally, his inventive, intricate plots move on so easily and entertainingly that the reader, guided without effort through the maze, may put the book down believing it to be a clever SF-thriller and nothing more. The fact that what Dick is entertaining us about is reality and madness, time and death, sin and salvation — this has escaped most readers and critics. Nobody notices; nobody notices that we have our own homegrown Borges, and have had him for thirty years.”
— Ursula K. Le Guin, The Language of the Night

Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27

Zimbabwe crash involving church minibus kills 27
August 29, 2026
At least 27 people were killed in a minibus crash in central Zimbabwe after the vehicle carrying churchgoers collided head-on with a truck, police said Saturday. Seven people were injured.
Police spokesperson Paul Nyathi said members of a popular Indigenous African Christian denomination, known for wearing white robes, were traveling to a conference on Friday when their minibus collided with a truck on a major highway near the town of Chivhu, about 140 kilometers (87 miles) south of the capital, Harare.
The foreign-registered haulage truck was overtaking another vehicle when it collided with the minibus. Both vehicles were carrying an "unspecified" number of passengers, Nyathi said in a statement.
Footage shared on social media by public broadcaster ZBC showed the mangled minibus charred to a shell.
Zimbabwe faces road safety crisis
Authorities say 94% of road accidents occur due to human error. Many Zimbabweans rely on privately operated minibus taxis, known locally as kombis, for everyday transportation. The vehicles are often criticized for carrying more passengers than allowed.
Zimbabwe’s roads are also riddled with potholes after years of underfunding and neglect, while driving standards can be poor.
In April, at least 18 people were killed when a minibus burst into flames on a highway in southern Zimbabwe. Earlier that month, a woman and her five children were killed when their vehicle collided with a haulage truck on another highway linking Zimbabwe and South Africa.
Road crashes kill about 300,000 people across Africa each year, accounting for roughly a quarter of the global road death toll, according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The continent has the world’s highest road fatality rate, the commission says.
This is despite Africa’s 1.5 billion people accounting for only about 3% of the world’s vehicle fleet.

In Ein Kerem, Israel’s most unlikely wellness retreat becomes a source of healing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
17:39:19 UTC
02:39:19 KST

By our second morning at the Khan Ein Karem Boutique Hotel, something had already begun to shift. Roi and Tomer, the hotel’s warm and attentive hosts, understand this quiet rhythm perfectly. Their hospitality philosophy is simple: Give visitors tranquility, space, and a nourishing breakfast, then let the valley do the rest.
What Adi and I discovered over the weekend is that Ein Kerem’s deepest wellness offering isn’t the landscape alone but the remarkable concentration of people who have chosen to build their lives inside it. In a country navigating complex realities and social fractures, Ein Kerem holds an unusual number of individuals who have each developed their own philosophy of healing and chosen to share it openly with those who arrive.
“It is a capsule of this multicultural, interreligious encounter that is so special and sadly almost doesn’t exist in Israel,” Roi told us over breakfast at the hotel’s inviting dining table. “Here, when you go out and start walking, you meet. You have no choice.” Meeting, as our weekend unfolded, turned out to be the most restorative act of all.
Food for the soul: Café Itah
On Friday morning, Adi and I made our way down the stone stairs to Café Itah – meaning “woman” in Aramaic – a courtyard kitchen that operates as a model of social healing and community hospitality. Our host, Moti Levi, a local contractor who lives a minimalist lifestyle in renovated buses in nearby Givat Ye’arim, founded the café as a social enterprise under the Tirosh Association.
Its mission is to provide dignified, therapeutic employment for young women and teenage girls navigating personal crises, trauma, and institutionalization. The café also acts as a safety net for girls who age out of closed state welfare facilities at 18 and suddenly find themselves without shelter; Moti frequently steps in to give them a safe place to sleep.
Head chef Amit spent 12 years managing kitchens in high-end catering and luxury hotels, including the King David Hotel, before reshaping her career around a double purpose. Under her direction, the café delivers a genuinely high-level culinary experience – zucchini latkes, rich shakshukas, house-made pestos, and hand-preserved lemons – but the quality of the food is ultimately a vehicle for something deeper.
“I had no satisfaction in just working in a restaurant and serving food to a customer,” Amit said. “I wanted satisfaction in my heart at the end of the day – the satisfaction of doing something good for someone.” Of the kitchen itself, she added, “I am a very hyperactive person, and the kitchen is a place of creation to release that. The world of pastry and cooking is a therapeutic path.”
This approach demands a forgiving business model. Amit gives the girls time and space to process crises and anxiety attacks, noting that “in any other restaurant, they wouldn’t give you the space; they would just kick you out.” Her guiding rule: “The customer is temporary… but for her, this is her life. My girls come before the customer.”
Anchoring this support system is Avraham, a 60-year-old retired village resident who sits on a wooden bench in the courtyard each day between noon and 4 p.m. – a calm, steady figure the girls can sit beside to regulate their breathing when anxiety rises mid-shift.
The impact runs deep. One young woman told us she’d once spent an entire year shut inside her home, paralyzed by depression; another said, “I never managed to hold a job for five days a week… but here it’s like family. You aren’t treated like a robot; you are seen as a human being first.”
Sitting in the sun-kissed courtyard over this exceptional food, you understand that its therapeutic value is inseparable from the well-being of the hands that prepared it.
The scribe of lost stories: Avshalom Eshel
Between the village’s stone alleys and the ridge where the Music Center awaits, we met one of Ein Kerem’s most remarkable figures: Avshalom Eshel, who moves between the hassidic religious world and the creative world of arts as though they were never separate.
Avshalom is officially a sofer stam – a traditional Jewish scribe who writes Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzahs by hand. He playfully reinterprets the Hebrew acronym STAM as “Stories, Tricks, and Plots.” Outside his studio hangs a sign describing his daily mission: “Conductor of roads for lost stories.”
Inside, he directs theatrical plays, including an upcoming production of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov’s The Seven Beggars. His own return to religion was sparked by reading Rabbi Nachman’s stories and falling in love with a religious woman who happened to sit beside him on a bus – an encounter that led to their marriage and six children.
His calligraphy, he explained, is a spiritual remedy for the modern age. Teivah in Hebrew means both “ark” and “word.” Since a physical ark can no longer shelter a person from the flood of modern noise and anxiety, Avshalom crafts tiny “arks” out of positive words, writing them by hand on parchment to give to visitors as a portable refuge. Every person, he teaches, is like a single letter in a Torah scroll; if even one letter is cracked or missing, the whole scroll is invalid. “This is our medicine,” he said, “to return and be parts of one big story.”
That philosophy runs through his workspace: a building that houses a secular yeshiva downstairs and a joyful, “hippie” Orthodox synagogue upstairs. Before we spoke, he picked up his sitar – a stringed musical instrument – letting its resonant tones settle the room, then pressed our personalized parchment tags into our hands.
Because Avshalom lives intentionally offline and refuses a smartphone, our visit ended with him offering his wife’s WhatsApp number – a fitting close for a man whose life is devoted to genuine human connection.
Sacred soundscapes and open tables
On Friday afternoon, we visited the Eden-Tamir Music Center on the village’s upper ridge, welcomed by Prof. Rami Eden (son of co-founder Bracha), Dr. Dror Semmel, and longtime host Saleh. Founded in 1968 by the piano duo Bracha Eden and Alexander Tamir, the center has anchored Jerusalem’s classical music scene for nearly six decades.
Its intimate 120-seat hall houses a rare fortepiano – a replica of an 1819 Viennese instrument built by master craftsman Paul McNulty – whose lighter, softer sound lets us hear Beethoven and Schubert nearly as their first salon audiences did, without the volume of a modern grand piano. The center still hosts chamber concerts every Saturday morning and biweekly Friday performances for young Israeli artists.
During our Shabbat walk, we found a striking blend of art and tradition at the Jewish House, the local Chabad House run by Rabbi Shaya and Nechemi Kedelburg. Housed in a restored stone building that doubles as an art gallery and vintage boutique, it felt unlike any conventional Chabad house – artistic, localized, and rooted in Ein Kerem’s bohemian character.
Over a long Shabbat conversation, we watched secular artists, traditional residents, and international travelers share the same table, a quiet proof that belonging can be one of the most powerful forms of harmony.
The gathering table
On Thursday evening, we dined at the Ein Kerem Courtyard Restaurant, one of the village’s few kosher establishments, over baked cauliflower with tehina and cheese-stuffed phyllo.
The meal set the tone for how Ein Kerem functions as a crossroads where social boundaries dissolve. On any afternoon, its limestone alleys host Christian priests beside barefoot anthroposophical families, secular tech workers, and haredi (ultra-Orthodox) families who’ve driven in from central Jerusalem for a change of pace.
That spirit peaks every Thursday night in the courtyard of Avshalom’s building, where wooden tables go up under the open sky for 80 to 100 people – an evening of cholent, live theater, and acoustic jam sessions that bypass political and religious divides entirely. Among the regulars is a woman who drives every week from Ofakim, in the South, just to be part of it.
As the weekend closed, Adi and I sat on the Khan Hotel’s upper balcony watching the sun cast long shadows across the terraces, our Shabbat table catered by chef Eli Fadida of Beit HaKerem and the celebrated Pasha in Talpiot.
Community, it turns out, is the oldest and most effective wellness intervention. Ein Kerem doesn’t offer it packaged; it offers it in the raw, unscheduled way of a village where the streets are too narrow to walk without meeting someone. The healers, scribes, chefs, musicians, and rabbis who have built their lives here are its greatest therapeutic asset. We left rested, fed, and quietly altered, carrying what the valley gave us back into the city above – the way water carries minerals from ancient stone.
