Reports of US funding cuts to Kurdish armed forces raises concerns over regional stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:24:22 UTC
01:24:22 KST

The Trump administration is planning to cut funding to the Peshmerga, the armed forces of the Kurdistan Regional Government, according to a BBC report that called the Peshmerga "a key Middle East ally that helped the US defeat the Islamic State group (IS) and is now facing punishing attacks from Iran, according to four sources familiar with the matter."
Kurdish media Rudaw said Washington had not informed the Peshmerga of a plan to cut funding.
Discussions and concerns about the US reducing funding for the Peshmerga have been key issues for years. The Peshmerga have played a key role over the years fighting ISIS and securing the autonomous Kurdistan Region. However, efforts to reform them have not proceeded as planned. In addition, the US is withdrawing from Iraq on September 30.
A bit of history helps explain the issues involved.
The Kurdish Peshmerga have been an important military force in the Middle East in the last decade. The Peshmerga date back to the Kurdish national movement of the twentieth century. Following the establishment of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq after the 1991 Gulf War, the Peshmerga became the region's official security force. However, the force remained divided between the two dominant Kurdish political parties: the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), whose military formation became known as Division (or Unit) 80, and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), whose forces were organized as Division (or Unit) 70. This division complicated command and control despite cooperation against common threats.
US expands military assistance after Kurdish forces halts ISIS advance
The rise of ISIS in 2014 highlighted both the strengths and challenges facing the Peshmerga. Kurdish forces played a decisive role in halting ISIS's advance, defending Erbil, protecting displaced civilians, and later participating in the campaigns to liberate Sinjar, Kirkuk, and areas surrounding Mosul.
Their battlefield performance led the United States and the Global Coalition to significantly expand military assistance, training, and equipment programs. There had been an effort to reform the forces before 2014. The concept was to move them away from party affiliation toward a neutral Peshmerga ministry. The ISIS war and the 2017 Kurdistan Independence referendum delayed this effort.
A central component of that effort by the international community to support the Peshmerga has been the Kurdistan Training Coordination Center (KTCC) in Erbil. Established by coalition partners during Operation Inherent Resolve, the KTCC has coordinated multinational training programs, standardized instruction, and helped professionalize Kurdish units. Coalition members have trained thousands of Peshmerga soldiers in infantry tactics, staff planning, leadership, logistics, and specialized military skills while also advising the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs on broader institutional reform.
I witnessed this firsthand on visits to the region. The training was paying off. The Peshmerga Ministry was trying to modernize.
However, the region faces many crises. Baghdad has sought to weaken the region economically. There have been threats from Iran and Iranian-backed militias. Turkey has also operated in areas near the border. The KDP and PUK can’t get along in the regional parliament. Everything is on hold due to local political squabbles. The result is that international support is sometimes either taken for granted or not leveraged to its full potential.
BBC wrote that “the US Department of Defense has told leaders of Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region in recent meetings that the administration is not planning to renew an expiring agreement that provides security assistance to the Peshmerga, the Kurdish security force.”
Funding cut may embolden Iran
The report notes that “Kurdish officials fear the funding cut would create a power vacuum and embolden Iran, which has fired hundreds of missiles and drones into Iraqi Kurdistan since US President Donald Trump started the war with Tehran.” Yerevan Saeed, the director of the Global Kurdish Initiative for Peace at American University, told the BBC that "the US would be cutting off the Kurds, who shed so much blood to help the Americans achieve their goals in Iraq and the wider Middle East…This is going to be a big win for Iran, China, and Russia if the Kurds are left so exposed."
The report added that the Peshmerga has around 180,000 troops in Iraqi Kurdistan and they “received $61m (£45m) in the fiscal year 2026 for weapons, military training and stipends through the Pentagon's counter-IS program.”
For such a large force, this isn’t a lot of funds. However, the US is dealing with many issues in the region. It is trying to deal with Gaza and Lebanon and the war with Iran.
BBC notes that “the Pentagon signed the initial memorandum of understanding giving military assistance to the Peshmerga in 2016 and renewed it in 2022. A final decision on security engagement between the US and Kurdistan is still being reviewed, according to one source familiar with the Pentagon's thinking. The US is considering ways to maintain some security support in both Iraq and Iraqi Kurdistan after the troop withdrawal, the sources said.”
According to Kurdish media outlet Rudaw, “Washington has not officially informed the Kurdistan Region's Peshmerga ministry of plans to halt financial assistance as a security agreement nears expiry, three informed sources told Rudaw on Saturday, after the BBC reported that the United States had told Erbil the deal would not be renewed.” The report noted that "regarding the termination of the aid, the US has told the Ministry of Peshmerga nothing officially," a senior ministry official told Rudaw’s Soran Hussein on Saturday.

====================================================================================================

Jerusalem's L3 opens after years of delays, turning one light rail line into a network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:24:15 UTC
01:24:15 KST

Living in central Jerusalem can be defined by a few key characteristics: the shuk, the noise, and, of course, the light rail.
Nearly a full year after we here at The Jerusalem Post bemoaned the temporary loss of the Haturim station, the payoff has arrived, and the L3 segment – the first section to open as part of the broader Green Line project and currently highlighted in yellow – opened to the public this week, running from Haturim to the Malha Mall.
The city went all in on the yellow branding, with balloon arches at every station, yellow signs, and lemon-flavored popsicles marking the grand opening.
The line’s opening was headlined by a who’s who of the Jerusalem infrastructure world, and was celebrated by Transportation Minister Miri Regev, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion, and Cfir CEO Oren Cohen.
The L3 route spans seven kilometers, running from Haturim station west through the Central Bus Station and the Navon rail station, before heading south to the Knesset and Hebrew University’s Givat Ram campus. It then stops at Teddy Stadium and Pais Arena before ending near the Malha Mall and the expanding Gav Yam tech park. The segment adds 12 stations to the network alongside the existing Haturim interchange and the Central Bus Station/Navon hub.
What matters most is that for the first time, Jerusalemites can transfer from one light rail line to another, and residents finally get to see what all that construction and noise has been about.
“It’s very reliable and convenient, and I don’t have to worry about missing my bus because, you know, it actually comes on time,” one passenger said after the launch. “Getting to Malha is a breeze now.”
Red Line recently expanded
The Red Line, the city’s first light rail corridor, has operated for 15 years, with recent expansions creating a vital link between Neve Yaakov and Hadassah Ein Kerem, carrying 200,000 riders daily.
However, as is common for public transport projects worldwide, the launch faced severe delays. Globes reported that the Green Line’s L3 phase opened 10 years later than planned, whereas earlier projections had envisioned the entire line being fully completed by 2025.
The delays over the past few years were compounded by the rounds of fighting with Iran, which disrupted construction and pushed the project’s timeline further.
The venture was initially approved by City Council in 2016, with tenders issued soon afterward, and construction has stretched across nearly a decade. The Green Line is also following a pattern familiar to residents: the Red Line’s extensions, initially slated for completion in 2023, were repeatedly pushed back before opening.
For residents along the route, the wait has meant years of construction, detours, and disrupted access to streets and businesses in areas including Givat Mordechai, Pat, and Jaffa Road.
But whether the delays were over a decade or just one year, the L3 is finally here, and Israel’s officials have been eager to frame the Green Line as a turning point for Jerusalem, even if some passengers found themselves decidedly underwhelmed.
“It smells like plastic which was just poured into a mold,” one passenger stated. “Also, it’s somehow already dirty, and I’m not surprised.”
For Mayor Moshe Lion, the opening marks a transformation in the city’s public transit landscape. “Jerusalem is moving from a city that has a light rail to a city with a light rail network,” he said, noting that the L3 marks the first step toward a fully interconnected transit grid.
“Together with the expanding park-and-ride facilities, this will soon become the city’s transportation backbone, transform its appearance and quality of life, connect neighborhoods, employment centers, and major institutions, and enable drivers to leave their private vehicles at home, and thus reduce traffic congestion and air pollution. L3 is not the finish line. The network will expand with additional lines, connect more and more parts of Jerusalem, and turn it into an accessible and advanced city like capitals and major cities around the world.”
Transportation Minister Miri Regev, who toured the line with Lion ahead of its opening, has similarly cast the project as part of a broader transportation revolution in the capital.
“Jerusalem continues to lead Israel’s public transport revolution and to demonstrate the direction in which we are taking transport in the major metropolitan areas: fast, efficient, interconnected, and accessible mass transit networks,” Regev said.
“The opening of the L3 line is a big step in our vision of connecting Israel and enabling all of its residents to reach their destinations quickly, comfortably, and safely.”
The next milestone is slated for December, when the L4 segment is set to link the Central Bus Station to Gilo in the south, the city’s largest neighborhood. This next phase will help more than 100,000 residents who are underserved by the light rail.
From there, the Green Line is expected to extend north toward Hebrew University’s Mount Scopus campus, scheduled to open by June 2027, running through French Hill and connecting the university’s two campuses by rail, which has been discussed by planners long before ground was even broken.
Looking to the future, the city has already begun construction on the Blue Line, set to run 24 km. from Ramot in the north to Gilo in the south, with 40 new stations.
However, that phase of the light rail isn’t projected to launch before 2029 or 2030, and the construction will bring several more years of the same street-level disruption residents just lived through with the Green Line.
Hopefully, the city will feel the same relief when that line opens as well.
Last week’s launch highlights Jerusalem’s success with surface light rail, contrasting with the far more complex and costly engineering of Tel Aviv’s $50 billion heavy underground metro system, which remains years away from completion.
While construction formally began with a cornerstone ceremony in December 2025, the tenders for the actual tunneling work are only now moving through pre-qualification, with operations not projected before the early-to-mid 2030s.
Bragging rights are great, but the stakes go further.
The light rail could eventually carry as many as 400,000 riders a day, easing a traffic problem that has only worsened, as Israel continues to suffer from some of the worst traffic congestion in the OECD.
For a city like Jerusalem, a genuine rail network does change who can live where and still remain connected to the heart of the city.
“Knowing that I don’t have to live right in the center of the city to benefit from the accessible transport will make living in Jerusalem easier in the long-term,” another passenger said.
One week in, it’s like the new stations have been with us all along, as commuters have already gotten used to checking updated schedules. The balloon arches have come down, but the trains keep on running.
For a city that has waited the better part of a decade for this moment, the milestone wasn’t really the ribbon-cutting, but the ordinariness of a new option simply existing.
The next test comes in December, when the line pushes farther south to Gilo. For now, Jerusalem has what it didn’t have a week ago: a network, not just a line.

Russian-American heads Trump's planned Caucasus trade route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:20:00 UTC
01:20:00 KST

Russian-American heads Trump's planned Caucasus trade route
August 29, 2026
Until recently, few people in the South Caucasus had heard of Konstantin Sokolov. Now the 52-year-old Russian-American businessman is at the center of new investment fund backed by US President Donald Trump.
In mid-July, Sokolov — who emigrated from Russia to the US at age 21 and later founded the investment firm IJS Investments in Chicago — was appointed to head a new investment fund of the US State Department.
The TRIPP+ EnterpriseFund, registered in the US as the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund and launched with more than $200 million (about €172.5 million) in capital, is expected to invest in countries across the South Caucasus and Central Asia and help finance the large-scale TRIPP infrastructure project, also known as the "Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity."
The "Trump Route" is a transit corridor that aims to connect Azerbaijan with its autonomous exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The ambitious infrastructure project is part of a peace deal that Armenia and Azerbaijan signed in August 2025 with US mediation. In early June 2026, Washington and Yerevan signed a framework cooperation agreement for the project.
Experts have said construction of the "Trump Route" fits Washington's strategy of creating a trade corridor between Europe and the region that bypasses existing routes through Russia and Iran.
Sokolov buys up Russian assets in Armenia
Long before he was appointed to head TRIPP+, Sokolov had already established a foothold in Armenia.
In 2024, he acquired Viva Armenia, the country's largest telecommunications provider. Despite its subsequent partial nationalization, Sokolov continued to expand his holdings. Recently, his companies also bought up the Armenian subsidiary of Russian telecom giant Rostelecom.
An even more significant deal, however, was carried out largely out of the public eye: the purchase of the Teghut copper-molybdenum mine. The mine, which holds an estimated 450 million metric tons of ore and has Armenia's second-largest reserves, had been taken over by Russia's state-owned VTB Bank after the company accumulated massive debts. VTB is now under Western sanctions. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's Armenian service, the deal was carried out through a third-party company.
"Sokolov wanted to avoid a direct deal with the Russian bank," said Mkrtich Karapetyan, a Radio Liberty journalist who has been investigating the flow of foreign capital into Armenia.
Sokolov: Trump supporter, MAGA backer
While Armenia's government and its supporters have welcomed the influx of Western capital into the country's infrastructure projects, the opposition has highlighted serious risks.
Mesrop Manukyan, a lawmaker from the opposition Armenia Alliance, is among Sokolov's most vocal critics in parliament. He said it's alarming that a US investor has been able to acquire major stakes in the finance, mining and telecommunications sectors in just a few years.
Manukyan's faction, which advocates close ties between Armenia and Russia, opposes the TRIPP+ project. It views the "Trump Route" as a disguised "extraterritorial corridor" and the "greatest threat" to Armenia's security.
Despite his extensive investments, Sokolov remains largely unknown to the Armenian public. There are no official photos of him, and he generally avoids interviews with the local press during business trips.
His most recent visit to the capital, Yerevan, was in early August, when he met with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan. He was accompanied by Aryeh Lightstone, senior adviser to US special envoy Steve Witkoff.
In Western media, however, Sokolov is known not only for his business ventures in the US and Switzerland but also for his political involvement. Sokolov is a major donor to the US Republican Party and a Trump supporter. According to The Associated Press, he donated about $11 million to Trump's MAGA movement over the course of a year.
'Compromise' between Moscow and Washington?
Benyamin Poghosyan of the Armenian think tank APRI sees two main reasons for Sokolov's appointment to head the fund.
The first is political. Appointing an American with Russian roots could be "a subtle gesture by Washington aimed at easing Moscow's fierce criticism of the project," he told DW.
The second, however, is pragmatic. "Perhaps Russia has nothing to do with it at all. Sokolov may simply have been chosen because he has a deep understanding of the business environment in the former Soviet Union — and because he knows Armenia and how its government works," said Poghosyan.
At the same time, the sheer scale of the investment and the financier's Russian roots are fueling speculation in Armenia. Social media users in the country are debating whether Sokolov, who was born in St. Petersburg, could be a secret "compromise figure" between Moscow and Washington. Supporters of the theory point to the ease with which US companies have acquired formerly Russian assets subject to Western sanctions.
Other observers have refuted the idea, noting that Sokolov has publicly and sharply criticized the Russian government and its war against Ukraine. The funds provided by the US State Department, running through 2036, are seen as flagging Washington's long-term strategic intentions in the region. During his visit to Yerevan, Aryeh Lightstone told Armenian news outlet CivilNet that the more than $200 million in initial funding could be viewed as a starting point for future investments.
Aram Sargsyan, head of the Republican Party of Armenia and an ally of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, also rejects the idea that Sokolov is a "compromise figure" for Moscow. He emphasized the practical value of Sokolov's background, seeing it as an opportunity rather than a cause for concern.
"Sokolov has significant business contacts, understands the Russian mentality perfectly, speaks the language and knows how to work with relevant Russian institutions," he said.
This article was originally written in Russian.

RSS chief’s visit to US denounced as ‘goodwill tour’ for Hindu nationalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:03:32 UTC
01:03:32 KST

RSS chief’s visit to US denounced as ‘goodwill tour’ for Hindu nationalism
Activists say Hindu nationalists have sought to mask far-right politics through broad appeals to the Indian diaspora.
An event in New York City featuring a prominent Hindu nationalist is being promoted as an invitation to send a positive message that “the world is one family”.
But an array of faith groups, advocacy organisations and unprivileged-caste organisations say they are not convinced. They fear Saturday’s rally, held at Madison Square Garden, is instead a high-profile effort to whitewash a record of discrimination and violence.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Oneness or Hindu supremacy? RSS chief Bhagwat’s secretive New York hosts
- list 2 of 3What is Hindutva, and what are the roots of this political movement?
- list 3 of 3Why India’s RSS is lobbying the West amid attacks on minorities at home
At issue is the Universal Oneness Celebration, hosted by the American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, a nonprofit that purports to advance “greater peace and harmony”.
One of its keynote speakers, however, will be Mohan Bhagwat, the leader of the Hindu paramilitary organisation Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). His organisation has been accused of embracing discriminatory policies and stoking violence against minorities, including India’s Muslim, Christian and Sikh populations.
Protests are expected outside Madison Square Garden to denounce Bhagwat’s appearance.
“This is a movement that has normalised mob violence against Muslims, attacks on Muslim men in relationships with Hindu women and the bulldozing of Muslim homes,” said Safa Ahmed, a Muslim community organiser in North Carolina who has travelled to New York to join the protests.
She told Al Jazeera she is sceptical about the event organisers’ claims about embracing the world as “one family”.
“They may speak about unity, but it’s in stark contrast with the bloody reality faced by minorities in India,” she said.
Overseas outreach
Advocates say that Hindu nationalist groups are working to expand their influence in the United States, where roughly 2.5 million Hindus live.
To do that, they have utilised a variety of appeals to soften the image of the RSS, such as celebrations of Hindu culture and campaigns to highlight anti-Hindu discrimination.
Sravya Tadepalli, the deputy executive director of Hindus for Human Rights, sees Saturday’s rally as part of that trend. Her group opposes the event.
“This is kind of a goodwill tour to improve the public image of the RSS, which is a fascist paramilitary organisation that has engaged in decades of communal violence against religious minorities in South Asia,” Tadepalli told Al Jazeera.
“The organisations behind this have pitched it as a broad appeal to Hindu history with an emphasis on inclusivity when, in reality, the RSS advocates for the exact opposite.”
Critics have pointed out, however, that Hindu nationalists have also sought to cultivate links with the global far-right, emphasising a shared belief in the purported threats posed by Islam and secular elites.
The RSS is widely considered the ideological parent of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has ruled India since 2014 and sought to remake the country along Hindu nationalist lines.
In remarks to the 2024 National Conservatism Conference in Washington, DC, BJP Vice President Ram Madhav said that conservatives in the West should view India as an example of how to defeat what he called the “left, liberal, Marxist, radical Islamist cabal”.
The Modi model
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who entered politics as an RSS cadre before becoming the head of the BJP, has championed Hindu nationalism throughout his leadership.
Like Bhagwat, he has also taken his message on the road, to speak to overseas supporters in the US.
In September 2019, for instance, the prime minister addressed a crowd of 50,000 at a “Howdy, Modi!” rally in the state of Texas.
The event underscored Modi’s appeal among Indians living abroad and was one of the largest such events in US history. US President Donald Trump, another far-right leader, even joined Modi on stage.
But such appearances were controversial too. Before becoming prime minister in 2014, Modi was banned from entering the US because of his leadership during a 2002 massacre of Muslim residents in the state of Gujarat.
Modi faced accusations of turning a blind eye to the slayings and even offering his support.
Even as he faces protests, though, Modi remains enormously popular in India, consistently ranking as one of the most popular leaders in the world. A survey this month from the magazine India Today found that he is also the top choice for prime minister in India, despite slipping approval ratings.
Divided diaspora
Still, outreach campaigns to rehabilitate the image of the RSS overseas have had limited success.
For instance, a 2024 survey found that, while Modi enjoyed near-majority support among Indian Americans for his performance as prime minister, 70 percent of respondents acknowledged that his rhetoric exemplified a growing threat to minorities in India.
Bhagwat’s planned appearance at Madison Square Garden has likewise ignited debate over his controversial commentary and leadership.
In a statement on Wednesday, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), an independent initiative within the federal government, called for Bhagwat’s visa to be revoked.
The commission warned that Bhagwat was “complicit in religious freedom violations”, along with other RSS members and Indian officials.
“Religious freedom conditions in India continue to deteriorate as violence and incitement are frequently used to target religious minority communities,” said USCIRF Chair Asif Mahmood. He urged the US to implement targeted sanctions.
When questioned about Bhagwat’s speech at a news conference this week, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani also spoke out against the RSS’s messaging.
“It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision of any country, frankly. And it is one that I find myself in deep opposition to,” Mamdani said, citing his identity as an Indian American.
He added that he does not “support the rally” but said he doubted the city had the jurisdiction to cancel a private event.
Ahmed, the community organiser from North Carolina, said she feels the backlash to Saturday’s event reflects a growing coalition in the Indian diaspora — one that brings together Hindu, Muslim, Sikh and unprivileged-caste voices.
“There is a vocal minority in the diaspora and a new, emerging majority who don’t believe in the politics of Modi and the RSS and who don’t want to see them gain traction here,” said Ahmed.
She predicted that Saturday’s event will ultimately backfire. “I’m very confident that Bhagwat will be met with a resounding rejection that he is not welcome.”

U.S. Army Received First XM30 Wolf IFV, Developed to Replace the Bradley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:01:12 UTC
01:01:12 KST

General Dynamics Land Systems has delivered the first prototype XM30 Wolf IFV to the U.S. Army for testing. The XM30 Wolf is currently competing with the XM30 Lynx as the future replacement for the Bradley IFV.
This was announced by Jeffrey Norman—a retired U.S. Army brigadier general who currently serves as director of strategy and development for General Dynamics Land Systems in the U.S.—on his LinkedIn page.
“We will continue to improve the XM30 Wolf every day through new software versions, new technologies that integrate easily via our modular, open system architecture, and an innovative digital design built from the ground up with upgradeability in mind,” he stated.
The XM30 is already the sixth U.S. Army program since the 1980s aimed at replacing the Bradley, while all previous programs have failed.
In early 2020, the Lynx KF41 from the Raytheon-Rheinmetall consortium and the Griffin III from General Dynamics Land Systems competed in the contest for a new infantry fighting vehicle.
However, both proposals were disqualified. The first due to the lack of a finished prototype, and the second due to non-compliance with requirements. Following this, the U.S. Army announced a relaunch of the program in 2021.
The Wolf is a new design that is likely based in part on existing solutions from the European ASCOD IFV developed by General Dynamics European Landsystems. The Lynx is based on the KF41 Lynx design, which Rheinmetall Landsysteme, together with partners from Hungary and Italy, manufactures for the Hungarian, Italian, and Ukrainian markets. However, the vehicle has been significantly modified to meet U.S. requirements.
Both vehicles feature a layout typical of infantry fighting vehicles and a two-person crew seated side-by-side behind the engine and transmission compartment. The troop compartment at the rear of the hull is designed to carry six infantrymen.
Instead of a turret, the prospective IFV features an unmanned combat module that does not protrude into the hull. It is armed with a Northrop Grumman XM913 50 mm cannon, developed specifically for this project, which fires 50×228 mm ammunition. The cannon is paired with a standard 7.62 mm M240 machine gun.
The vehicles can also be equipped with an additional 12.7 mm Browning M2A1 heavy machine gun in a remotely controlled combat module mounted on the turret roof. The armament is complemented by a universal launcher for TOW or CCMS-H family anti-tank guided missiles, as well as for loitering munitions.
The level of armor protection has not been disclosed, but it is expected to be robust and modular. The protection package is complemented by Elbit’s Iron Fist active protection system, which was also selected for the M2A4ED1 Bradley.
The XM30 is expected to enter service in the early 2030s, gradually replacing the upgraded Bradleys in combat units.

The tendency of conspiracy theorists to police others online is associated with narcissistic traits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:00:32 UTC
01:00:32 KST

People who heavily endorse conspiracy theories often take on the role of online “social vigilantes,” seeking to correct the perceived ignorance of others. New research suggests that this tendency to act as self-appointed enforcers of truth online is largely driven by feelings of superiority and a desire for self-enhancement. The findings were published in Personality and Individual Differences.
Conspiracy theories often provide people with a dual sense of identity. Believers tend to view themselves as part of a privileged minority that has uncovered hidden truths, while also casting themselves as heroic underdogs fighting against powerful forces. Earlier research established that believing in conspiracy theories is closely tied to narcissism and feelings of intellectual superiority.
For instance, a review covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that one of the strongest personality traits linked to conspiracy beliefs is a tendency to act antagonistic and superior to others. Along similar lines, a 2022 review indicated that narcissistic desires to feel special and dominant make conspiracy narratives especially appealing, as they allow believers to feel uniquely insightful.
This prior research set the stage for a new question. Does this sense of superiority motivate conspiracy theorists to actively police and attack others on the internet? The research, led by Achilleas Piliousis, a PhD candidate in the Department of Journalism and Mass Communications at Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, investigated how and why people transform their private conspiracy beliefs into aggressive online behavior.
“The idea for this research originated from an observation that had intrigued me for several years, particularly in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic,” Piliousis said. “I noticed that some people who endorsed conspiracy beliefs—for example, about vaccines or climate change—did not simply express their views. They would also attack, disparage, or publicly shame those who disagreed with them, while portraying themselves as people who had ‘seen the truth’ and dismissing others as ‘sheep’ or ‘asleep’.”
“This led me to wonder whether conspiracy thinking might sometimes be associated with such online behaviors through social vigilantism, that is, the belief that one possesses superior knowledge or insight while simultaneously feeling a responsibility to expose, correct, or even police those perceived as ignorant or misinformed,” Piliousis explained.
To explore this idea, the researchers conducted three separate studies. The first study included 139 Greek adults and measured their general conspiracy thinking along with their belief in specific conspiracy theories about climate change and cancer. The participants also completed surveys measuring their levels of social vigilantism, dogmatism, intellectual humility, and narcissism. Piliousis and his colleagues found a moderate positive association between all the conspiracy variables and social vigilantism. Even when accounting for general arrogance, stubbornness, and close-mindedness, holding conspiracy beliefs remained a strong predictor of wanting to aggressively correct others.
The second study tested whether these vigilante tendencies actually translate into confrontational online habits. The research team surveyed 116 Greek participants, asking them about their beliefs in climate change conspiracy theories and their daily online behaviors. This included their willingness to argue online, their intent to participate in online shaming, and how they would comment on hypothetical Facebook posts about climate change.
One post featured factual information, while the other featured misinformation. The results indicated that climate change conspiracy beliefs indirectly predicted both a willingness to argue online and a desire to participate in online shaming, suggesting that the drive to act as a norm enforcer pushes believers toward aggressive digital habits.
“One key takeaway is that conspiracy thinking seems to be more than simply believing in particular conspiracy theories,” Piliousis noted. “When it becomes a broader lens through which people interpret the social world, it may shape how individuals perceive themselves and others.”
To see if these patterns held up in a different cultural context, the researchers conducted a third study with 188 participants from the United States. In this round, the team focused on general conspiracy thinking and asked participants about their actual frequency of getting into conflicts on social media over the past twelve months. They also wanted to see if specific types of narcissism were driving this behavior. As a result, they measured two distinct aspects of grandiose narcissism: narcissistic admiration, which is the desire to be seen as a great personality, and narcissistic rivalry, which involves an antagonistic desire to see others fail.
The findings from the American sample mirrored the earlier results. Conspiracy thinking indirectly predicted online argumentation, shaming intentions, and actual social media conflict, again acting through the channel of social vigilantism. Interestingly, when the researchers factored in narcissistic admiration, the statistical link between conspiracy thinking and social vigilantism weakened substantially.
“One finding that I found particularly interesting was the role of the agentic facet of narcissism, particularly narcissistic admiration,” Piliousis said. “Our findings suggest that self-enhancement motives may play an important role in these relationships.” Rather than acting as selfless heroes trying to save an unwitting public from danger, conspiracy theorists might engage in online enforcement largely to serve their own egos.
As Piliousis explained, “the adoption of a social vigilante role among conspiracy theorists may partly reflect self-focused motives, such as self-enhancement, self-affirmation, and the pursuit of status.”
The authors noted a few limitations in their work. “The nature of our data does not allow us to establish causal relationships,” Piliousis said. “Our findings indicate associations between the variables, but they cannot tell us what causes what. For this reason, longitudinal studies are needed to examine the direction of these relationships and provide stronger evidence for our theoretical proposal.”
The studies also relied heavily on self-reported intentions rather than directly observing how participants behaved on social media platforms. People might claim they would engage in online shaming, but they may not always follow through in a real-world setting. Future research could look at real comment sections and public conflicts to see how these dynamics play out in everyday life.
It is also an open question how the confrontational style of these social vigilantes affects passive observers on the internet. A highly aggressive approach to spreading conspiracy theories might make the ideas seem more visible and widespread, or it might backfire and push people away by coming across as overly hostile.
The study, “Conspiracy thinking and online surveillance: The rise of the “social vigilante”,” was authored by Achilleas Piliousis and Antonis Gardikiotis.

Andrey Belousov: NATO nuclear expansion leaves Russia no choice but to respond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
16:00:18 UTC
01:00:18 KST

Andrey Belousov: NATO nuclear expansion leaves Russia no choice but to respond
RT: It is well known that the United States has stationed nuclear weapons in NATO countries in Europe since the 1950s as part of a nuclear‑exchange programme. Why has the issue of removing US nuclear weapons from the region become a matter of fundamental importance at this moment?
Andrey Belousov: First and foremost, it must be noted that the problem of US nuclear weapons on the territory of European states and Turkiye has long been the subject of bilateral meetings on strategic stability, including at the beginning of the mid‑1990s. For the record, under presidential initiatives in the early 1990s, Russia reduced its non‑strategic nuclear arsenal four‑fold and kept the remainder at central storage bases.
We could reasonably expect symmetrical moves from the United States. Yet the actions taken by the US in the early 2000s – such as the withdrawal of nuclear weapons from Greece and the United Kingdom, and partially from Italy and Germany – seemed more like a tactical concession or a trick, without changing the military‑political context in Europe. After all, the US nuclear weapons withdrawal from Greece was fully compensated by their presence in Turkiye, and those withdrawn from the UK were replaced by its own nuclear arsenal of the United Kingdom – which is the main and most important ally, strategic ally of the United States.
In contrast, the measures taken to remove and reduce US nuclear weapons in Italy and Germany did not significantly enhance security, trust, or predictability, because the practice of US nuclear weapons in Europe and joint NATO nuclear missions continued unchanged. In short, if we keep talking about this, we must remember that at that time the United States consistently followed a line to enhance its strategic capabilities, primarily through the implementation of plans and programmes not directly related to strengthening its nuclear potential, most of which was under the arms‑control bans at the time – Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty and Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty.
By the mid‑1990s, the US began implementing its Global Missile Defence configuration, which envisaged deploying one of its segments – the third positional sector – in Europe. At the same time, the concept of a global lightning‑strike was being implemented, under which the US could use non‑nuclear strategic carriers to strike any target anywhere on Earth.
We should also mention the development of new nuclear delivery systems and, finally, a programme to create laser anti‑satellite air‑based systems. This also included the development of heavy strike UAVs that, by their technical characteristics, fell under the criteria of the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, but were not covered by it. It was also a key element of enhancing US strategic capacity.
Accordingly, during that period of reshaping strategic stability from a military‑security view, Russia’s priority was to mitigate the risks and threats that could arise from the execution of the projects and programmes I mentioned. It does not mean that the issue of US non‑strategic nuclear weapons in Europe fell out of Russian diplomatic focus, let alone the Russian military, which could not ignore this problem in its defensive planning.
As tensions with the United States and its satellites increased, Russia sharpened the issue of removing American nuclear weapons from Europe, and the complete withdrawal of that armament from European territory to national territory.
Today, however, we live in entirely different, more complex and dangerous conditions. The United States, with the support of its closest partners and allies, has disintegrated the system of arms‑control agreements on nuclear disarmament. The very important treaty on missile defence, essential for strategic stability, has been discarded. The removal of political and international‑law restrictions on the unchecked buildup of nuclear arsenals, together with Washington’s steps to create a missile‑defence system for the country combining land, sea, air and space segments – now all under the “Golden Dome for America” programme – coupled with the deep modernisation of U.S. nuclear potential, upgrading nuclear warheads and creating new carrier systems for intermediate‑ and shorter‑range missiles, has led to a radical deterioration of the military‑political situation both regionally and globally.
Naturally, this has had a profoundly negative impact on the strategic environment.In fact, the negative factors are not limitк ed to the present situation. Factors that must be considered in analysing the current modern context also include NATO’s provocative positioning as a nuclear alliance and the continuous attempts of member states to expand that alliance eastward. Moreover, plans for advanced and extended deterrence, and the expansion and deepening of NATO’s joint nuclear missions, are increasingly being implemented. All of this must be considered together to understand the environment in which we live now.
And, undoubtedly, these aspects compel us to give enhanced attention, during this historical period, to the non‑strategic US nuclear weapons deployed in Europe, as well as those of US allies in NATO – France and the United Kingdom. As a result, in the current conditions the factor of the total nuclear arsenal or the combined nuclear potential in the region takes on special importance in Russia’s military‑security context. The involvement of new states, NATO’s schemes for practising nuclear usage and discussing the possibility of deploying such weapons on their territory, and the introduction of new multifunctional aircraft platforms as delivery systems, increase the threat to Russia. The reason is that nuclear warheads can be moved quickly and covertly from permanent locations to points from which their use could have the greatest effect, including an attack on strategically important targets in the European part of Russia.
To summarise, I would like to note that all of this confirms that the European component of US nuclear forces, as well as the nuclear weapons of its allies, is designated for carrying out strategic objectives specifically, which poses critical risks for our country. This compels us to a corresponding military‑technical response. On the diplomatic front, our current efforts are focused on sparking an international discussion on the extremely destabilising nature of NATO’s joint nuclear mission practice, and on encouraging the United States to take steps toward removing its nuclear weapons from Europe.
RT: Andrey Ivanovich, what arguments, in your view, could persuade the American side and European countries alike to agree to remove this weapon?
Andrey Belousov: Here we can offer an entire battery of arguments – political, diplomatic, military, economic, international‑law and even historical in nature – grounded in the present state of inter‑state relations and the overall military‑political environment in the world.
The core of our arguments is, in principle, well known, because it is based on our doctrinal documents, our foreign‑policy concept, the fundamentals of national‑security strategy and military doctrine. Most of them relate to the fact that the international community is essentially faced with a choice: will inter‑state relations continue to develop in a confrontational paradigm that threatens a direct armed conflict between nuclear powers and the use of nuclear weapons, or will prudence prevail among our opponents, allowing the leading powers to reach an agreement on concrete joint measures to prevent escalation and avert a catastrophic scenario for the entire world?
Obviously, unlike our opponents and most Western countries, Russia does not stand at a crossroads. We have repeatedly expressed, at various levels and on different international platforms – including the UN – our readiness to cooperate with all interested states to maintain peace, strengthen regional security, and ensure strategic stability. Moreover, our statements are regularly reinforced by concrete initiatives. Recall that one of the founding principles of Russia’s foreign‑policy course in international and regional security remains the principle of equal and indivisible security. A key part of that principle is the non‑acceptance of a situation in which one state or a group of states creates comfortable conditions for itself – or a privileged status – at the expense of lowering the security level or damaging the security of other states.
From that widely recognised principle, which is set out in a host of international multilateral documents, Russia has recently put forward a whole set of key initiatives. These include proposals for the United States and its NATO allies to introduce a mutual moratorium on the deployment of intermediate and shorter range missiles. Another initiative, launched in late 2021 and early 2022, was the establishment of a security guarantee on the western front in the form of an agreement with the United States and NATO allies. Yet another initiative was a proposal, unfortunately still unrealised, to convene a summit of heads of state, the United Nations Security Council’s permanent members, to discuss urgent problems in international security. Among the latest proposals is the one put forward by Russian President Vladimir Putin on September twenty second of last year to preserve the legacy of the START Treaty through voluntary limits.
It is obvious that if these initiatives were implemented they would act as deterrents, contributing to the prevention of a new arms race and creating favourable conditions for the renewal of strategic dialogue between Russia and the United States, with the prospect of involving other nuclear powers. Unfortunately, most of our ideas were either rejected, received no adequate response, or were simply ignored. The only exception, perhaps, was the initiative to have leaders of the nuclear powers sign a joint declaration on preventing nuclear war and halting the nuclear arms race, which was carried out on January third 2022. Yet even this document is not clearly worded. In terms of practical implementation and compliance with its provisions by Western states, the matter largely remains at the level of empty declarations, which raises serious concerns and deep disappointment.
In short, our opponents – primarily in Europe – must decide where we are headed next. In that context, it is far more important to bring forward arguments that are conditioned by the course of the historical process associated with establishing a new multipolar world order in which the imperative is the abandonment of global dominance by any one state or bloc of states. The new system of geopolitical coordinates, in whose formation Russia actively participates, does not allow perpetual escalation, the accumulation of unresolved contradictions critical to international security, or the further erosion of trust between the emerging centres of power, whose dangerous balance risks armed conflict. Furthermore, this system of coordinates does not allow continuous fuelling of a conflict‑generating potential in international relations and an uncontrolled arms race. It is also unacceptable, in a new world order, to create security systems aimed at a single state or predicated on bloc‑based confrontation. Rather, the new order dictates the necessity for mutually beneficial cooperation and constructive collaboration between states.
The quest, above all, is for political‑diplomatic solutions to the most urgent regional and global problems, strict adherence to the fundamental principles of the UN, the goals and tasks of the global community, respect for international law, and the recognition by every member of the international community of its responsibility for the fate of the world and international security.
RT: how could these negotiations – and the withdrawal of the weapons themselves – be organized if, in an optimistic scenario, the US side agreed with this position?
Andrey Belousov: That’s a very interesting question. At this point the organizational aspects of such negotiations, or even the procedure for removing US weapons from Europe, are secondary. The key issue now is Washington’s unwillingness to find a principled agreement to discuss this problem with a view of reaching any real agreement on the matter. What is needed is an openness to start and conduct negotiations without tying them to the question of Russia’s non‑strategic nuclear weapons, which, unlike US weapons of this class that can be used operationally against our country, do not pose a direct strategic threat to US territory.
It is obvious that Washington’s attempts to initiate a dialogue on our non‑strategic nuclear arsenal serve a single purpose – shifting the international community’s focus away from the danger posed by US nuclear weapons in Europe, and more broadly, from the missile‑nuclear programs and plans that Washington is implementing. Speaking of that danger, it cannot be overlooked that Washington’s persistence in trying to launch discussions about Russia’s non‑strategic nuclear weapons – those that do not threaten US territory – at various multilateral disarmament forums repeatedly suggests that US military strategists are seriously considering the possibility of using nuclear weapons on the European theater of operations. In fact, Europe is being viewed as a probable military theater.
Obtaining, through negotiations or discussions on strategic stability, objective data on Russia’s non‑strategic nuclear weapons via the implementation of some intrusive transparency practices – or reducing or even completely eliminating them – would increase the likelihood of a scenario in which the US and its European allies use nuclear weapons. I hope Europe will recognize the danger of such a strictly operational‑planning approach that Washington adopts toward the territory of its allies.
In a principled sense, regarding the conditions for launching any substantive US dialogue, there are three points that must be understood. First, what must precede such negotiations? Our country’s leadership – and the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs – has repeatedly stated their position on this issue. Our delegations have mentioned it both in the First Committee of the UN General Assembly and at the recently held 11th Conference on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. To create a favorable climate for starting US negotiations, it is essential that they first, not in words but in action – declaratively and through concrete steps – demonstrate that they are ready to irreversibly abandon an anti‑Russian course and to resolve the most critical issues in international security together with us, starting with the elimination of fundamental contradictions and the root causes of the current crisis in interstate relations, and ending with questions of arms control, disarmament, and non‑proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.
Second, it is important to understand what the nature of the negotiations should be. We have always and continue to insist on a mutually respectful dialogue built on trust and the consideration of all participants’ interests. It is unacceptable for Russia to be subjected to fabricated claims and unsubstantiated demands, or for the discussion to be conducted in the style of an ultimatum. The conversation must be substantive and equal, with both sides fully aware of the danger of rising tension, loss of trust, the degradation of bilateral relations, and of their individual and collective responsibility for humanity’s future.
Third, the content of the negotiations and their ultimate goal. Russia rejects mere performative speeches that, under the pretext of making the world safer, drag us into another propaganda campaign aimed at enhancing the US image or maintaining its reputation at our expense or that of our close partners and allies.
In the strategic sphere, for us a constructive dialogue aimed at achieving long‑term and indisputable agreements on the entire complex of factors affecting strategic stability is crucial. Removing some specific, extremely technical issues from the interdependent framework of the sector will not help move forward or achieve the required agreements and understandings.
Another important point I would like to emphasize concerns the nature and content of the dialogue: we will never, under any circumstances, start a serious conversation on US terms only to make an effort to address American security issues. The starting point of any strategic‑stability negotiations must be a clear recognition of the inviolability of the principle of equal and indivisible security, and no exceptions can be made from strict adherence to this principle.
RT: Nevertheless, American media outlets are reporting a potential expansion of the number of participants in the program. What risks and threats could such plans create, given that among European countries Poland – and the Baltic states as well – have expressed interest in hosting U.S. weapons?
Andrey Belousov: It is a very important issue from the standpoint of our country’s security, and essentially it concerns maintaining strategic balance and strategic stability. In answering the first question, I already partially addressed your question, which touches on this issue.
The involvement of an ever‑growing number of NATO member states in schemes that envisage the practical use of nuclear weapons against Russia primarily is fully in line with NATO’s nuclear status and the logic of the trans‑Atlantic linkage, whose key element today is precisely nuclear dimension. Securing a nuclear status for NATO is not merely a declaration or a sign lacking substance or implying any action. On the contrary, one must clearly understand that such a status is concrete. It means that nuclear weapons, their possible use, and the concept of nuclear deterrence – as understood by the military‑political establishment of NATO and the European Union states – have become a fundamental means by which westerners ensure their security.
It is important to note that the security views of Europe’s current elites differ sharply from the narratives and concepts we tried to align with the West and jointly implement at the end of the last century and at the beginning of this one. The main distinction lies in our opponents refusal to create a security architecture in Europe together with Russia in favor of attempts to build a regional security system aimed at our country. The results of this radical shift – so to speak – are now evident.
Currently, the minds of our Western opponents, under significant influence, are shaped by a new view of how regional and international security should be ensured, induced by pressure from the United States. The concept of “peace through force,” which seems long out of date and paradoxical at its core but is actively promoted by Washington, has been adopted.
Returning to the question of involving ever more states in joint nuclear missions and expanded, now even advanced, deterrence schemes, we again note that this process fully fits within the logic of the aforementioned approach. More importantly, the “peace through force” concept is in sharp contradiction with the rapidly accelerating and now irreversible process of the emergence of a multipolar world order. Western states collectively, fearing the loss of their leadership and dominant position in the world, strive to preserve it by any means. When political and economic measures fail, they repeatedly resort to the tried‑and‑true method of creating a real military threat to their global competitors, backed by continuous modernization and unrestricted buildup of military potential, developing new means and methods of warfare.
Thus they bet on overwhelming military superiority, which requires mastering and implementing the most advanced scientific‑technical achievements. This is precisely what the United States and its closest allies are doing now. After all, the practice of joint nuclear missions, and indeed the rehearsal of any other combat systems, is no longer carried out with outdated technology or the old algorithms and tactics developed in the 1950s and 60s. It is executed at a completely new technological level that would guarantee indisputable advantages both on the local theater of operations and in large‑scale conflicts.
The drive to obtain overwhelming military advantage largely through the modernization and scaling of nuclear potential – in which NATO states are involved – leads to a breach of strategic balance and creates risks and threats to our country’s defense and security. Accelerated Western implementation of such nuclear plans, with active assistance from allies, will bring about the most severe consequences in the military‑political and strategic spheres. One such consequence could be a new arms race, not limited to nuclear weapons.
RT: What could Russia’s potential response to such actions look like?
Andrey Belousov: Regarding countermeasures, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s statement on the expiry of the New START Treaty on February fourth unambiguously notes that the parties to the treaty are free to decide on subsequent steps. Yet, our country intends to act responsibly and prudently, charting its line on strategic offensive arms based on a thorough analysis of the overall situation – the analysis of US military policy and the overall strategic environment – which, among other things, includes the actions of American allies.
We are talking about a combination of political‑diplomatic and military‑technical compensatory measures aimed at maintaining strategic balance and mitigating potential additional threats to Russia’s military security.

'I am sure of myself': A look back at Dolly Parton's unspoken feminist legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-29
15:57:29 UTC
00:57:29 KST

'I am sure of myself': A look back at Dolly Parton's unspoken feminist legacy
Beloved country star Dolly Parton was many things to her fans, including an actor, singer, philanthropist and entrepreneur. But after her death on Tuesday at the age of 80, some admirers are remembering her as something she never overtly claimed: feminist icon.
Twelve "Women of the Year" are pictured smiling on the January 1987 cover of "Ms." magazine, co-founded by feminist pioneer Gloria Steinem. They include a US senator, a renowned novelist, a former nun who helped Central American refugees and, smiling brightest of all, Dolly Parton.
The beloved country superstar, who died this week at 80, never embraced the feminist label. She eschewed it when asked, just as she carefully avoided political labels.
But when Parton was building her groundbreaking career in music, more telling were Parton’s life choices, social alliances and especially her lyrics – words that made clear how fiercely independent the woman beneath the wig and rhinestones truly was, and what she believed in.
“People who haven’t listened to Dolly Parton or to feminism may be surprised to learn that they go together,” Steinem wrote in that 1987 magazine issue. “She has used her business sense to bring other women and poor people along with her. And her flamboyant style has turned all the devalued symbols of women to her own ends.”
“If feminism means each of us finding our unique power, and helping other women to do the same,” Steinem wrote, “Dolly Parton certainly has done both.”
Parton may not have claimed to be a feminist, but her female fans claim her as an icon with pride and affection.
“She didn’t tell us she was a feminist,” says Lynn Melnick, author of “I’ve Had to Think Up a Way to Survive: On Trauma, Persistence, and Dolly Parton”.
“She showed us – in her actions and her words and in her songs. And I think that’s why people loved her so much.”
At the Newport Folk Festival in 2019, a cheeky Parton, then in her early 70s, drew delighted cheers when she sang lyrics skewering double standards: “My mistakes are no worse than yours just because I’m a woman.”
Parton had just explained to the crowd that the song was a reference to a frank conversation she’d had with her husband soon after marriage, when he asked if she’d been with other men.
“When you boys get married you want us to be just as pure as snow – well, sometimes we’re not!” she told the crowd. “This is for you, gals, and your boys just gotta take it, OK?”
The remarks were vintage Parton, making a point without alienating anyone. She was, after all, about relatability.
“One thing about Dolly is that no matter what side of the political spectrum you’re on, you think she’s with you,” Melnick says.
“Everyone claims her. And so as a feminist I always thought, well, obviously she’s a feminist, and the more I read about her and wrote about her, it was just undeniable – first of all because of how she lived her life completely on her own terms.”
She and Carl Dean met in 1964 and were married for nearly 60 years. But they both gave each other a lot of space and freedom to live their own lives. After she convinced Dean to attend an awards show early on in her career, they both quickly realized it was just not his thing.
"He said, 'Look, now I want you to do everything you want to do and I wish you the best, but don't ever ask me to go to another one of these damn things 'cause I ain't going,'" Parton recalled.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Read moreEmbraced across divides, Dolly Parton leaves a lasting legacy
To music writer Evelyn McDonnell, Parton’s looks – the eyelashes, the big hair, the curves – served as an invisible cloak, helping her freely express progressive feminist views while leaning into the ultra-feminine.
“She took the objectification of being a pop star and embraced it,” says McDonnell, editor of the music anthology “Women Who Rock” and a professor at Loyola Marymount University. “It was like her magic cloak – she could be saying feminist things and doing feminist things and modelling a life and a voice that was outspoken, progressive, political. But you saw the package and you’re like, ‘Oh, okay.’ It made it safe.”
“She knew she was blonde and pretty, and that it was always going to work against her,” says music writer Caryn Rose. “So she figured out how to make it work FOR her. There's not anything more feminist than that.”
McDonnell says Parton’s values are clear from songs like “9 to 5”, which she wrote for the movie in which she starred with Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda about a tyrannical boss who made a sport out of sexual harassment.
“It’s all about feminism, right? About women in the workplace, economic empowerment, pushing back against the male supervisor, uniting women’s voices,” she says.
Equal pay was just one of the issues Parton wrote about. She also, Melnick notes, addressed reproductive justice, teen pregnancy and "all of these very feminist issues ... she was just doing the work quietly, in her songs”.
One such song was “The Bargain Store", from 1975. “I may have just what you’re looking for, if you don’t mind the fact that all the merchandise is used," Parton wrote. “But with a little mending, it could be as good as new.”
Parton said later that country radio shunned the song because they took it to be about prostitution, when it was really about healing after a relationship.
Then there was “Down from Dover,” about a teenage single mother. “I wrote that back during a time when people didn’t talk about unwed mothers,” Parton told Vulture in 2023. “They wouldn’t play that on the radio.”
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Melnick posits that Parton exemplified so-called third-wave feminism, which gained currency in the ’90s with a focus on individual choice. A feminism where one could wear big heels, big hair and sparkly rhinestones.
And that’s exactly how Parton framed her looks in a 1977 interview with Barbara Walters: “It's certainly a choice.”
Parton said later that people had warned her against talking to Walters, who they said would chew her up and spit her out.
But a 31-year-old Parton, with quiet confidence and a generous smile, emerged looking far better than her interlocutor, who relied largely on sexist assumptions.
Walters asked if she was faithful to her husband, and why she was even married if she was constantly travelling. She even asked Parton if her famous breasts were real – saying an assistant wanted to know.
Walters then asked Parton to stand up and display her body. She did so, politely.
"But do you ever feel that you're a joke?" Walters asked.
Parton easily explained why she was comfortable with the jokes about her – because she was, in fact, in on them.
"Oh, I know they make fun of me, but actually, all these years, the people have thought that the joke was on me, but it's actually been on the public," she said.
“I know exactly what I am doing and I can change it at any time,” Parton added.
“I make more jokes about myself than anybody ... I am sure of myself as a person and I am sure of my talent. I am very content. So I can afford to diddle around with makeup and clothes and stuff because I am secure with myself.”
And what could be more feminist than that?
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Israeli settlers stage new attack on home in West Bank's Qusra, witnesses say
QUSRA, West Bank, Aug 29 - Dozens of masked Israeli settler militants attacked homes surrounding the occupied West Bank village of Qusra on Saturday, the first major attack since a siege by settlers in the area earlier this month drew an international outcry.
The settlers surrounded a Palestinian home, throwing stones while seven Palestinians were trapped inside, according to witnesses who spoke to Reuters.
Saddam Oday, one of those trapped, said the Israeli military fired tear gas into the home and detained the residents inside while letting him go. He said the Israeli military had not detained any of the settlers and had allowed them to leave.
The owner of the house, Luay Bayruti, said when the military arrived they handcuffed, blindfolded and beat those inside, before later releasing them.
The Israeli military said in a statement that troops and border police forces had arrived on the scene to remove "rioters" and protect the residents inside the house.
The military did not immediately respond to a request for comment on why they had reportedly fired tear gas at the house and detained and beaten the residents.
In his first public statement on Qusra, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he condemned the violence in Qusra and blamed a "handful of rioters".
"I strongly condemn the criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Qusra and Jalud," said Netanyahu, referring to a separate incident in a neighbouring village.
The United States had previously pressured Netanyahu to publicly condemn the militant settlers who had besieged Palestinians in their homes, U.S. and Israeli officials told Reuters around two weeks ago.
The Israeli government has previously blamed a "fringe minority" for settler violence, a characterisation disputed by findings from rights groups.
A U.N. inquiry in June found that Israeli authorities are directly involved in settler attacks that have killed, injured and displaced Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. The Israeli mission in Geneva rejected the report's findings.
RESIDENT REPORTS NEAR-DAILY ENCROACHMENTS
Bayruti said that after calling the Israeli military for help, he and six others were trapped inside the home for more than an hour as settlers threw stones.
Bayruti showed a Reuters reporter his bandaged arm, which he said had been injured by a stone during the attack.
Oday, a medic, said four of those trapped had suffered injuries due to the tear gas, and two had suffered injuries from the stones thrown by settlers.
The attack occurred a few hundred yards away from three homes to which settlers laid siege this month, drawing international condemnation and a massive Israeli military deployment that residents say has kept them effectively trapped in their homes.
"They spotted the residents working on their house, which is still under construction and they started throwing rocks," said Loui Ridi, a Palestinian-American whose home was one of the three under siege this month. He said he watched Saturday's attack occur from his home.
Ridi said he had seen near-daily encroachments of Israeli settlers into the area surrounding his home, despite the heavy Israeli military presence in the area.
SETTLER VIOLENCE ON THE RISE
Rights groups say the increasing settler presence on the edge of Palestinian villages, like Qusra, is part of a wider effort by settlers to seize more land from Palestinians, further eating into territory where Palestinians aim to establish a state.
Violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank has increased, with some emboldened by the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has overseen a massive settlement expansion in the territory.
U.N. bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the area as disputed rather than occupied. REUTERS

At least 37 killed after Russian strike hits an ammunition depot near Kyiv, triggering massive explosions. Many of the victims were residents of a nearby care home.
The Russian army struck the village of Myla on the outskirts of Kyiv on the evening of August 28, setting fire to a warehouse where ammunition was being stored. The fire triggered a series of detonations, sending flames into nearby private homes. The explosions were powerful enough that authorities shut down traffic entirely on the Zhytomyr highway between the 15th and 32nd kilometer markers. Nearly 400 people were evacuated from the area affected by the strike.
Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said Saturday morning that at least 27 people had been killed in the Russian strike on Myla, in Kyiv region’s Bucha district. Another 42 people, including four children, were injured to varying degrees. Among the dead was Taras Didych, head of the Dmytrivka community in the Kyiv region, who had been helping rescue people from the fire.
Update. As of 2:00 p.m. Saturday, 37 people are known to have died in the Russian strike, Tymur Tkachenko wrote.
About 50 residential buildings were damaged. The heaviest damage was to a nearby care home for elderly and disabled residents, where 20 people died, according to local social media pages.
Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the care home had been damaged. “Those who allowed this must certainly bear responsibility for their decisions. Investigators from the National Police and the Security Service of Ukraine are conducting a pretrial investigation, and a criminal case has been opened over official negligence. There are rules: ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential buildings. There will definitely be appropriate conclusions,” the president of Ukraine said.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi called what happened in the Bucha district the result of “criminal negligence,” recalling the “terrible tragedy in Vyshneve,” which he said “did not serve as a lesson.” Russian forces struck a Ukroboronprom warehouse in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, in July. The resulting detonation damaged 300 residential buildings and killed nine people.
The Kyiv region declared August 30 a day of mourning for those killed in the Russian strike.
Russia’s Defense Ministry stated that its drones struck an ammunition warehouse belonging to the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point in the village of Myla, where components for FP-1/FP-2 UAVs were stored. 10,000 young leaders from 191 countries invited to youth festival in Russia
Organizers of the International Youth Festival have completed the selection process for participants in this year’s event, which will take place in Yekaterinburg, Russia, from September 11 to 17, 2026.
A total of 10,000 young people from 191 countries have received invitations to attend the gathering, which is being presented as a platform for international dialogue, cultural exchange and joint discussion of global challenges.
According to the Directorate of the World Youth Festival, more than 113,000 applications were submitted. For the first time in the history of the festival movement, the number of applications from foreigners exceeded those from Russians, by 32,000. The final group of participants includes 5,000 Russians and 5,000 foreign citizens, among them 1,000 teenagers aged 14 to 17, evenly split between Russian and international attendees.
“Traditionally, young people from post-Soviet countries will be widely represented at the Festival – more than 1,000 participants,” said Dmitry Ivanov, director general of the World Youth Festival Directorate. “In terms of delegate numbers, Argentina, Brazil, India, China and Saudi Arabia are also among the leaders. Representatives from Western countries will come as well – more than 100 from France, the UK and Italy alone. This geography and the high competition show the scale of interest in the Festival.”
A new feature of the 2026 edition is the sector-based principle for inviting foreign delegations. Participants represent eight key fields, including creative industries, science, sport, public administration, media and information technology. Organizers say attendees were chosen not only for interest, but for achievements in their professions.
Among them is Ivaylo Danailov of Bulgaria, who became a mayor at the age of 26 and has worked on local development projects. “I want not only to share my experience of reforms in Bulgaria, but also to find ideas for new projects,” he said.
Another participant, Christian Bahati of the Republic of the Congo, runs a major mining company and founded a charitable organization in 2019 to support poor communities in neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo. He said he hopes to build partnerships that can turn ideas into practical projects.
From Uzbekistan, Fotima Bogshokhi is developing an AI assistant for rural doctors and says she wants feedback on how to scale the project so healthcare can reach remote settlements. Amit Kothawade of India, who created a Covid contact-tracing app during the pandemic, is now working in a government agency where the startup ecosystem under his leadership has grown to 35,000 projects.
The event will also include bloggers and social media creators. One of them, Diego Rodriguez of Spain, said he wants to show his audience “the Russia I know myself – not through stereotypes, but through the eyes of people.”
Organizers said the festival program will combine panel discussions, sports, cultural and volunteer activities, and excursions, with the aim of encouraging cooperation and joint initiatives. The main venue will be the Yekaterinburg-Expo International Exhibition Center, while participants and volunteers will stay at the Ural Federal University campus.
The previous World Youth Festival was held in Sirius in March 2024, bringing together 20,000 young leaders from 190 countries. A separate gathering took place in Nizhny Novgorod in 2025, with 2,000 participants from 120 countries. Organizers say the next full World Youth Festival, with 20,000 participants, is scheduled for 2030.

RSS supremo Mohan Bhagwat speaks in New York amid criticism
Mohan Bhagwat, the chief of Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) — a right-wing Hindu nationalist group in India — gave an address at New York City's Madison Square Garden on Saturday as part of an event which was earlier denounced by the US city's mayor Zohran Mamdani and triggered a call for sanctions against RSS members by a US panel on religious freedom.
Bhagwat talked about pluralism and diversity in his address at the "Universal Oneness Celebration" organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue.
"When discussing the United States of America, one word that frequently comes up in conversation is 'pluralism.' On the other hand, when referring to Bharat (India), the phrase most often discussed is 'unity in diversity,'" he said, adding that unity and diversity was "embedded in the DNA of the people of India."
The controversial RSS has been organizing foreign visits in an attempt to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary outfit involved in attacks on minorities.
At a conference of interfaith leaders earlier on Saturday, Bhagwat alluded to a question some Muslim individuals posed to him asking whether RSS would drive Muslims out of India considering the group's vision of a "Hindu Rashtra (nation)."
"I told them, 'No, that is not Hindutva. If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslim in Bharat (India), he ceases to be a Hindu," Bhagwat said.
Critics have accused the group of promoting the political ideology of Hindutva, which means "the essence of being Hindu," and seeks to define Indian national identity and culture in terms of Hindu values.
Do your duty to US, Bhagwat tells Indian Americans
At Madison Square Garden, Bhagwat told Indian expats to be loyal to the US, which he described as their "karma bhumi" (place of duty).
"What is our duty? You are in America. You live in America. You earn in America. So you are America, and you should behave true to America," the RSS chief said, adding that "the diaspora has a duty to their karma bhumi. They must fulfil that."
He told the expats that if they had the "urge" to do something for their "janma bhumi" (place of birth), which was India, they could do it after fulfilling their duty to the US.
"It is not prohibited," Bhagwat said.
